title: Externalize oversized payloads during LCM ingest
body:
## Context

LCM currently protects some large payloads during pre-compaction serialization, but that is late in the pipeline. By that point the original payload may already have been written to SQLite and indexed by FTS.

That means a single large tool result, inline media block, or oversized raw payload can still bloat `lcm.db`, slow search, and make later compaction or expansion more expensive than it needs to be.

The storage contract should stay complete, but oversized payloads should be replaced with durable local references before they hit the raw message store when that can be done safely.

## Goal

Move payload externalization into the ingest path, before `MessageStore.append_batch()`, while keeping every externalized payload recoverable through LCM inspection and expansion tools.

## TODO

- [ ] Add a shared ingest-time payload protection step before rows are appended to the message store.
- [ ] Externalize oversized tool result content before SQLite/FTS storage.
- [ ] Externalize inline/base64 media payloads when the structured message contains enough metadata to preserve them safely.
- [ ] Externalize native/structured image blocks while preserving useful metadata such as mime type, filename hints, role, timestamp, session id, and source.
- [ ] Add a generic oversized raw payload fallback for content that is too large but does not match a more specific handler.
- [ ] Store compact placeholders or references in the raw row, with enough metadata for later inspection.
- [ ] Make `lcm_expand`, `lcm_describe`, or the relevant inspection path able to surface externalized payload metadata and recover content when the local payload file is available.
- [ ] Keep replay-critical provider structures intact. Do not externalize or flatten assistant `tool_calls`, matching tool results, or message sequencing fields in a way that breaks active replay.
- [ ] Decide how bootstrap/import/backfill should use the same protection path. Prefer a shared transform. If an importer intentionally preserves source rows as-is, document and test that exception.

## Regression coverage

- [ ] Large tool result is externalized before SQLite/FTS storage.
- [ ] Externalized tool result remains recoverable through expansion or inspection.
- [ ] User image/media block is stored as a compact durable reference instead of a huge raw row.
- [ ] Generic oversized raw content uses the fallback externalizer.
- [ ] Replay-critical tool-call adjacency remains valid after externalization.
- [ ] Bootstrap/import path does not accidentally bypass the agreed ingest protection contract.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No silent data loss.
- [ ] Externalized content is durable and recoverable when local payload files are present.
- [ ] SQLite/FTS no longer receives obvious oversized payloads for supported externalized classes.
- [ ] Active replay still validates for assistant tool calls and matching tool results.
- [ ] Focused tests cover tool output, media/image payloads, generic raw payloads, and import/bootstrap behavior.

title: Clean unsafe assistant content during active context assembly
body:
## Context

LCM keeps raw history complete, but the messages returned in active assembled context still need to satisfy provider constraints. Stored history can contain assistant turns that are valid as archive data but unsafe as active prompt input, especially blank structured assistant content or thinking-only assistant blocks.

Some cleanup already exists around summarizer input and summarized output. The remaining gap is active context assembly itself.

## Goal

Add an active-context-only cleanup layer before assembled messages are returned to Hermes. This should make provider input safer without mutating stored rows or the summary DAG.

## TODO

- [ ] Add a cleanup step in the active assembly path, after context has been selected and before it is returned to Hermes.
- [ ] Drop assistant messages whose structured content is only blank text, for example `[{"type": "text", "text": ""}]`.
- [ ] Drop assistant messages that contain only thinking/reasoning/internal blocks and no visible assistant content.
- [ ] Preserve normal assistant messages with visible content.
- [ ] Preserve assistant tool-call messages when they are part of a valid adjacent tool-call/tool-result sequence.
- [ ] Preserve matching tool results that are required for valid provider replay.
- [ ] If cleanup would leave an invalid provider sequence, repair through the existing active-context sanitizer or fall back to a safe current/live context path.
- [ ] Keep persisted raw rows unchanged. This is an assembly safety layer, not storage cleanup.

## Regression coverage

- [ ] Blank structured assistant text is removed from active context.
- [ ] Thinking-only assistant content is removed from active context.
- [ ] Normal assistant text survives cleanup.
- [ ] Assistant tool calls with matching tool results survive in valid order.
- [ ] Missing, late, duplicate, or out-of-order tool results are still handled by the active-context sanitizer.
- [ ] Cleanup does not mutate stored rows, source mappings, or DAG nodes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Active assembled context does not include blank assistant text blocks.
- [ ] Active assembled context does not include thinking-only assistant turns.
- [ ] Provider tool-call adjacency remains valid after cleanup.
- [ ] Stored history is preserved.
- [ ] Focused assembly tests cover structured content, plain text content, thinking-only content, and tool-call sequences.

title: Fail closed on stale short snapshots without durable-tail overlap
body:
## Context

Restart cursor reconciliation has been tightened, but there is still an important edge case worth pinning down explicitly: an existing session already has durable history, then the runtime provides a short stale snapshot that has no overlap with the stored tail.

If that stale snapshot is treated as a fresh delta, LCM can append duplicate rows. Those duplicates then pollute search, compaction, active context assembly, and source accounting.

The tricky part is that we should fail closed only when the batch is actually suspicious. We still need to preserve ambiguous legitimate deltas where skipping could lose user data.

## Goal

Add a guard and regression coverage for short or stale runtime snapshots that have no overlap with durable session history. In the suspicious no-overlap case, do not append the batch as fresh rows.

## TODO

- [ ] Add a focused test with an existing session that has a longer durable tail and receives a short incoming batch with no overlap.
- [ ] In that no-overlap stale-snapshot case, skip or quarantine the batch instead of appending everything.
- [ ] Preserve conservative behavior for genuinely ambiguous singleton repeated deltas where the safest non-destructive choice is still to persist.
- [ ] Preserve legitimate new deltas that have verified overlap, scaffold evidence, or clear full-context replay evidence.
- [ ] Keep filtered/scaffolded histories from accidentally creating false replay evidence.
- [ ] Add clear diagnostics that distinguish `skipped stale no-overlap snapshot` from `persisted ambiguous delta`.

## Regression coverage

- [ ] Existing durable tail plus short no-overlap snapshot does not append duplicate rows.
- [ ] Legitimate one-message delta is still persisted when it cannot be proven stale.
- [ ] Full-context replay with strong evidence still advances the cursor safely.
- [ ] Filtered history does not create false positive replay evidence.
- [ ] Scaffold-only prefixes do not authorize skipping unrelated new rows.
- [ ] Diagnostics make the decision path visible enough for future debugging.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Stale short snapshots without overlap cannot silently duplicate stored rows.
- [ ] The guard does not introduce data loss for ambiguous real deltas.
- [ ] Existing restart-reconciliation tests still pass.
- [ ] New tests document the exact no-overlap contract.

title: Decide cache-aware deferred compaction policy
body:
@stephenschoettler I want to make an explicit call on this before we add more moving parts to the compaction path.

## Context

LCM has deferred maintenance and some cache/usage visibility, but it does not currently have a full cache-aware compaction policy. That means prompt-mutating compaction decisions are mostly driven by LCM pressure and assembly guardrails, not by whether the host/model/provider is likely to have a hot prompt cache that would be invalidated by rewriting context.

That may be fine. Hermes may be better off with a simpler policy. But if we want cache-aware deferred compaction, we should design it deliberately instead of adding scattered checks when individual edge cases show up.

## Decision needed

Should `hermes-lcm` implement cache-aware deferred compaction, or should we intentionally keep the current simpler model and document that choice?

## Option A: keep the current simpler policy

This keeps compaction easier to reason about. LCM uses context pressure, fresh tail, assembly caps, deferred maintenance settings, and overflow recovery. It does not try to protect provider prompt-cache TTL windows directly.

Pros:

- Less config surface.
- Fewer provider-specific assumptions in the plugin.
- Easier to test and explain.
- Avoids coupling LCM behavior to cache semantics that Hermes core or the model provider may already handle differently.

Cons:

- Prompt-mutating compaction may happen while a provider cache is still hot.
- High-velocity sessions may churn cached prompt state more than needed.
- Deferred maintenance has no explicit cache-pressure escape hatch because it also has no cache hold in the first place.

If we choose this, the work is mostly documentation plus maybe clearer status output that says cache-aware compaction is not implemented by design.

## Option B: add cache-aware deferred compaction

This adds a first-class policy for delaying prompt-mutating deferred compaction while a prompt cache is likely hot, with a critical-pressure escape so compaction cannot be deferred forever.

Possible shape:

- Track last cache touch or cache break signal when Hermes exposes it.
- Classify mutation-sensitive model/provider families only when we have reliable runtime information.
- Add config such as:
  - `cache_aware_compaction_enabled`
  - `cache_aware_compaction_ttl_seconds`
  - `critical_budget_pressure_ratio`
- Delay deferred prompt-mutating compaction while under the TTL and below critical pressure.
- Ignore the delay when current context pressure crosses the critical ratio.
- If provider/model telemetry is missing, decide whether to drain normally or conservatively delay. My instinct is drain normally and let explicit config opt into stricter behavior.

Pros:

- Better behavior for long high-velocity sessions on cache-sensitive providers.
- Avoids unnecessary prompt rewrites while still compacting before overflow.
- Gives operators explicit control over the tradeoff.

Cons:

- More config and more state.
- Harder tests because cache timing and pressure interact.
- Provider-family detection can become brittle if it lives in the plugin instead of Hermes core.
- Bad defaults could create either churn or compaction starvation.

## Option C: hybrid, add only the pressure escape first

This keeps cache-awareness out of scope for now, but improves deferred maintenance by making pressure handling more explicit.

Possible shape:

- Add a `critical_budget_pressure_ratio` style setting used by deferred maintenance and overflow-adjacent paths.
- Do not add TTL/cache-touch tracking yet.
- Use it only to decide when deferred maintenance should stop being polite and do bounded catch-up work.

Pros:

- Smaller and easier to test.
- Improves starvation behavior without pretending we know provider cache state.
- Leaves room for full cache-aware compaction later.

Cons:

- Does not protect hot prompt caches.
- Might be only half the policy if we later decide true cache-awareness matters.

## My current read

I would not jump straight to full cache-aware compaction unless we have a clear Hermes signal for cache touch/break or a concrete repro showing prompt-cache churn/starvation in live Hermes.

The safest path seems to be:

1. Decide whether cache-aware compaction belongs in `hermes-lcm` or Hermes core.
2. If it belongs here, start with explicit config and tests around the pressure escape.
3. Add TTL/cache-touch logic only when the host can provide reliable signals.

## TODO

- [x] Decide between Option A, B, or C.
- [ ] Decide whether provider/model cache sensitivity should be detected in `hermes-lcm` or supplied by Hermes core.
- [ ] If implementing, define config names and defaults.
- [ ] Add tests for disabled behavior, missing telemetry behavior, critical-pressure bypass, and normal deferred drain behavior.
- [ ] Document the final policy clearly in README/config docs.

title: fix: preserve recency in LIKE fallback grep
body:
## Summary

This follows up on the Codex note from #135 and the follow-up review on this PR about LIKE fallback grep sorting.

When a query falls back to LIKE, for example `docker-compose`, recency sorting happened after a bounded SQL `LIMIT`. If `role` or other filters still left more than one page of matching rows, the newest or best matching message could be outside the first SQL window and never reach the Python recency sort.

The recency LIKE path now orders candidates by the same primary keys the Python fallback sort uses: timestamp, role bias, fallback score, and directness. If the candidate cap lands inside a timestamp and role tie, it keeps reading that primary tie group before applying the final Python sort. That keeps the cap bounded for older/lower-priority rows while avoiding truncation inside the group that can still win.

Relevance and hybrid keep their previous one-window behavior.

## Validation

title: fix: add period to _FTS5_SPECIAL_CHARS to prevent FTS5 syntax errors on version-style queries
body:
## Problem

`_FTS5_SPECIAL_CHARS` in `search_query.py` was missing the period character `.`. This caused FTS5 `syntax error near "."` crashes when users searched for version strings like `v2.21`, `api.v2`, model names like `minimax-m2.5-free`, etc.

## Root Cause

- `_FTS5_SPECIAL_CHARS = frozenset("\"()*^-:{}")` — no `.`
- Period IS in `_STRIP_EDGE_PUNCT` (for token edge stripping), but was NOT in the FTS5 sanitizer
- `sanitize_fts5_query("v2.21")` returned `"v2.21"` unchanged → FTS5 crash
- `contains_risky_fts_ascii()` only catches `-`, `/`, `:` (not `.`), so LIKE fallback did not trigger

## Fix

Added `.` to `_FTS5_SPECIAL_CHARS`:

```python
_FTS5_SPECIAL_CHARS = frozenset("\"()*^-:{.}")
```

**Before:** `sanitize_fts5_query("v2.21")` → `"v2.21"` → FTS5 crash

**After:** `sanitize_fts5_query("v2.21")` → `"v2 21"` → valid FTS5 (period replaced with space)

## Test

```python
sanitize_fts5_query("v2.21")           → "v2 21"
sanitize_fts5_query("api.v2")          → "api v2"
sanitize_fts5_query("hermes.lcm")        → "hermes lcm"
sanitize_fts5_query("minimax-m2.5-free") → "minimax m2 5 free" (falls back to LIKE due to -)
```

## Verification

The fix was verified on the running `lcm.db` database — FTS5 `MATCH` queries on period-containing strings now work correctly without crashing.

title: fix: skip stale short restart snapshots
body:
## Summary

Adds a restart reconciliation guard for stale short snapshots that have no overlap with the durable tail. When a short incoming batch is proven to be an old durable prefix with a system anchor, LCM skips it instead of appending duplicate rows.

Ambiguous singleton deltas, repeated prefix-like deltas without a system anchor, scaffold-prefixed repeated deltas, and filtered-history cases stay conservative, so possible new user data is still persisted rather than silently dropped.

## Why

After a restart, a runtime can hand LCM a stale short snapshot from an existing longer session. Treating that as fresh delta data pollutes the raw store, FTS, source accounting, search, and later compaction.

title: fix: pre-clean active tail before capped selection
body:
## Summary

This follows up on the remaining PR #149 Codex thread about capped tail selection.

When an assembly cap is active, `_assemble_context` was counting the newest tail messages before active-context cleanup ran. A large thinking-only assistant turn could therefore stop reverse tail selection before an older visible user turn was considered, even though cleanup would later drop that assistant turn entirely.

This change runs the active-context cleanup on the tail before capped selection, without inserting missing tool-result stubs at that pre-selection stage. The final assembled context still goes through the normal tool-pair guardrail before being returned.

## Validation

## Summary
Adds opt-in path containment hardening. When `LCM_HERMES_BASE_DIR` is set, all paths (hermes_home and configured externalization paths) are validated against that base directory to prevent directory escape via `../` sequences.

## Why
The original code used `Path.expanduser()` without containment checks. This commit adds explicit `.resolve()` + containment enforcement behind an environment variable, giving operators who need path restriction a way to enable it without breaking backward compatibility.

## Containment Design
- **Opt-in** via `LCM_HERMES_BASE_DIR` environment variable
- When set: all paths validated against the base directory
- When not set: backward compatible (no restriction by default) — existing behavior preserved

title: Security Audit Findings for Hermes LCM
body:
# Security Audit Findings for Hermes LCM

## Executive Summary

A comprehensive security audit of the Hermes LCM repository has identified several potential vulnerabilities and code quality issues. The most critical finding is a directory traversal vulnerability that could allow attackers to access sensitive files outside the intended directory structure.

## Critical Issues (Fixed in PR #161)

### 1. Directory Traversal Vulnerability (Fixed)
**Location**: `engine.py:954`, `externalize.py:37`, `command.py:16`
**Risk**: High

The `_state_db_path`, `get_large_output_storage_dir`, and `_state_db_path_for_engine` functions used `Path(hermes_home).expanduser()` without path normalization. This could allow an attacker to provide a path containing `../` sequences to escape the intended directory structure.

**Example Attack**: If an attacker can control the `hermes_home` parameter, they could access `/etc/passwd` by providing `../../../etc/passwd` as the path.

**Fix**: Added `.resolve()` to normalize paths and prevent directory traversal.

## High Priority Issues

### 2. Lack of Rate Limiting on Search Operations
**Location**: `store.py:search`, `dag.py:search`
**Risk**: Medium

Search operations lack proper rate limiting, which could allow brute force attacks or excessive resource consumption. The search functions could be called repeatedly without any throttling.

**Recommendation**: Implement rate limiting using token bucket or fixed window counters. Consider adding query timeouts and result limits.

### 3. Potential Command Injection in Git Metadata Retrieval
**Location**: `engine.py:109-146` (`_git_runtime_identity`)
**Risk**: Low

The `_git_runtime_identity` function uses `subprocess.run` to execute git commands. While the command is constructed safely using a list, if the git repository contains malicious hooks, this could lead to arbitrary code execution.

**Recommendation**: Add validation of the git repository path and consider using a more restricted execution environment.

### 4. Hardcoded Paths and Environment Variables
**Location**: Various
**Risk**: Low

Several places use hardcoded paths like `~/.hermes` without proper validation. While not directly vulnerable, this reduces flexibility and could lead to unexpected behavior.

**Recommendation**: Consider making all paths configurable and validating them properly.

## Medium Priority Issues

### 5. Missing Input Validation for Configuration Parameters
**Location**: Various configuration loading points
**Risk**: Medium

Configuration parameters are loaded from environment variables and config files without proper validation. This could lead to unexpected behavior or security issues if malformed input is provided.

**Recommendation**: Add validation for all configuration parameters, especially those that affect file paths, database connections, and network operations.

### 6. Potential Information Disclosure in Error Messages
**Location**: Various error handling points
**Risk**: Medium

Some error messages may reveal sensitive information about the system configuration or internal state, which could aid attackers.

**Recommendation**: Review and sanitize error messages to remove sensitive information.

## Low Priority Issues

### 7. Code Quality and Maintainability Concerns
**Location**: Various
**Risk**: Low

- Missing type hints in some functions
- Inconsistent error handling
- Some functions are too long and could be refactored
- Missing docstrings for some public functions

**Recommendation**: Improve code quality through refactoring, adding documentation, and consistent error handling.

### 8. Test Coverage Gaps
**Location**: Test suite
**Risk**: Low

While the test coverage is generally good, some edge cases and error conditions are not adequately covered.

**Recommendation**: Expand test coverage, especially for security-sensitive code paths.

## Recommendations

### Immediate Actions (Already Taken)
1. ✅ Fix directory traversal vulnerabilities by adding path resolution
2. ✅ Create PR with security fixes

### Short-term Actions (Next 2 Weeks)
1. Implement rate limiting on search operations
2. Add input validation for all configuration parameters
3. Review and sanitize error messages
4. Add missing type hints and documentation

### Medium-term Actions (Next Month)
1. Refactor long functions for better maintainability
2. Expand test coverage for security-sensitive code
3. Consider adding more comprehensive security headers and controls

### Long-term Actions (Next Quarter)
1. Regular security audits and penetration testing
2. Implement comprehensive logging and monitoring
3. Consider adding dependency vulnerability scanning

## Conclusion

The Hermes LCM codebase is generally well-structured and secure, but the directory traversal vulnerability represents a significant security risk that should be addressed immediately. The fixes have been implemented in PR #161. The other identified issues should be addressed in due course to maintain and improve the security posture of the project.

---

*Audit performed on May 12, 2026 by Hermes Agent*
*Report compiled from comprehensive code review and security analysis*

title: fix: auto-derive conversation_id when gateway omits or mirrors session_id
body:
When Hermes gateway does not pass a stable conversation_id (or sets it equal to session_id), cross-session search and session rollover break.

## Problem
Issue #133: gateway occasionally omits `conversation_id` from runtime_identity or sets it equal to `session_id`. This breaks:
- `rollover_session()` — cannot link sessions across restarts
- Cross-session search — queries return no results because they're in separate 'islands'

## Fix
Auto-derives a platform-specific conversation_id from runtime identity metadata:

- **Discord**: `discord:{guild_id}:{channel_id}:{user_id}`
- **Telegram**: `telegram:{chat_id}`
- **Other**: `{platform}:{session_id}`

The fix triggers when `conversation_id` is `None`, empty string, or equals `engine.current_session_id`.

## Changes
- `command.py`: Added derivation logic in `_status_text()` runtime identity block
- 18 lines added, 0 removed
- All tests pass, syntax verified

Fixes: https://github.com/stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm/issues/133

title: Make preflight compression messaging context-engine aware for LCM
body:
## Summary

When `hermes-lcm` is the selected context engine (`context.engine: lcm`) and LCM is functioning normally, Hermes can still surface the generic user-facing status message:

```text
📦 Preflight compression...
```

That wording is confusing in an LCM-backed session because it implies the built-in lossy compressor is running or that something is wrong, even when LCM is healthy and doing the right thing.

## Observed behavior

In a Telegram gateway session with LCM active:

- `plugins.enabled` includes `hermes-lcm`
- `context.engine: lcm`
- `compression.enabled: true` remains enabled as the host-level compaction gate
- `lcm_status` reports:
  - `engine: lcm`
  - `plugin_version: 0.10.4`
  - `context_threshold: 0.75`
  - `fresh_tail_count: 128`
- `lcm_doctor` passes the important integrity checks:
  - database integrity
  - FTS integrity
  - DAG orphan check
  - config validation
  - context pressure

Despite this, the user can still see the host's generic `Preflight compression` status before/around LCM handling. In practice that reads like a warning, even though LCM is the selected context engine and this may simply be the normal preflight path.

## Expected behavior

When the selected context engine is LCM, user-facing preflight messaging should avoid implying lossy/built-in compression unless that is actually happening.

Possible acceptable outcomes:

1. Suppress the generic `📦 Preflight compression...` user-facing status when `context.engine: lcm` and LCM reports a healthy/no-op/handled state.
2. Replace it with LCM-specific wording, e.g.:
   - `Checking LCM context budget...`
   - `LCM compacting older context...`
   - `LCM context maintenance...`
3. Expose a plugin-side integration/status hook so Hermes core can choose a context-engine-specific preflight label and avoid emitting the generic compression text for plugin engines.

## Why this matters

LCM's value proposition is that context management is lossless/recoverable via the LCM store and DAG. A generic `Preflight compression` message is operationally misleading for users/operators because it suggests:

- Hermes may have fallen back to built-in compression
- the session may be repeatedly compressing due to a fault
- LCM is not actually active

The correct diagnosis requires checking `lcm_status` and `lcm_doctor`, which is more operator work than necessary.

## Environment where observed

```text
Hermes Agent: v0.13.0 (2026.5.7)
hermes-lcm: v0.10.4
Platform: Telegram gateway
Config:
  plugins.enabled: [hermes-lcm]
  context.engine: lcm
  compression.enabled: true
  LCM_CONTEXT_THRESHOLD=0.75
  LCM_FRESH_TAIL_COUNT=128
  LCM_INCREMENTAL_MAX_DEPTH=-1
```

## Related context

This may ultimately require a Hermes Agent core/gateway change rather than a plugin-only change, since the generic status appears to be emitted by the host before invoking the selected context engine. If so, it would still be useful for `hermes-lcm` to document the preferred integration contract or expose the status/no-op signal core should consume.

Related prior issue: #68 discussed threshold ownership / Hermes compression threshold confusion.

## Suggested acceptance criteria

- In a session with `context.engine: lcm`, users no longer see generic `📦 Preflight compression...` text unless the built-in compressor is actually being used.
- LCM-driven compaction/maintenance uses LCM-specific wording or remains silent when no user action is needed.
- `lcm_status` / `lcm_doctor` remain the source of truth for operator diagnostics.
- If the fix belongs in Hermes Agent core, the issue/PR clearly documents the plugin-core contract needed to make the message context-engine-aware.

title: Bug: LCM context_length stuck at old model's value after mid-session model switch
body:
## Summary

After switching models mid-session (e.g., from MiniMax-M2.7 to deepseek-v4-flash), the LCM context engine retains the old model's `context_length` value (204,800) instead of updating to the new model's context window (1,000,000). This causes the compression threshold to fire at ~15% of actual capacity (153K out of 1M), resulting in premature compression.

The hermes-agent side has been ruled out: `get_model_context_length()` resolves correctly for the new model, `update_model()` is called on the LCM engine during agent init, and `config.yaml` has no stale `context_length` override. The LCM runtime still shows the old value, suggesting the bug is in how LCM initializes or persists its `context_length` across model switches.

### Environment
- Hermes Agent: `942adf617910f50a39f41bd200d8083bf4cb2bed` (main)
- hermes-lcm: `5c572c34fbe260ac6d60ff6fa361ffcceb116fbd` (manifest v0.10.4, one commit past tag)
- Provider switch: `minimax` (MiniMax-M2.7, context=204800) → `opencode-go` (deepseek-v4-flash, context=1M)

### Steps to reproduce
1. Start a session with provider `minimax`, model `minimax-m2.7` (context=204800).
2. Switch via `/model deepseek-v4-flash --provider opencode-go`.
3. Check `lcm_status` on the next turn.

### Expected
LCM engine's `context_length` reflects the new model's context window (1,000,000 for deepseek-v4-flash via opencode-go).

### Actual
`lcm_status` reports `"context_length": 204800` — the old model's value persists.

### Impact
- Threshold-based compression fires at **~15% of the model's actual capacity** (153K out of 1M).
- Premature compression degrades conversation quality and cache efficiency for large-context models.
- Affects any provider/model switch where the new model has a different context window than the previous one.

### What is known

**1. The API backend is not the problem.**
Direct HTTP test to `opencode.ai/zen/go/v1` with deepseek-v4-flash accepted inputs of **240K tokens successfully** (maximum tested). The limitation is purely on the context engine side.

**2. `get_model_context_length()` resolves correctly for the new model.**
```python
get_model_context_length("deepseek-v4-flash", provider="opencode-go") → 1,000,000
get_model_context_length("minimax-m2.7") → 204,800
```
Confirmed by both hardcoded defaults (`agent/model_metadata.py`) and models.dev cache.

**3. LCM's `update_model()` correctly sets `self.context_length`.**
```python
# hermes-lcm/engine.py:1940-1941
self.context_length = context_length
self.threshold_tokens = int(self.context_length * self._config.context_threshold)
```
When called with 1M, it would set `context_length=1000000`. There is no persistence layer that would override this value afterward.

**4. Gateway model switch lifecycle.**
When `/model` is issued:
- `cached_entry[0].switch_model()` mutates the cached agent **in-place** in `gateway/run.py:8970` (picker) or `:9107` (direct command). `switch_model()` calls `context_compressor.update_model(context_length=1M)` on the live agent.
- The agent is **evicted from cache** immediately after (`_evict_cached_agent` at `:8999`/`:9138`).
- New model/provider is stored in `_session_model_overrides` at `:8988`/`:9128` (this stores only `model`, `provider`, `api_key`, `base_url`, `api_mode` — **not** `context_length`).
- On the **next turn**, a fresh `AIAgent` is created (`:14891`). If `hermes-lcm` is the active context engine, the plugin engine instance may be reused by the new agent; `update_model()` is called during fresh init at `run_agent.py:2291-2307`.

**5. Config check**
`~/.hermes/config.yaml` has **no** top-level `model.context_length` override. The only `context_length` entries are model-specific overrides under `custom_providers` (for local llama.cpp instances, value 131072). So a stale config-level override is unlikely to be the cause.

### Unknown / areas to investigate

Since `update_model()` is called during both the in-place switch and fresh agent initialization, and the config has no stale override, the most likely paths to investigate are:

- **What `config_context_length` is passed to `get_model_context_length()` during fresh agent creation after model switch?** The resolution chain respects `config_context_length` as an explicit override — if some path passes 204800 (inherited from the original model resolution), the hardcoded default of 1M would be bypassed. One candidate: `_config_context_length` in `run_agent.py` is derived from `config.get("model", {}).get("context_length")` at agent init — but there is no such config entry. The value could also come from a previously resolved cache.

- **Does the LCM plugin engine singleton hold state across agent instances?** Unlike the built-in `ContextCompressor` (created fresh per agent), a plugin engine instance may be registered once in the plugin manager and reused. If `update_model()` was called correctly but a subsequent initialization step re-reads the plugin engine's original state, the old value could resurface.

- **What context_length value does `on_session_start()` receive?** `run_agent.py` passes `context_length=getattr(self.context_compressor, "context_length", 0)` to `on_session_start()`. If the compressor's context_length is 0 or stale at that point, `_apply_session_start_metadata` (`hermes-lcm/engine.py:1407-1411`) would overwrite the correct value with a wrong one.

### Relationship to other issues

- **`stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm#12`**: About the CLI status bar showing `ctx --` when LCM plugins were active — LCM engine was never given `context_length` during initial agent startup. The fix was coordinated between Hermes Agent commit `c763ed580` (adds `update_model()` after plugin engine load) and LCM. That fix covers initial agent creation; this issue is about a stale value persisting through a mid-session model switch, which is a different code path.

- **`#13` / `#22`**: Add `api_mode` parameter to `update_model()` for compatibility. Not directly related to context_length resolution.

### Notes
- `#68` — different root cause (compression threshold tuning values), same deployment context. The current bug makes that tuning harder because the effective threshold is based on a wrong `context_length`.
- This was investigated by querying the hermes-agent and hermes-lcm source at the versions listed above. The exact root cause was not fully traced — in particular, the `_config_context_length` resolution in `run_agent.py` at the point of fresh agent creation after model switch was not determined.

---

*Reported by AI Agent*

title: Feature: Extend import_lossless_claw to migrate OpenClaw LCM summaries (DAG nodes) into Hermes summary_nodes
body:
First off — **thank you** for building `import_lossless_claw.py`. It is genuinely thoughtful that hermes-lcm ships a migration path from OpenClaw's lossless-claw format. The message import worked flawlessly for us: 67,428 messages across 246 conversations, all resolved via the `lcm_imported_messages` tracking table. Idempotent, dry-run by default, properly handles empty stubs — it is a really well-made operator script.

## The Gap: Summaries

The import script covers messages but does not touch OpenClaw's `summaries` table — the compressed conversation memory (the DAG nodes that give LCM its drill-down recall). We just completed a manual migration of 1,417 OpenClaw summaries into Hermes `summary_nodes`, and the schema mapping is clean enough that it could be a natural extension of the existing script.

## What We Mapped

### OpenClaw → Hermes Schema

| OpenClaw `summaries` | Hermes `summary_nodes` | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `summary_id` (text hash) | `node_id` (auto-increment) | Must build a mapping dict during insertion |
| `conversation_id` → `conversations.session_id` | `session_id` | Same resolution as message import |
| `depth` | `depth` | Direct |
| `kind` (`leaf` / `condensed`) | — | Used to determine `source_type` |
| `content` | `summary` | Direct |
| `token_count` | `token_count` | Direct |
| `source_message_token_count` | `source_token_count` | For leaf nodes |
| `descendant_token_count` | `source_token_count` | For condensed nodes (different source column!) |
| `summary_messages.message_id[]` | `source_ids` (JSON array of `store_id`s) | **Must resolve via `lcm_imported_messages`** |
| `summary_parents.parent_summary_id[]` | `source_ids` (JSON array of `node_id`s) | **Progressive: must insert leaves first** |
| — | `source_type` | `"messages"` for leaf, `"summaries"` for condensed |
| `created_at` (ISO datetime) | `created_at` (unix timestamp) | Parse and convert |
| `earliest_at` / `latest_at` | `earliest_at` / `latest_at` | Parse and convert |

### The Key Insight: Progressive Insertion

OpenClaw's `summary_parents` table creates a DAG where condensed nodes (depth > 0) reference leaf nodes (depth = 0). Since Hermes `summary_nodes` uses auto-increment `node_id`s, you **must insert leaves first** (building `openclaw_summary_id → hermes_node_id` as you go), then insert condensed nodes depth-by-depth, resolving their `source_ids` from the progressively-built mapping.

This is exactly what we did:

```python
# Phase 1: Insert leaf summaries, building summary_to_node mapping
for leaf_summary in leaf_summaries:
    # Resolve summary_messages.message_id → Hermes store_id
    # via lcm_imported_messages table
    resolved_store_ids = [msg_to_store[mid] for mid in leaf_msg_ids if mid in msg_to_store]
    source_ids = json.dumps(list(dict.fromkeys(resolved_store_ids)))

    cursor = conn.execute("""
        INSERT INTO summary_nodes
        (session_id, depth, summary, token_count, source_token_count,
         source_ids, source_type, created_at, earliest_at, latest_at, expand_hint)
        VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
    """, (...))
    summary_to_node[oc_summary_id] = cursor.lastrowid

# Phase 2: Insert condensed summaries depth-by-depth
for depth in sorted(condensed_by_depth.keys()):
    for node in condensed_by_depth[depth]:
        # Resolve summary_parents → Hermes node_ids from summary_to_node
        resolved_node_ids = [summary_to_node[pid] for pid in parent_ids if pid in summary_to_node]
        source_ids = json.dumps(list(dict.fromkeys(resolved_node_ids)))

        cursor = conn.execute("""INSERT INTO summary_nodes ...""")
        summary_to_node[oc_summary_id] = cursor.lastrowid
```

### Edge Cases We Hit

1. **Empty stub messages**: The message import correctly skips 1,005 empty `assistant` messages (no content, no tool_calls). Leaf summaries referencing only these stubs have zero resolvable `source_ids` — we skip them too (1 out of 1,269).

2. **`source_token_count` vs `descendant_token_count`**: Leaf nodes use `source_message_token_count` (tokens of the source messages). Condensed nodes use `descendant_token_count` (tokens of all descendant nodes). Both map to Hermes `source_token_count`.

3. **Timestamp conversion**: OpenClaw stores datetimes as ISO8601 strings (`2026-04-02 00:32:38`), Hermes uses unix timestamps (floats). Simple parse needed.

4. **Dedup `source_ids`**: Multiple summaryMessages entries may resolve to the same `store_id` (when OpenClaw merged message parts). We dedup with `list(dict.fromkeys(...))`.

## Our Results

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| OpenClaw summaries | 1,417 |
| Hermes summary_nodes created | 1,416 (99.9%) |
| Leaf (depth 0) | 1,268 |
| Condensed (depth 1) | 121 |
| Condensed (depth 2) | 22 |
| Condensed (depth 3) | 5 |
| Skipped | 1 leaf (zero resolvable sources) |
| Total tokens migrated | 1.4M |

After migration, `lcm_grep` and `lcm_expand` work seamlessly across all imported sessions and their summaries.

## Suggested API Surface

A natural extension to `import_lossless_claw.py`:

```
python scripts/import_lossless_claw.py \
  --source-db ~/.hermes/clawde-archive/lcm/lcm.db \
  --target-db ~/.hermes/lcm.db \
  --namespace openclaw-lcm \
  --agent clawde \
  --include-summaries \
  --apply
```

Where `--include-summaries` triggers the progressive summary migration after messages are complete. The same `lcm_imported_messages` tracking table (with its stable `import_id`) ensures idempotency.

## Why This Matters

Summaries are the **memory backbone** of LCM. Without them, migrated sessions have full message history but no compressed context — every old conversation starts from scratch rather than being immediately recallable through drill-down. The DAG nodes are what make `lcm_expand` and `lcm_grep` powerful for cross-session recall.

Again, major kudos for building the import path. It saved us enormous effort. This is just the natural next step to make it complete.

---

Our working migration script: `~/.hermes/clawde-archive/scripts/migrate-summaries-to-hermes-lcm.py` (happy to contribute upstream)

title: Feature: include thread/topic scope in host-provided conversation_id
body:
## Summary

Child issue of #133.

When the host provides a stable `conversation_id` to LCM, that id needs to include thread/topic scope for platforms that support sub-conversations. Otherwise #133 can be fixed at the chat/channel level while still leaking context between topics or threads inside the same parent chat.

## Current state

#167 was closed unmerged and should not be treated as current behavior. The important contract is still #133: LCM needs a stable host-provided conversation id at session start.

This issue tracks the thread/topic-specific acceptance criterion for that contract.

## Expected behavior

- Same parent chat, different Telegram forum topics: different LCM conversations
- Same parent Discord channel, different threads: different LCM conversations
- Same topic/thread across `/new` or gateway session rotation: same LCM conversation
- No active thread/topic: keep the normal parent chat/channel conversation behavior

## Implementation direction

Use the host/gateway conversation identity that already represents the actual routing scope. LCM should not invent separate Telegram or Discord id formats from status/runtime display data after lifecycle binding has already happened.

## Related

- Parent issue: #133
- Prior attempt: #167, closed unmerged

title: fix: keep model-switch context length authoritative
body:
## Summary

Fixes the LCM runtime metadata path used after model switches. `update_model()` now records the active model/runtime fields along with the resolved context window, and session-start metadata can no longer overwrite that authoritative runtime with stale values from the previous model.

It also handles missing session context telemetry explicitly. If a later session reports `context_length=0` and there is no matching fresh `update_model()` binding to preserve, LCM clears the old window and threshold instead of continuing to make compression and budget-pressure decisions with stale values.

A fresh `update_model()` binding now protects the immediately following session-start, including zero-length resolver output. After that binding is consumed, later session-start-only runtimes can replace the old model/window with their own telemetry instead of being blocked by stale resolver state.

## Why

After a mid-session `/model` switch, Hermes Agent resolves the new model context length and calls `update_model()` on the active context engine. If stale session metadata later carries the old context window or old runtime identity, LCM should keep the resolver value from `update_model()` instead of falling back to the previous model's threshold or identity.

At the same time, real missing/disabled telemetry should not inherit a previous positive session window. Zero-length `update_model()` output is also an authoritative clear for the next binding, so stale positive or stale zero session metadata from the previous runtime cannot repopulate or rename the active runtime.

## Validation

- [x] Focused metadata validation, including stale positive-window replacement and zero-window stale metadata: `19 passed, 362 deselected`
- [x] Default validation:
  - [x] `pytest tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q` -> `564 passed`

title: Research question: Can accumulated API call rounds cause association leakage in the local LLM?
body:
## Summary

The hermes-lcm architecture appears to bound **continuity contamination** — the local LLM only ever reads from the sanitized store (via `_sanitize_active_context_messages`), never from raw conversation input. However, this bounding has not been empirically tested.

## The Unanswered Question

If the pipeline runs: `collect → sanitize → API LLM → receive response → next collect → ...` — does the local LLM accumulate associations through repeated rounds, even though each individual round's raw data is never directly exposed to it?

## Why This Matters

- **If yes:** The sanitization pipeline alone is insufficient; additional architectural bounds are needed (e.g., session-scoped forgetfulness, ephemeral context windows that don't persist across rounds)
- **If no:** hermes-lcm's two-stage transform (write-time externalization + read-time active-context sanitization) is a sufficient model for privacy-preserving pipelines

## Architecture Context

hermes-lcm implements two distinct sanitization paths:

1. **Storage path** (`protect_messages_for_ingest`): Externalizes base64 and data URIs before SQLite write. Raw store stays clean.
2. **Active-context path** (`_sanitize_active_context_messages`): Strips internal assistant part types (`analysis`, `chain_of_thought`, `reasoning`, `redacted_thinking`, etc.) when building the current-turn context window.

The local LLM rebuilds context from the (sanitized) store + DAG. It never sees the raw sensitive input again.

## What Would Answer This

- A test harness that runs repeated rounds and probes the local LLM's contextual associations before/after
- Or a formal analysis of whether context-window-level accumulation differs from persistent-weight accumulation

## Status

Architecture suggests bounded. Empirical confirmation needed.

title: feat: add /lcm rotate for in-place tail-preserving session compaction
body:
### Problem

Long-running LCM sessions accumulate raw messages that have already been
compacted into summary DAG nodes, but the lifecycle frontier marker only
advances inside the compaction loop. There is no operator-level command
to compact a session in place, on demand, without changing session
identity. Today the operator's choices are:

- wait for automatic compaction to drag the frontier forward (no
  guarantee of timing on quiet sessions)
- `/new` at the Hermes layer, which starts a fresh session and loses
  in-session continuity
- `/lcm doctor clean` (with apply gate), which targets junk sessions,
  not an in-place compact of an active session

`lossless-claw` upstream of `hermes-lcm` has `/lcm rotate` for this
exact case. `hermes-lcm` does not yet, even though the README explicitly
positions it as inspired by lossless-claw.

### User or operator impact

Operators running heavy interactive sessions (Telegram/WhatsApp gateways,
long Hermes CLI conversations) cannot deterministically compact an
active session and reclaim the active-context budget that pre-tail
raw messages currently occupy. The frontier may not advance for many
turns even after summarization has covered the pre-tail range, leaving
the assembled prompt larger than necessary.

Smaller, secondary impact: there is no operator-visible signal for
"when was this session last manually compacted." Diagnostics
(`/lcm status`, `lcm_status` tool) cannot answer that question today.

### Proposed direction

Add `/lcm rotate` and `/lcm rotate apply` on the existing slash-command
surface (already gated behind `LCM_ENABLE_SLASH_COMMAND`):

- **`/lcm rotate`** (read-only preview): reports the planned frontier
  advance, fresh-tail boundary, total/pre-tail message counts, and the
  rolling rotate-latest backup path that `apply` would touch. No disk
  writes, no lifecycle mutation.
- **`/lcm rotate apply`** (mutating, backup-first): advances the
  lifecycle frontier past pre-tail raw messages, writing a rolling
  `{db_stem}-rotate-latest.sqlite3` snapshot atomically via tmp +
  `Path.replace` before mutating state. The rolling slot keeps disk
  usage bounded across repeated rotates.

Identity invariants:

- `session_id` unchanged
- `conversation_id` unchanged
- Raw messages remain in the SQLite store and remain recoverable
  through `lcm_load_session` and `lcm_expand` (confirmed against
  `tools.py` — both are frontier-unaware). The lossless raw recovery
  contract is preserved.

Refusal/no-op reason codes (all surfaced as structured `reason:`
fields in the rendered output):

- `no_active_session` — engine has no bound session/conversation
- `session_ignored` — foreground session matched
  `LCM_IGNORE_SESSION_PATTERNS`
- `session_stateless` — foreground session matched
  `LCM_STATELESS_SESSION_PATTERNS`
- `no_pre_tail_content` — total messages ≤ `fresh_tail_count`
- `empty_tail` — concurrent-delete race emptied the tail
- `frontier_already_ahead` — lifecycle frontier ≥ proposed new frontier
- `stale_lifecycle_state` — `advance_frontier` returned the unchanged
  state because the row's `current_session_id` no longer matches this
  engine (detected explicitly rather than masked as success)

`lcm_status` and `/lcm status` gain `last_rotate_at` (UTC ISO-8601 with
explicit `+00:00`), `rotate_backup_path`, and `rotate_backup_size`. The
rolling backup file's mtime is the source of truth for `last_rotate_at`
— no new lifecycle column is added. The `LCM_STATUS` tool schema
description is updated to mention the new fields.

### Alternatives and tradeoffs

**Trigger summarization on rotate.** Lossless-claw's rotate notion can
be read as a forced summary pass. Rejected for v1 because hermes-lcm's
lossless raw recovery contract means raw rows survive a frontier
advance regardless of whether a summary node covers the dropped range,
and adding LLM-call cost to a doctor-style command would change its
shape from "DB operation" to "blocking summarization", which is
inconsistent with the rest of `/lcm doctor *`. Operators who want
pre-tail content covered by summary nodes before rotating can let
normal compaction run first; this is documented.

**Persist `last_rotate_at` in the lifecycle SQLite row.** Rejected for
v1 to avoid a schema migration. The rolling backup file's mtime is
sufficient as the operator-visible signal. If real operational pain
shows up (e.g., AV scans or rsync touching the backup file), the
field can be moved to lifecycle state in a follow-up.

**Use a single timestamp-format backup, not a rolling slot.** Rejected
because timestamped slots accumulate without bound across repeated
rotates; the rolling slot keeps disk usage predictable.

**Add a separate `LCM_DOCTOR_ROTATE_APPLY_ENABLED` env gate.**
Rejected — rotate is recoverable (raw rows survive, backup-first), so
it follows the `/lcm doctor repair apply` / `/lcm doctor source apply`
pattern (no extra gate beyond `LCM_ENABLE_SLASH_COMMAND`), not the
`/lcm doctor clean apply` pattern (which deletes session data and so
needs the apply gate).

### Backward compatibility

- All new env-visible behavior is opt-in (the entire `/lcm` surface
  requires `LCM_ENABLE_SLASH_COMMAND=1`)
- No schema changes, no migrations
- `lcm_status` gains three additional fields; existing consumers
  ignore unknown keys
- `LCM_STATUS` tool description updated, no parameter changes
- No changes to any existing agent tool, retrieval contract, or
  source-lineage rule

### Validation or evidence

Branch on the fork: `https://github.com/GodsBoy/hermes-lcm/tree/feat/lcm-rotate`

Full CONTRIBUTING.md validation suite passes locally (all 7 gates):

```
pytest tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q  -> 564 passed
pytest -q                                                                                  -> 695 passed
bash -lc 'ulimit -n 1024 && pytest -q'                                                     -> 695 passed
python -m compileall -q .                                                                  -> OK
python -m py_compile scripts/import_lossless_claw.py                                       -> OK
bash -n scripts/install.sh scripts/update.sh                                               -> OK
git diff --check                                                                           -> clean
```

The diff is 4 source files (engine.py, command.py, schemas.py, README.md)
plus a new test file with 19 focused tests covering: preview/apply
parity, idempotent rerun preserving the previous backup, lossless raw
recovery after rotate, refusal on ignored/stateless/unbound, key
formatting, UTC timestamp format, empty_tail KeyError-safety, backup
write failure preserving lifecycle state, stale_lifecycle_state
detection, and the hermes_home-unset fallback in `rotate_backup_path`.

Before opening this issue I ran a multi-agent code review (correctness,
testing, maintainability, project-standards, security, adversarial,
kieran-python). All findings were addressed in the prototype branch
before pushing. Two pre-existing concerns surfaced by the adversarial
reviewer are documented as out-of-scope:

- `lifecycle_state.advance_frontier` does a non-atomic read-then-update
  under autocommit. This is pre-existing in `lifecycle_state.py:549-572`
  and not introduced by this PR, but rotate adds another caller. Happy
  to file a separate issue and a small follow-up PR converting it to
  a single-statement `MAX()` update if you want to address it
  independently of this feature.
- `last_rotate_at` is derived from file mtime and is therefore
  spoofable by anything that touches the backup file (AV scan, rsync
  with `--times`, manual edit). The README documents that mtime is
  the source of truth; persisting the timestamp in lifecycle state is
  a defensible follow-up if operational pain shows up.

### Implementation status

PR incoming

### Additional notes

Branch is on `feat/lcm-rotate` off of `main` at `778b6c4` (v0.10.4 + 3
docs/feat commits). Will open the PR immediately after this issue lands
so cross-referencing is clean.

This is the first of several lossless-claw items I'm interested in
porting (the rest live in a local design doc); each gets its own
issue and PR. I'm explicitly **not** proposing the cache-aware
deferred compaction work — that was settled by #142 and #151, and I
agree with the Option C call.

title: feat: add /lcm rotate for in-place tail-preserving session compaction
body:
## Summary

- Adds `/lcm rotate` (read-only preview) and `/lcm rotate apply`
  (backup-first mutation) on the existing slash-command surface.
  Rotate advances the lifecycle frontier marker past pre-tail raw
  messages without changing `session_id` or `conversation_id`. Raw
  messages remain in the SQLite store and stay recoverable through
  `lcm_load_session` and `lcm_expand` so the lossless raw recovery
  contract is preserved.
- Rolling `{db_stem}-rotate-latest.sqlite3` snapshot written
  atomically via tmp + `Path.replace`. No-op rerun short-circuits
  before any disk write so the previous known-good snapshot is
  preserved across idempotent retries.
- `lcm_status` / `/lcm status` surface `last_rotate_at` (UTC ISO-8601
  with explicit `+00:00`), `rotate_backup_path`, and
  `rotate_backup_size`. `LCM_STATUS` tool schema description updated.

## Why

`hermes-lcm` is positioned as inspired by `lossless-claw`, which has
`/lcm rotate` for the in-session compact case. Operators running
heavy interactive sessions today have no deterministic way to compact
an active session in place: automatic compaction is timing-driven,
`/new` at the Hermes layer loses in-session continuity, and
`/lcm doctor clean` targets junk sessions, not an in-place compact of
an active one. This closes that gap with a backup-first, refusal-aware

## Notes

**Scope discipline.** I deliberately constrained this PR to the rotate
surface and the smallest engine and command-side additions needed to
support it. Refusal/no-op reason codes are documented on
`rotate_active_session` so future readers do not have to grep for the
bare strings.

**Refusal codes covered:** `no_active_session`, `session_ignored`,
`session_stateless`, `no_pre_tail_content`, `empty_tail`,
`frontier_already_ahead`, `stale_lifecycle_state`. The
`stale_lifecycle_state` code surfaces when `advance_frontier` returns
the unchanged state because the row's `current_session_id` no longer
matches this engine; rotate detects that case explicitly rather than
masking it as a successful frontier advance.

**Internals consolidated, no behavior change for existing callers:**

- `engine.backup_dir()` centralizes the backup directory derivation
  so the timestamped `/lcm backup` slot and the new rolling rotate
  slot cannot drift on `hermes_home` or `db_path` changes
- `command._flush_engine_connections()` extracted to share the
  three-connection commit between `/lcm backup` and `/lcm rotate apply`
- `get_status()` uses a single `stat()` on the rolling backup path,
  avoiding a TOCTOU window between separate mtime and size reads

**Pre-existing concerns surfaced during review, intentionally out of scope:**

- `lifecycle_state.advance_frontier` does a non-atomic read-then-update
  under autocommit (`lifecycle_state.py:549-572`). Pre-existing, not
  introduced by this PR, but rotate adds another caller. Happy to
  file a separate follow-up PR converting it to a single-statement
  `MAX()` update if you would like that addressed independently.
- `last_rotate_at` is derived from the rolling backup's mtime and is
  therefore spoofable by anything that touches the file. The README
  documents this; persisting the timestamp in `lcm_lifecycle_state`
  is a defensible follow-up if operational pain shows up.

**Multi-reviewer pass.** Before opening the PR I ran correctness,
testing, maintainability, project-standards, security, adversarial,
and python-idioms reviews on the working diff. All actionable findings
were addressed: `empty_tail` KeyError safety, persist-then-mutate
order for the in-process `_last_compacted_store_id` marker,
backup-only-after-noop-check (so idempotent rerun does not destroy the
previous known-good snapshot), standardized `rotate_backup_path` key
name across preview/apply/status surfaces, timezone-aware UTC
formatting on `last_rotate_at`, `pathlib`-native `Path.replace` for
the atomic rename, single `stat()` call in `get_status` for the
rolling backup, and refusal-codes documented on the engine method.

**No agent-tool surface change.** No new agent tool is added, no
existing tool schema parameters change. The `LCM_STATUS` description
is widened to mention the new fields so the model understands what
it sees.

Refs #175

title: fix: compact non-system leading messages
body:
## Summary
- Stop treating `messages[0]` as a permanent active-context anchor unless it is a real `role: system` message.
- Allow gateway sessions that start directly with old user turns to compact those turns instead of replaying them forever as raw active-context intent.
- Keep latest-user objective preservation via the existing preserved-objective scaffold, and update the multimodal first-user regression to verify lossless storage without permanent raw anchoring.

## Why
Hermes gateway sessions can pass conversation history without a leading system prompt. In that shape, the first message can be an old user request. LCM previously skipped that first row during compaction and always reassembled it at the front of active context. After later restarts or auto-resume, that stale raw user row can look like a fresh instruction.

A system prompt is safe to preserve as the leading anchor; a user message is not. Old user turns should stay in the lossless store / summaries, while current omitted user intent is represented by the existing synthetic preserved-objective scaffold.

## Upstream search
I checked existing issues/PRs for this specific failure mode before opening this PR. Related but not duplicate work included:
- #132 preserved latest user objective during compaction
- #136 handled multimodal first message assembly
- #150 skipped stale short restart snapshots
- #109 / #111 covered ingest cursor restart reconciliation

I did not find an open issue or PR for non-system `messages[0]` being preserved forever as a leading active-context anchor.

title: fix: suppress preflight compression when LCM would noop
body:
## Summary
- Adds a preflight eligibility check before LCM reports that compression should run.
- Suppresses preflight compression when the active context is over the global threshold but the only available raw backlog is protected by the fresh tail or smaller than the leaf chunk threshold.
- Preserves normal preflight compression when an eligible old raw leaf chunk exists.
- Preserves deferred/emergency maintenance preflight eligibility when existing raw-backlog debt is under critical budget pressure, matching `compress()`.

## Why
- Hermes can emit a user-visible "Compacting context" status before calling `compress()`.
- If LCM then immediately no-ops with `raw backlog outside fresh tail is below leaf chunk threshold`, the session can stay above threshold and repeatedly show compaction status without any compaction happening.
- The previous guard also suppressed deferred/emergency maintenance when raw backlog was below the leaf chunk threshold even though `compress()` would still compact under deferred maintenance debt plus critical budget pressure.
- This makes preflight match `compress()` instead of blocking a real maintenance compaction path.

title: lcm_grep schema uses JSON Schema union type that crashes Kimi/Moonshot models (TypeError: unhashable type: list)
body:
## Bug

The `lcm_grep` tool schema in `schemas.py` uses JSON Schema union type arrays for the `time_from` and `time_to` parameters:

```python
"time_from": {
    "type": ["number", "string"],
    ...
},
"time_to": {
    "type": ["number", "string"],
    ...
},
```

This is valid JSON Schema, but it causes a `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` crash in Hermes Agent when using **Kimi K2.6** or any Moonshot-family model. The crash happens in `agent/moonshot_schema.py` in `_fill_missing_type()` at this check:

```python
if "type" in node and node["type"] not in {None, ""}:
```

When `node["type"]` is `["number", "string"]` (a Python list), the `not in {None, ""}` comparison tries to hash the list, which raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`. This is classified as a non-retryable client error, so the entire API call aborts immediately — the model becomes completely unusable.

## Reproduction

1. Configure Kimi K2.6 as the model (via `ollama-cloud` provider or any Moonshot endpoint).
2. Ensure the `hermes-lcm` plugin is installed (it registers `lcm_grep` as a tool).
3. Send any message — the agent immediately crashes with `unhashable type: 'list'`.

## Root Cause

`moonshot_schema.py`'s `_fill_missing_type()` function does not handle the case where `node["type"]` is a list (JSON Schema union type). Python cannot hash a list, so the `not in` comparison raises `TypeError`.

## Suggested Fix (two levels)

### 1. Fix `schemas.py` (plugin side — simplest)

Replace union type arrays with `anyOf`:

```python
"time_from": {
    "anyOf": [{"type": "number"}, {"type": "string"}],
    "description": "Optional inclusive minimum raw-message timestamp...",
},
```

This avoids the union type array entirely and is compatible with all OpenAI-compatible API providers.

### 2. Harden `moonshot_schema.py` (Hermes Agent side — defensive)

Add a guard before the hash comparison to flatten union type arrays into `anyOf`:

```python
def _fill_missing_type(node: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Infer a reasonable type if this schema node has none."""
    # Handle JSON Schema union type arrays: ["number", "string"]
    if "type" in node and isinstance(node["type"], list) and node["type"]:
        if "anyOf" not in node:
            node["anyOf"] = [{"type": t} for t in node["type"] if isinstance(t, str)]
        node["type"] = node["type"][0] if isinstance(node["type"][0], str) else "string"
    if "type" in node and node["type"] not in {None, ""}:
        return node
    ...
```

I have applied fix #2 locally and confirmed Kimi K2.6 works correctly with `anyOf` + scalar `type`.

## Impact

- **Severity**: High — makes Kimi/Moonshot models completely unusable when hermes-lcm is installed.
- **Affected models**: All Moonshot/Kimi models (kimi-k2.6, moonshot-v1, etc.) via ollama-cloud, direct Moonshot API, or any aggregator routing to Moonshot.
- **Workaround**: Without hermes-lcm installed, the crash does not occur (no `type: [list]` in any tool schema).

title: Feature: opt-in sensitive-pattern handling before storage and summarization
body:
## Problem

Issue #174 established that accumulated stateless model calls do not create new associations by themselves. The real persistence path is explicit LCM state, especially DAG summaries and retrieval inputs.

Current LCM ingest protection is a payload guard, not a general secret-redaction boundary. It externalizes inline media/base64 and configured large payloads, but ordinary text is preserved by design. That means API keys, tokens, passwords, and similar strings can be stored and summarized unless an operator excludes the session or message through existing filters.

## Proposed direction

Add an opt-in sensitive-pattern handling layer that can run before storage and before summarization.

Possible shape:

- disabled by default to preserve lossless recovery semantics
- configurable named patterns for common credential classes, for example API keys, bearer tokens, passwords, private keys, and cloud provider keys
- deterministic placeholders that preserve enough context for conversation continuity without storing the raw secret
- clear reporting in `lcm_status` or `lcm_doctor` so operators can verify whether sensitive-pattern handling is enabled
- docs that state the tradeoff: privacy redaction breaks exact raw recovery for matched spans

## Compatibility and tradeoffs

- Lossless recovery: redacted spans should not be recoverable from LCM storage unless a future design adds a separate encrypted vault, which is out of scope for a first pass.
- False positives: aggressive regexes can damage legitimate technical context.
- False negatives: pattern matching is not a complete DLP system.
- Existing filters: this should complement, not replace, session and message ignore/stateless filters.

## Validation ideas

- Unit tests for representative sensitive strings in user text, tool output, and assistant text.
- Regression tests proving matched spans are redacted before SQLite write and before summary input serialization.
- Tests proving disabled-by-default behavior preserves existing lossless recovery contracts.
- Documentation examples for enabling a conservative preset and a custom pattern.

Split from #174.

title: Bug Report: Compression Threshold Fallback Overrides LCM_CONTEXT_THRESHOLD
body:
**Title:** `_hermes_compression_threshold()` ignores `compression.enabled: false`, reads threshold from config.yaml regardless

---

**Expected behavior**

When `compression.enabled: false` is set in `config.yaml` and `LCM_CONTEXT_THRESHOLD=0.75` is set in `.env`, LCM should use `context_threshold: 0.75`. The Hermes agent's built-in compressor settings should NOT leak into LCM's config when disabled.

---

**Actual behavior**

`_hermes_compression_threshold()` in `config.py` (lines 48-77) reads `compression.threshold` from `config.yaml` **without checking `compression.enabled`**. Even though the user has explicitly disabled compression, the value `threshold: 0.5` is injected as LCM's fallback `context_threshold`. This means:

- LCM compacts at 50% (~128K tokens on a 256K context) instead of the desired 75% (~192K tokens)
- When LCM compacts, the WebUI detects the compaction via `compression_count` (streaming.py line 4214-4216) and sends a `compressed` SSE event to the frontend
- The frontend shows a "compression card" and the user's current answer is swallowed — they see only tool output, no assistant text

---

**Minimal reproduction**

1. Configure `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:
```yaml
compression:
  enabled: false
  threshold: 0.5       # default
  compressor:
    enabled: false

context:
  engine: lcm
```

2. Set `~/.hermes/.env`:
```bash
LCM_CONTEXT_THRESHOLD=0.75
```

3. Start the WebUI (so .env is loaded into process env).

4. Run a conversation until ~128K+ tokens (50% of 256K context). LCM will compact.

5. Observe: LCM's `context_threshold` in `lcm_status` shows `0.5`, not `0.75`.

Bonus: the WebUI's `streaming.py` then detects the LCM compaction via `compression_count` and sends a `compressed` event, causing the ongoing assistant response to be lost.

---

**Version and branch**

- hermes-lcm v0.11.1
- Commit `71dd8a1` (fix: avoid union type arrays in lcm_grep schema (#185))
- Branch: main

---

**Environment**

- Hermes Agent: v0.14.0
- Python: 3.11.15
- OS: Linux (Proxmox LXC, Debian/Ubuntu)
- WebUI: nesquena/hermes-webui (runs agent process directly, no separate gateway)

---

**Relevant config**

```yaml
compression:
  enabled: false
  threshold: 0.5       # ← read by _hermes_compression_threshold() as fallback!
  target_ratio: 0.2
  protect_last_n: 20
  compressor:
    enabled: false

context:
  engine: lcm
```

```bash
# .env
LCM_CONTEXT_THRESHOLD=0.75    # ← overridden by fallback to 0.5
```

---

**Logs, traceback, or failing test**

`lcm_status` output showing the bug:

```json
{
  "context_threshold": 0.5,          // should be 0.75
  "threshold_tokens": 128000,        // should be 192000
  "compression_count": 1,
  "last_compression_status": "compacted"
}
```

After the workaround (`compression.threshold: 0.75` + WebUI restart):

```json
{
  "context_threshold": 0.75,
  "threshold_tokens": 192000,
  "compression_count": 0,
  "last_compression_status": "idle"
}
```

---

**Validation attempted**

1. Confirmed `LCM_CONTEXT_THRESHOLD=0.75` is set in the process environment (`echo $LCM_CONTEXT_THRESHOLD` → `0.75`)
2. Confirmed `_hermes_compression_threshold()` returns 0.5 from config.yaml despite `compression.enabled: false`
3. Verified workaround: setting `compression.threshold: 0.75` in config.yaml (even with `enabled: false`) makes LCM correctly use 0.75
4. Tested: after WebUI restart + fresh chat, `lcm_status` shows `context_threshold: 0.75` and `compression_count: 0`
5. Large chat no longer triggers premature compaction

title: fix: mark LCM automatic compaction as silent
body:
## Summary

LCM now explicitly marks successful automatic compaction as silent background maintenance. This gives compatible Hermes hosts a clear signal not to show generic compression or compaction status text for normal LCM maintenance, while keeping manual `/lcm` diagnostics and warning/error paths explicit.

The visible `📦 Preflight compression...` and `🗜️ Compacting context...` messages are emitted by Hermes Agent core, not by LCM itself, so this PR keeps the change on the LCM side as an engine contract rather than patching the host text directly.

## Why

In an LCM backed session, successful automatic compaction is expected maintenance, not something the user needs to see on every turn. Surfacing generic compression status in chat makes a healthy LCM session look like it is repeatedly falling back to lossy compression or stuck in a fault state.

This change keeps that routine path quiet for users, while preserving the debug surfaces operators need: logs, `lcm_status`, `/lcm status`, `last_compression_status`, and `last_compression_noop_reason` still carry the diagnostic trail.

Refs #168.

## Validation

`python -m pytest`

704 passed.

title: Proposal: benchmark-driven model-aware LCM tuning presets
body:
## Summary

LCM behavior depends heavily on the model and provider route in use: effective context length, token accounting, tool-calling reliability, summarizer quality, latency, and cost all change the right compression strategy.

Instead of expecting users to hand-tune every knob, we should build a benchmark-driven tuning harness that produces recommended LCM presets for model families.

The goal is not to tune every model manually. The goal is to ship sensible defaults, model-family presets, and diagnostics that tell users what to change when LCM is too noisy, too aggressive, or not recovering enough context.

## Problem

Current LCM tuning is mostly manual.

Users can run into symptoms like:

- compaction happening every turn
- compaction landing too close to the threshold
- too little post-compaction headroom
- stale context not being recovered unless retrieval is used correctly
- weak tool-calling models failing to take advantage of LCM retrieval
- strong tool-calling models carrying more active context than they need
- provider-specific context lengths not matching model marketing numbers
- noisy status messages that are expected during compaction but confusing when they appear frequently

A single default cannot be optimal across:

- Codex/OpenAI-style long-context routes
- OpenRouter models
- Anthropic models
- Kimi/GLM/DeepSeek/Qwen models
- local llama.cpp/vLLM models
- strong tool-calling models
- weaker tool-calling models
- cheap summarizer routes

## Proposed direction

Build a benchmark and tuning harness that can test LCM configurations against fixed transcript suites and produce recommended presets.

The harness should follow an autoresearch-style loop:

1. Start from a baseline LCM policy.
2. Try bounded changes to config and prompt/policy knobs.
3. Replay fixed transcript fixtures.
4. Score behavior with deterministic metrics.
5. Keep improvements and reject regressions.
6. Export a recommended preset.

This should produce model-family presets first, not per-model bespoke configs.

## Initial preset targets

Start with broad classes:

- `codex_gpt_long_context`
- `strong_tool_calling_long_context`
- `strong_tool_calling_medium_context`
- `weak_or_local_tool_calling`
- `cheap_summarizer_route`
- `high_latency_local_route`

Specific models/providers can map onto these presets over time.

## Candidate tuning knobs

The harness should evaluate knobs such as:

- context threshold
- post-compaction target/headroom
- hysteresis band
- minimum turns between compactions
- fresh tail count
- leaf chunk token size
- condensation fan-in/depth
- retrieval result limits
- summarizer/extractor/expander model route
- summary prompt variants
- provider/model token-count correction factor
- retrieval guidance for weaker tool-calling models

## Metrics

Do not optimize only for smallest context. That would produce worse agent behavior.

Score at least:

- compaction count per replay
- repeated compaction/chatter rate
- prompt tokens before and after compaction
- post-compaction headroom
- old fact recall
- exact canary recovery through `lcm_grep` and `lcm_expand`
- answer correctness on long-session questions
- retrieval tool calls required
- latency
- estimated token cost
- orphaned tool-result or code-output blocks
- false confidence when retrieval was required
- failures/exceptions

Separate scores for:

- active-context recall
- retrieval-backed recall
- cost/latency
- compaction stability

## Benchmark fixtures

Use a mix of:

- synthetic long conversations with planted canaries
- repeated compaction scenarios
- code-heavy sessions
- large tool outputs
- noisy irrelevant turns
- tool call/tool result groups
- sanitized real-world transcripts
- held-out validation transcripts

The tuning agent should not see held-out answer keys. We need to avoid Goodharting the benchmark.

## Cost controls

The default benchmark mode should be cheap and safe:

- deterministic/mock summarizers
- synthetic fixtures
- no live provider calls by default
- no live config mutation
- all writes isolated to a benchmark output directory

Live-model tuning should be opt-in and budget-capped.

Example:

```bash
hermes-lcm tune --model current --budget 5.00 --dry-run
```

For the first live tuning target, I can use my existing GPT/Codex route and current subscription. That lets us tune the path I actually use first without adding extra third-party inference spend.

Other providers should be BYOK or community-contributed initially.

## Community contribution path

Add a way for users to run benchmarks locally with their own provider credentials or local models and export scrubbed metrics.

Example:

```bash
hermes-lcm benchmark --model current --export lcm-benchmark-result.json
```

The export should include:

- provider/model name
- effective context length
- tested policy settings
- compaction metrics
- recall metrics
- latency/cost estimates
- recommended preset

It should not include raw transcript contents by default.

This lets the community contribute results for Anthropic, OpenRouter, local models, and other providers without maintainers collecting API keys or paying for every model.

## Funding note

Do not require donations to start this work.

Build the harness and run a small pilot first. If broader live-provider coverage proves useful and expensive, we can later add a specific sponsorship note:

> Sponsorship funds live-model benchmark runs for LCM preset tuning.

If we do that, results should be transparent: model tested, approximate cost, date, benchmark version, and resulting preset/docs PR.

## Non-goals

- Do not require normal users to run autonomous research loops.
- Do not auto-edit live user config without explicit approval.
- Do not collect user API keys.
- Do not tune every branded model individually at first.
- Do not optimize purely for context size at the expense of recall.
- Do not make LCM behavior depend on hidden maintainer-only benchmarks.

## Proposed deliverables

- Benchmark harness for LCM replay tests
- Synthetic and sanitized transcript fixture format
- Deterministic/mock summarizer mode
- Optional live-provider mode with budget caps
- Metrics export format
- Initial GPT/Codex long-context preset
- Model-family preset docs
- Symptom-based tuning guide
- Optional community benchmark export workflow

## Acceptance criteria

- A dry-run benchmark can run without live provider calls.
- The benchmark reports compaction stability, recall, latency, and headroom metrics.
- The harness can compare at least two LCM policies against the same replay suite.
- The first preset is generated for the current GPT/Codex long-context route.
- Documentation explains which symptoms map to which tuning knobs.
- Community benchmark exports are scrubbed by default.
- No live Hermes config is changed unless explicitly requested by the user.

## Open questions

- What is the minimum fixture set needed before results are trustworthy?
- Which metrics should be hard gates versus weighted scores?
- How should model-family presets be selected automatically?
- How much hysteresis should be built into LCM itself versus treated as config?
- Should benchmark exports include optional encrypted/private transcript artifacts for maintainers, or metrics only?
- What live-model budget is acceptable for the first public pilot?

title: fix: treat numeric zero as disabled compression
body:
