title: [v1·externalize 5/5] bounded atomic threshold full sweeps
body:
## Summary - add opt-in **bounded atomic threshold full sweeps**: after threshold activation, drain the eligible raw prefix in configured leaf-sized chunks instead of stopping when the first pass relieves pressure - condense the summary frontier only after raw history is drained and only while it exceeds `LCM_SUMMARY_PREFIX_TARGET_TOKENS` (`0` derives one leaf budget) - bound the whole invocation to **12 leaf/condensation passes and 120 seconds**, cap provider/extraction timeouts to the remaining wall budget, **persist each completed pass**, and publish exactly one newly assembled active context - surface passes, duration, before/after tokens, stop reason, and budget exhaustion in status telemetry - deterministic, content-scrubbed incremental-vs-sweep benchmark included We maintain Martian Engineering's Lossless Claw and are porting the proven pattern into Hermes-LCM. Fixes #379 Part of #375 ## Why Incremental compaction relieves pressure one leaf at a time — correct, but on a long backlog it means many turns each pay a compaction pass before the prompt reaches its steady-state size. When an operator opts in, a threshold crossing instead drains the whole eligible backlog in one bounded, crash-safe invocation: every pass persists before the next begins, so an interruption loses at most one pass, and only one assembled context is published at the end. ### Where this hooks into the pipeline ```mermaid flowchart LR I[Ingest] --> C[Compact] --> D[Condense] --> ES[Escalate] --> A[Assemble] --> R[Retrieve] C -->|bounded passes:
12 passes / 120 s,
each pass persisted| C classDef hot fill:#b45309,stroke:#7c2d12,color:#fff class C,D hot ``` Synchronous and independent of deferred/background compaction (#287 stays a separate discussion). **Stacked on #381** (token-bounded fresh tail) — please merge/rebase that dependency first. ## Benchmark (re-run post-rebase — deterministic, reproduced exactly) `python scripts/benchmark_threshold_full_sweep.py` on the committed synthetic workload: - incremental: 1 summary call, 1 publication, 6,680 → 5,659 tokens - threshold full sweep: 5 summary calls, 1 publication, **6,680 → 1,355 tokens**, stop reason `summary_prefix_target_reached` - all 24 planted synthetic facts remained provider-visible and recoverable in both runs - neither run exhausted its pass/wall budget (Synthetic assembly/compaction benchmark — not a provider-quality, billing, or latency claim.) ## Validation - [x] restacked onto the rebased #381 (`fd6958d`), which sits on current `main` (`31675c6`) — zero conflicts - [x] full `pytest -q` — **1624 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed**; 3 failures are the known macOS baseline (1 tokenizer-dependent + 2 `/var` vs `/private/var`), reproduced identically on the untouched upstream clone at `31675c6` — Linux CI is the canonical gate - [x] `ruff check .` — pass - [x] `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going` — diff/compile/shell gates, focused pytest, benchmark smoke, stress smoke, and **stress release all pass**; the full-suite variant carries only the same three macOS baselines. The low-fd full-suite variant wedged environmentally on an 8-thread `threading.Barrier` migration test under heavy host load and was terminated; that test passes 3/3 in isolation on this branch (same phenomenon root-caused on the sibling #381 run — local-load artifact, not a code defect) - [x] deterministic benchmark re-run post-rebase — numbers above reproduced exactly (Fork workflow runs need maintainer approval — validation output above is locally reproducible until then.) ## Notes - Disabled by default (`LCM_THRESHOLD_FULL_SWEEP_ENABLED=false`); no background worker, no deferred- maintenance coupling, no live profile or DB migration. - First-pass summary failures keep existing fail behavior; later failures publish only already-persisted progress and report a partial stop. - **Merge order**: stacked on #381. Overlap: your #370 rewrites the same `compress()` hunks — happy to rebase this (and #381) after #370 lands; the rebase cost is ours.

title: Design: temporal rollups + natural-time retrieval (lcm_recent) — day/week/month memory over LCM history
body:
## What Add **calendar-time memory** to hermes-lcm: day/week/month rollup summaries built from existing leaf/ condensed summaries, plus a natural-time retrieval tool (`lcm_recent`) that answers "what did we work on yesterday / last week / on 2026-07-01" without content-keyword guessing. We maintain Martian Engineering's Lossless Claw and are porting the proven pattern into Hermes-LCM (part of #375's parity direction; this is the design issue first, per CONTRIBUTING — the staged PR train follows, stacked and referencing this issue). ## Why Today retrieval is content-indexed (`lcm_grep`, `lcm_describe`, `lcm_expand`): excellent for "find the linker error", blind for "summarize yesterday". Agents and operators both reach for time-shaped recall constantly, and the DAG already contains everything needed — it just has no calendar aggregation. In our Lossless Claw deployment the equivalent feature became one of the most-used recall surfaces. ## Design **Schema** (new `SCHEMA_VERSION` step, idempotent `ensure_*` helpers per the `db_bootstrap.py` pattern): - `lcm_rollups` — `rollup_id`, `period_kind` (`day|week|month`), `period_start`, scope (per-conversation for dailies; global aggregates for week/month), `summary`, `token_count`, `status` (`building|ready|stale|failed`), `built_at`, `source_fingerprint` - `lcm_rollup_sources` — rollup → contributing summary-node ids (provenance + staleness detection) - a small state row for last-build cursors per period kind **Builder** — daily rollups synthesized from that day's leaf/condensed summaries (target ~5k tokens, hard cap ~15k), then week/month aggregates built **from the dailies** (~20k cap). New ingest marks the affected day `stale`; rebuilds happen inside the **existing synchronous maintenance seams** — this proposal adds **no background thread** (deliberately consistent with the staged posture in `docs/async-background-compaction.md`; a worker loop, if ever wanted, is its own discussion). Synthesis rides the existing summarize-with-escalation auxiliary path, so the circuit-breaker and spend-guard already govern it. **Tool surface** — `lcm_recent`: parses `today | yesterday | 7d | week | month | date:YYYY-MM-DD` (+ relative windows), returns ready rollups; when a rollup is absent/stale/disabled it **falls back to the existing leaf-summary retrieval** — degrade is always "what you have today", never an error. Build-state introspection: either a small `lcm_rollup_debug` tool or an extension of `lcm_inspect` — maintainer preference welcome (question 2 below). **Config** — `LCM_TEMPORAL_ROLLUPS_ENABLED=false` (default off, standard `_EnvFieldSpec` entries); token targets configurable. Zero LLM calls when disabled; zero when serving already-built rollups. ```mermaid flowchart LR I[Ingest] -->|marks day stale| RB[RollupBuilder
maintenance-seam, bounded] RB --> RS[(lcm_rollups /
sources / state)] R[lcm_recent
natural-time query] --> RS R -.->|absent/stale| F[existing leaf-summary
retrieval fallback] ``` ## Staged PR train (stacked, each the smallest reviewable unit) 1. schema + `RollupStore` — **no behavior change** 2. `RollupBuilder` + ingest/maintenance wiring (flag-gated) 3. `lcm_recent` tool + schemas + retrieval-tools docs 4. introspection + `/lcm` command surface + operator-guide docs Each PR: checkbox validation, docs in-PR, deterministic tests; the builder PR includes a synthetic token-shape benchmark. ## Questions 1. Daily rollups per-conversation with global week/month aggregates (our production shape) — or would you prefer global dailies too? 2. `lcm_rollup_debug` as its own tool vs. folding into `lcm_inspect`? 3. Any naming preferences before the train lands (`lcm_recent` vs `lcm_timeline` etc.)?

title: Design: pluggable embeddings + semantic/hybrid retrieval — provider abstraction, BLOB vector store, staged train
body:
Title: Design: pluggable embeddings + semantic/hybrid retrieval — provider abstraction, BLOB vector store, staged train ## What Add **opt-in semantic and hybrid retrieval** to hermes-lcm: a pluggable embedding provider (`voyage` HTTP / `ollama` / `fastembed` local / `none`), a dependency-free vector store (float32 BLOBs in regular tables), a dry-run-first backfill command, and `semantic`/`hybrid` modes on the existing retrieval tools — with recall proven by a committed eval script, and a docs guide covering **free** (Voyage free tier) and **local no-signup** (fastembed/Ollama) setups. We maintain Martian Engineering's Lossless Claw and are porting the proven pattern into Hermes-LCM (the largest remaining piece of #375's parity direction; design issue first per CONTRIBUTING — the stacked PR train follows, referencing this issue). ## Why `lcm_grep` is FTS/BM25: exact-term recall is excellent, paraphrase recall is not ("have we discussed auth token rotation?" misses "credential refresh"). In our Lossless Claw deployment, hybrid retrieval (FTS ∪ KNN → rerank) measurably lifted recall on a stratified query set. LCM's summary corpus is the ideal target: thousands of dense leaf summaries, not millions of chunks. ## Design decisions (and the data behind them) **1. Vector math: brute-force cosine over float32 BLOBs in a regular table is the DEFAULT.** No new hard dependency, no SQLite extension. `sqlite-vec` is an optional accelerator only (`LCM_SQLITE_VEC_ENABLED=false`): it is pre-1.0/alpha and — decisively — **cannot load on macOS stock-Python** (Apple compiles SQLite with `SQLITE_OMIT_LOAD_EXTENSION`), which many Hermes users run. Benchmark on the corpus sizes that matter: **Benchmark** (median ms, top-50 cosine, unit-normalized float32 BLOBs in SQLite; 1 warmup + 5 measured; Homebrew Python 3.12, numpy 2.5.1, sqlite-vec 0.1.9; full method + raw data ship with the train): *D = 512* | N | pure-python | bounded-scan (2k) | numpy cold | numpy warm | sqlite-vec | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 5,000 | 47 | 21 | 5.8 | 0.07 | 2.9 | | 20,000 | 191 | 19 | 30 | 0.70 | 11 | | 50,000 | 461 | 18 | 61 | 1.8 | 28 | *D = 1024* | N | pure-python | bounded-scan (2k) | numpy cold | numpy warm | sqlite-vec | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 5,000 | 90 | 39 | 6.8 | 0.41 | 5.7 | | 20,000 | 342 | 33 | 27 | 1.4 | 22 | | 50,000 | 845 | 34 | 69 | 3.6 | 58 | Reading: against a 300 ms interactive budget, **unbounded pure-Python fails past ~20k vectors** (845 ms at 50k×1024); **numpy meets budget everywhere even cold-loading the matrix from SQLite per query** (≤69 ms; warm cache is a 15–80× optimization we can add without changing the contract); the **bounded pure-Python scan holds ~20–40 ms** at any corpus size (coverage-limited, clearly reported); sqlite-vec performs well **but hard-fails on stock/system Python** — verbatim: `AttributeError: 'sqlite3.Connection' object has no attribute 'enable_load_extension'`. Hence the ladder: **numpy (optional import) → bounded pure-Python scan → FTS-only**, with sqlite-vec strictly an opt-in accelerator. Degrade ladder: numpy (optional import, tokens.py-style non-blocking loader) → bounded pure-Python scan over the most recent N vectors → FTS-only. Search NEVER errors because embeddings are missing. **2. Provider abstraction is LCM-owned** (the host has no embedding endpoint to borrow): `LCM_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER` ∈ `voyage` (raw HTTP, no SDK) | `ollama` (`POST /api/embed`) | `fastembed` (optional pip dep, ONNX, no torch) | unset → dormant. Model via `LCM_EMBEDDING_MODEL` (provider/model string, mirrors `model_routing.py`). Resilience mirrors `escalation.py`'s circuit-breaker + spend-guard. **Local-model downloads are never lazy**: fastembed's first-use model fetch happens only via an explicit warmup command / backfill preflight (bounded — this is #371's lesson applied at larger scale), never on an interactive tool call. **3. Model identity is fingerprinted.** `lcm_embedding_profile` locks dimensions at registration; vectors from different models never mix; switching provider/model marks the corpus invalid and status/doctor report "semantic disabled until re-backfill". **4. Staging follows `docs/async-background-compaction.md`'s posture**: dual flags (`*_enabled` / `*_worker_enabled`), one-shot manual backfill command first (dry-run default), fingerprint-validated, no background thread in the core train. **5. Interactive latency is budgeted.** Query-embed and rerank calls each get a hard ~2–3 s timeout → degrade to FTS-only with an explicit `degraded_*` flag in the result. Auth errors surface; transient errors degrade. **6. Hybrid algorithm** (ported semantics): FTS(BM25) top-K ∪ KNN top-K, dedup by node id → optional Voyage `rerank-2.5` (token-budget-packed) → **reciprocal-rank fusion (k=60) fallback** when rerank is unavailable; filter-aware overfetch (post-KNN filters get k×10 candidates, cap 500); cosine confidence bands. History-only results remain byte-identical to today. **7. Proof, not vibes**: the search PR ships a minimal recall@k eval script with a committed stratified query set, so the recall claim is reproducible on any corpus. ## Cost/access story (the docs PR makes this a guide) - **Voyage free tier**: the Voyage-4 generation (voyage-4 / -large / -lite) and rerank-2.5 each carry 200M free tokens per model group, no credit card required — enough for years of a personal corpus. Hybrid query ≈ $0.001 beyond free; semantic-only ≈ $0.0001. - **Local, no signup**: `fastembed` (pip-only, ONNX) as the recommended local default; Ollama (`/api/embed`) for users who already run it. $0. - **Off** (default): nothing changes. ```mermaid flowchart LR I[Ingest] --> C[Compact] --> D[Condense] --> ES[Escalate] --> A[Assemble] --> R[Retrieve] P[embedding provider
voyage / ollama / fastembed] --> V[(lcm_embedding_*
float32 BLOBs)] BF[one-shot backfill
dry-run first] --> P R -->|semantic / hybrid modes
FTS ∪ KNN → rerank/RRF| V R -.->|degrade| F[FTS-only
today's behavior] ``` ## Staged PR train (stacked, smallest reviewable units) 1. schema + vector store + brute-force KNN + suppression/delete handling (no provider, no tools) 2. provider abstraction + config + warmup command (all-mocked HTTP tests) 3. one-shot backfill command (dry-run first) + advisory lock + fingerprints 4. semantic + hybrid modes + confidence bands + degrade flags + recall@k eval script + docs 5. docs: "Free & local embeddings" setup guide 6. (optional, post-acceptance) sqlite-vec accelerator; worker loop ## Questions 1. Comfortable with numpy as an OPTIONAL accelerator dependency (never required)? The benchmark shows where pure-Python alone stops being viable. 2. Preference between extending `lcm_grep` with `mode: semantic|hybrid` vs a separate tool? 3. Any provider you'd want first-class beyond voyage/ollama/fastembed?

title: [v1·temporal 1/4] rollup storage substrate (schema + RollupStore)
body:
## Summary - storage substrate for **temporal rollups** (design: #385 — train PR 1 of 4): `lcm_rollups` / `lcm_rollup_sources` / `lcm_rollup_state` tables via a new `SCHEMA_VERSION` step, plus a transactional `RollupStore` - day→week/month **staleness cascade**, windowed ready-rollup reads, build cursors, app-level source purge integrity (matches the repo's no-SQL-FK convention) - **no behavior change**: nothing constructs or calls `RollupStore` yet; the new `LCM_TEMPORAL_ROLLUPS_ENABLED` flag defaults off and is inert in this PR - 12 focused tests: migration idempotency, v5→v6 upgrade, newer-version refusal, CRUD/rebuild, staleness cascade, uniqueness, cursors, purge, config defaults/overrides We maintain Martian Engineering's Lossless Claw and are porting the proven pattern into Hermes-LCM. Design anchor: #385 (temporal rollups + `lcm_recent`) Part of #375 ## Why Time-shaped recall ("what did we do yesterday / last week") needs calendar aggregation the DAG doesn't have. Per #385, the train lands in the smallest reviewable units — this first PR is schema + store only, so the migration and data model can be reviewed in isolation before any behavior exists. ```mermaid flowchart LR RS[(lcm_rollups /
sources / state)] S1[PR-1 · this:
schema + RollupStore] --> RS S2[PR-2: builder +
maintenance wiring] -.-> RS S3[PR-3: lcm_recent] -.-> RS S4[PR-4: introspection] -.-> RS ``` ## Validation - [x] `pytest -q tests/test_rollup_store.py` — **12 passed** - [x] full `pytest -q` — **1618 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed**; 3 failures are the known macOS baseline, reproduced identically on untouched upstream `main` at `31675c6` - [x] `ruff check .` — pass - [x] `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going` — all gates pass (focused 409; benchmark + both stress tiers; the two full-suite variants carry only the same three macOS baselines — low-fd gate completed normally this run) - [x] five stale `SCHEMA_VERSION == 5` literals in `tests/test_lcm_core.py` now use the shared constant (version tracking only, no behavioral test change) (Fork workflow runs need maintainer approval — validation is locally reproducible until then.) ## Notes - Opt-in flag included here only so the config surface is stable across the train; it gates nothing until PR-2. - `lcm_rollup_sources` uses app-level integrity (transactional purge/replace in `RollupStore`), mirroring the existing summary-source convention rather than SQL FKs. - Heads-up: our embeddings design (#386) will also need a schema step; whichever train lands second rebases its version number — the migration steps are written to make that a two-line change. ### Schema-migration disclosure (adversarial-review follow-up) To be precise about the "no behavior change when disabled" claim: like every schema-backed feature in this repo, the migration is **unconditional** — opening an `lcm.db` with this build bumps `SCHEMA_VERSION` to the next value and creates the new tables even with the feature flag off. Those tables stay **empty** and nothing reads or writes them until the feature is enabled, so there is no *behavioral* change — but the on-disk schema does advance. One consequence worth stating: a user who tries this build and then rolls back to an older release will hit `refuse_schema_version_too_new` (the older build won't open a newer-schema DB). That is inherent to any additive schema step here, not specific to this PR; flagged explicitly so it's a conscious choice rather than a surprise.

title: [v1·temporal 2/4] rollup builder + bounded maintenance
body:
## Summary - **RollupBuilder** (design #385 — train PR 2 of 4, stacked on #387): UTC daily rollups synthesized from each day's leaf/condensed summaries, keyed by a node's **newest covered source-message timestamp** (`COALESCE(latest_at, created_at)`, matching `dag.py`'s source-window fallback); week/month aggregates built **from ready dailies only** - synthesis rides the existing **summarize-with-escalation** path and shares the engine's summary circuit breaker + spend guard; hard token caps via escalation's deterministic-truncate final rung - **two minimal flag-gated engine hooks**: post-ingest staleness marking, and bounded catch-up (`LCM_ROLLUP_BUILDS_PER_PASS`, default 2 — dailies before aggregates, oldest first) at the existing lifecycle-bind maintenance opportunity; the empty path is a single indexed query - **failure isolation**: a rollup failure marks the row `failed` and never affects the turn; everything inert with `LCM_TEMPORAL_ROLLUPS_ENABLED=false` (default) - 9 focused tests: time keying, deterministic output, caps + oversize fallback, ready-only aggregation + refingerprinting, end-to-end staleness→bounded rebuild, flag-off inertness (spy on zero queries), failure isolation We maintain Martian Engineering's Lossless Claw and are porting the proven pattern into Hermes-LCM. Design anchor: #385 · Stacked on: #387 · Part of #375 ## Why PR-1 gave rollups a home; this PR fills it — bounded, synchronous, and quietly. No background thread (consistent with `docs/async-background-compaction.md`'s staged posture): stale rollups catch up a few per pass inside maintenance work the engine already does. ```mermaid flowchart LR I[Ingest] -->|mark day stale
flag-gated| RS[(lcm_rollups)] M[lifecycle-bind maintenance
≤ builds_per_pass] --> RB[RollupBuilder
escalation-capped] RB --> RS ``` ## Validation - [x] focused builder + store tests — **21 passed** - [x] full `pytest -q` — **1627 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed**; 3 failures are the known macOS baseline (same three as #387, reproduced on untouched upstream `main`) - [x] `ruff check .` — pass - [x] `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going` — all gates pass (focused 409, benchmark + both stress tiers; full-suite variants carry only the same three baselines) (Fork workflow runs need maintainer approval — validation locally reproducible until then.) ## Notes - Merge order: #387 first (this stacks on it). - Rollup scope = the active DAG session id, so ingest staleness and rollup selection share one key. - LLM spend: zero when disabled; when enabled, rollup synthesis is governed by the same circuit breaker + spend guard as regular summarization — it cannot outspend the budget you already granted.

title: [v1·temporal 3/4] lcm_recent natural-time retrieval
body:
## Summary - **`lcm_recent`** — natural-time retrieval over LCM history (design #385 — train PR 3 of 4, stacked on #388): `today | yesterday | Nd | week | month | date:YYYY-MM-DD | last Nh`, parsed to UTC `[start, end)` windows - serves **ready** day/week/month rollups newest-first, with per-rollup token lines, provenance (which rollups served, status), limit clamping, and the shared 20k-char response ceiling - **transparent degradation is the load-bearing behavior**: missing/stale/disabled rollups and sub-day windows fall back to existing depth-0 summary retrieval in the same window — never an error, and provenance says `fallback: true` - serving is **read-only and makes zero LLM calls** (building stays in #388's bounded maintenance) - 66 focused tests: every period form, invalid inputs, ready/stale/disabled/sub-day modes, scopes, bounds, provenance; docs with three usage examples We maintain Martian Engineering's Lossless Claw and are porting the proven pattern into Hermes-LCM. Design anchor: #385 · Stacked on: #388 (which stacks on #387) · Part of #375 ## Why This is the PR the first two exist for: "what did we work on yesterday / last week" becomes a single tool call that answers from prebuilt rollups when they exist and behaves exactly like today's retrieval when they don't. ```mermaid flowchart LR Q[lcm_recent
natural-time query] --> P[UTC window parser] P -->|ready| RS[(lcm_rollups)] P -.->|absent / stale /
disabled / sub-day| F[existing leaf-summary
retrieval fallback] ``` ## Validation - [x] focused `lcm_recent` + public-registration/packaging contracts — **66 passed** - [x] full `pytest -q` — **1652 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed**; 3 failures are the known macOS baseline, reproduced identically on untouched upstream `main` (isolated-HOME run) - [x] `ruff check .` + `git diff --check` — pass - [x] `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going` — all gates pass (focused 409, benchmark + both stress tiers; full-suite variants carry only the same three baselines) (Fork workflow runs need maintainer approval — validation locally reproducible until then.) ## Notes - Merge order: #387 → #388 → this. - Beyond the spec'd files, the repo's hard-coded public-tool surfaces (`engine.py` tool list, `__init__.py`, `plugin.yaml`) needed registration-only lines so the tool is reachable and the synchronized tool-contract suite stays valid — no engine lifecycle/compaction behavior touched. - `week`/`month` serve only exact calendar aggregates; any non-ready row in the window forces the fallback (conservative by design — no partially-fresh answers).

title: [v1·embeddings 1/5] embedding vector storage substrate + KNN ladder
body:
## Summary - **embedding storage substrate** (design #386 — embeddings train PR 1, benchmark-driven): `lcm_embedding_profile` (dim locked at registration, immutable) / `lcm_embedding_meta` (model-fingerprinted) / `lcm_embedding_vectors` (float32 BLOBs) via a new schema step - **the #386 compute ladder, exactly as benchmarked**: NumPy full scan when importable (with a `(model, max(rowid), row_count)` matrix cache invalidated on writes — correctness never depends on the cache), bounded most-recent pure-Python scan otherwise, `coverage: full|bounded|none` reported on every result - L2-normalization on write; DELETE+INSERT under one transaction (no upsert); filter-aware overfetch (k×10 cap 500) with post-scan joins for time/conversation filters; app-level purge for hard-deleted nodes - **default-off and inert**: nothing constructs the store yet — no provider, no HTTP, no tool wiring (train PRs 2–4) - 14 tests incl. hand-computed cosine ordering, NumPy-absent fallback, bounded-window enforcement, cache invalidation, migration idempotency/upgrade/version-guard We maintain Martian Engineering's Lossless Claw and are porting the proven pattern into Hermes-LCM. Design anchor: #386 · Part of #375 ## Why Per #386's benchmark: NumPy meets a 300 ms interactive budget even cold-loading 50k×1024 from SQLite (≤69 ms), unbounded pure-Python fails past ~20k vectors, and sqlite-vec can't load on stock/system Python — so the store is dependency-free by default with NumPy as an optional accelerator and an honest `coverage` signal when running bounded. This PR is the data model + math only, reviewable in isolation before any behavior exists. ```mermaid flowchart LR VS[(lcm_embedding_profile /
meta / vectors BLOB)] L1[NumPy full scan
+ matrix cache] --> VS L2[bounded pure-Python scan
coverage: bounded] -.fallback.-> VS L3[coverage: none
callers stay FTS-only] -.fallback.-> L2 ``` ## Validation - [x] `pytest -q tests/test_vector_store.py` — **14 passed** - [x] full `pytest -q` — **1620 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed**; 3 failures are the known macOS baseline, reproduced identically on untouched upstream `main` - [x] `ruff check .` — pass - [x] `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going` — compile/shell/diff gates, focused pytest (409), benchmark smoke, both stress tiers pass; the two full-suite gates hit a known local-load-only wedge in an 8-thread Barrier migration test (frozen logs, terminated; the test then passed 3/3 in isolation and a fresh bounded full run showed only the same three baselines — same phenomenon documented on #381/#384) (Fork workflow runs need maintainer approval — validation locally reproducible until then.) ## Notes - **Schema-version heads-up**: this PR and the temporal train's #387 independently claim the next schema version (`v6_embeddings` vs `v6_temporal_rollups`). Whichever lands second renumbers to v7 — isolated to a two-line constant change here by design. Happy to rebase whichever order you merge. - Upstream `main` has no `summary_nodes.suppressed_at` column today; the post-scan join enforces suppression when the column exists and is valid without it (hard-deleted summaries are always excluded; purge removes their vectors). - `conversation_ids` filters target `summary_nodes.session_id`; `since` uses `COALESCE(latest_at, created_at)` — matching DAG recency semantics. ### Schema-migration disclosure (adversarial-review follow-up) To be precise about the "no behavior change when disabled" claim: like every schema-backed feature in this repo, the migration is **unconditional** — opening an `lcm.db` with this build bumps `SCHEMA_VERSION` to the next value and creates the new tables even with the feature flag off. Those tables stay **empty** and nothing reads or writes them until the feature is enabled, so there is no *behavioral* change — but the on-disk schema does advance. One consequence worth stating: a user who tries this build and then rolls back to an older release will hit `refuse_schema_version_too_new` (the older build won't open a newer-schema DB). That is inherent to any additive schema step here, not specific to this PR; flagged explicitly so it's a conscious choice rather than a surprise.

title: [v1·temporal 4/4] rollup operator introspection + /lcm rollups
body:
## Summary

- operator-facing surfaces for temporal rollups (design #385 — **final train car, 4 of 4**, stacked

title: test: preflight noop-reset assertion fails on current main
body:
## Summary

The current `origin/main` fails one committed test in a clean, isolated runtime:

```text
tests/test_lcm_engine.py::TestEngineABC::test_positive_preflight_clears_prior_noop_status
```

The same failure appears on both current temporal and embeddings train tips, but reproduces unchanged on their exact base (`31675c6ed54abd747578b4da4b1589d81b18384a`), so it is base debt rather than a regression in either train.

## Reproduction

```bash
sandbox=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$sandbox/home" "$sandbox/hermes"
HOME="$sandbox/home" HERMES_HOME="$sandbox/hermes" NOISEGATE_DISABLE=1 \
  python3 -m pytest \
  tests/test_lcm_engine.py::TestEngineABC::test_positive_preflight_clears_prior_noop_status \
  -q -o addopts=
```

Observed:

```text
assert instance.should_compress_preflight(eligible_messages) is True
E  AssertionError: assert False is True
```

## Expected

Either the fixture should remain deterministically eligible under the supported tokenizer/runtime matrix, or the assertion should be made independent of tokenizer-sensitive character-to-token estimates.

## Scope

This issue only records the reproducible base failure so unrelated feature PRs do not inherit it. No fix is proposed here.

- **`docs/features-overview.md`** — every new feature family in one page: what it does, **why it exists, and the value it brings** (tables per family), a memory-pipeline diagram and an `lcm_grep` mode/degrade-path diagram (mermaid), a provider comparison covering the **Voyage free tier** (200M tokens on the voyage-4 family — verified against the [official pricing page](https://docs.voyageai.com/docs/pricing) on 2026-07-17, including the 200M-free reranker note) and the **fully-local options** (fastembed/Ollama), plus a pairing note for users who already run Voyage-backed code-search tools (one key serves both).
- **`docs/agent-config-profiles.md`** — copy-paste env profiles per agent shape: default chat, heavy tool-use coding agent, long-horizon personal agent, fully-local/air-gapped, cost-guarded cloud. Opens with a precise **"where configuration lives"** explainer (env-first precedence, the single supported `lcm:` YAML key, Hermes auxiliary-model inheritance — so operators know rollups go local when Hermes is local).
- **`README.md`** — the Documentation section becomes a complete map of `docs/`, and a short paragraph after Core capabilities introduces the three families with links.

Everything documented is **default-off**, and the docs say so prominently.

## Merge order

This PR is the caboose: it references features from all three trains and links `docs/embeddings-setup.md` (added in #395). Cleanest is to merge it **after the wave**; the README/docs hunks are additive, so cherry-picking early only costs two temporarily-dangling links.

## Try the whole wave in one checkout

To evaluate all 14 open PRs together without stacking them locally, an integration build (all trains + this docs PR's target state, on top of current `main`) is available on the contributor fork:

```bash
git clone -b release-test-2026-07-17 https://github.com/100yenadmin/hermes-lcm \
```

title: [v2 1/9] shared retrieval core (enabler)
body:
Part of the recall train (tracker: #375, "forever memory" follow-up to the #380–#395 wave). **Stacks on the wave** — cumulative from main like the prior trains; the slice diff for review is vs the wave head (`docs/embeddings-setup-guide` + subsequent fixes).

**This slice:** pure enabler refactor. Extracts the retrieval plumbing shared by `lcm_grep` (and the upcoming `lcm_recall`) into `retrieval_core.py`: RRF fusion, KNN invocation + node hydration, deadline helpers, snippet shaping. `tools.py` keeps thin wrappers, so every public contract, JSON shape, degrade path, and error string is byte-identical — full suite pass/fail set is unchanged vs base, verified by diffing sorted FAILED lists, not counts.

Zero behavior change; exists so two search surfaces never grow divergent ranking implementations.

title: [v2 2/9] content-aware raw-history chunk vectors
body:
Recall train slice 2 (stacks on the retrieval-core slice; tracker #375).

**This slice:** the verbatim-detail substrate — content-aware chunk embeddings of raw history, mirroring the embeddings train's discipline end-to-end: lazy marker-gated tables (`chunk_vectors_v1`, verified not trusted), identity-hashed profiles (task-scoped, so summary and chunk profiles coexist), dry-run-first leased backfill reusing the SAME lease/inflight/uncertain machinery (parameterized by corpus — the summary path is byte-identical, its 87 tests untouched), purge archiving, and the identical full|bounded|none KNN coverage contract.

- Chunking: turn-aligned (~600 tok, 1-sentence overlap on splits), policies `conversational` (user+assistant, default) | `heads` (+ tool-result head chunks & error-signature chunks) | `full`; every chunk maps to `lcm_expand(store_id, content_offset)` — lossless drill-down preserved.
- Providers: voyage (`voyage-context-4` mapping + contextualized-embed dispatcher w/ tested plain fallback), ollama, fastembed (local-first default posture unchanged).
- Real-data dry-runs (986MB / 347k-message imported archive): `conversational` = 92,990 chunks ≈ 29M tokens (≈$0 on voyage-context-3's free tier); `heads` = 261,406 chunks.
- +49 tests; full-suite failure set identical to base. Default-off: a stock install never creates the tables.

Known deferrals (follow-ups, noted in code): int8/Matryoshka storage (float32 today), live contextualized wire-shape exercise.

title: [v2 3/9] lcm_recall — cross-conversation memory search
body:
Recall train slice 3 — **the feature** (stacks on chunk-vectors; tracker #375).

**`lcm_recall`**: search the agent's entire memory across ALL conversations and all time by meaning. Three arms over the whole local DB — FTS (raw, all sessions) + summary KNN + chunk KNN (both unfiltered) — fused with RRF (chunk hits dedupe against FTS by store_id), optional `rerank-2.5-lite` stage (`LCM_RERANK_ENABLED`, default OFF pending our benchmark harness), then a soft prior: `final_score = rank × (1 + scope_bias·is_current_conversation) × recency(half-life 30d, floor 0.5)`. Scope/recency are ranking boosts, never filters. Honest degrade matrix mirrors `lcm_grep` (embeddings off → FTS arm with explicit reason). `lcm_grep` is untouched except one additive forward-pointer sentence; its param surface, degrade cells, and tests are byte-identical.

Design decision record: extending `lcm_grep`'s scope semantics was adversarially debated and rejected — it would reverse the reviewer-verified degrade cell (semantic × scope=all → raw-only) and jam soft-prior semantics into a hard-filter tool. A cold-agent reach-for test (8 scenarios) confirmed the dedicated tool wins exactly the "have I ever discussed…" class while grep keeps exact/known-range lookups; the description's not-for clauses come from that test.

One load-bearing find during acceptance: the summary arm inheriting `embedding_bounded_scan_rows=2000` made older archive vectors *structurally unreachable* (recency-bounded enumeration). Recall gets its own `recall_scan_rows` (default 25,000, deadline-guarded); regression-locked; grep unchanged.

Live proof on a real 347k-message / 3,872-summary imported archive, fresh session, real host: 8 hits, 7 cross-session over 5 distinct conversations, both canonical months-old memories recalled by a paraphrase query. 14 new tests; full-suite failure set identical to base.

title: [v2 4/9] LongMemEval retrieval-quality harness
body:
Recall-train companion (independent slice; stacks on the wave; tracker #375).

**LongMemEval retrieval harness** in the repo's benchmark culture: offline-first (explicit `fetch` step, HF dataset `xiaowu0162/longmemeval` PINNED at revision `2ec2a55`), retrieval metrics only (R@1/5/10, NDCG@10 against labeled evidence sessions — no LLM judge), deterministic stub / local-fastembed / voyage provider arms, aggregate-only exports.

Purpose: gate the recall train's quality knobs with OUR numbers instead of vendor claims — which arm wins (FTS / summary vectors / chunk vectors / hybrid RRF / +rerank), whether the reranker default earns its latency, and which chunk policy to recommend. First local numbers (25q, bge-small): FTS R@10 = 0.60; summary/hybrid vector arms R@10 = 0.84–0.88. README documents the MemDelta (arXiv:2606.29914) caveat: retrieval-benchmark verdicts flip with embedding/base-model choice, so we publish exact configurations.

16 tests; benchmarks/README section; full-suite failure set identical to base.

title: [v2 5/9] non-blocking FTS integrity scan on bind
body:
Operational fix (independent slice; stacks on the wave; tracker #375).

**Non-blocking FTS integrity scan on session bind.** Profiled on a 986MB/347k-row production-import DB: 100% of the cold-bind cost is the FTS5 `integrity-check` special command (the code's own comment cites #235); the existing 24h marker throttle helps, but every cache-miss (first bind + each expiry) blocked the bind synchronously — measured 10.3s warm-cache, minutes cold-cache.

Fix: on a throttled cache-miss, the cheap structural check stays synchronous (correctness gate), the deep scan moves to a daemon thread with its OWN connections (FTS5 integrity-check needs a writable handle — savepoint-rollback keeps it logically read-only; a separate brief connection stamps the marker). Corruption found in background is never auto-rebuilt: a persisted `fts_integrity_failed:<table>` flag surfaces through both doctor paths pointing at the explicit `/lcm doctor repair apply`. One scan per (db, table) with staleness unwedging; `LCM_FTS_INTEGRITY_BACKGROUND=false` restores the exact old behavior.

Measured: bind 10.257s → 1.721s on the same DB. +6 tests (dispatch/stamp, corruption→flag, kill-switch, single-flight, stale unwedge); sync-assertion tests pinned with the kill-switch, assertions unchanged.

title: [v2 6/9] interim schema-stamp remediation
body:
Operational fix (independent slice; stacks on the wave; tracker #375).

**Interim-build schema-stamp detection + guided remediation.** DBs touched by interim development builds carry `schema_version=6` with a v5 core and early-variant feature tables; current builds refused them with guidance ("upgrade the plugin") that is wrong for this case.

- `classify_version_mismatch()`: `interim_stamp` = core v5 shape matches EXACTLY and every extra table belongs to a known feature family — feature-table internal shape is deliberately not certified by the numeric stamp (each feature's marker-gated init owns that). Anything else stays `genuinely_newer` (refuses, safe direction).
- Refusal message now branches on the classification and names the remediation.
- `/lcm doctor repair schema-stamp [apply]`: dry-run default, backup-first, drops only family caches that FAIL their final-shape verifier (derived data — rollups rebuild from the DAG, vectors re-backfill; each drop reported with its rebuild hint), then resets the stamp. Refuses `genuinely_newer`.

title: [v2 7/9] proactive memory injection (default-off)
body:
Recall train slice 4 — the "it just has it" surface (stacks on #403; tracker #375).

**Proactive memory injection** (default-OFF: `LCM_PROACTIVE_RECALL_ENABLED`): at active-context assembly, LCM embeds the newest user message, runs the `lcm_recall` pipeline (k=6, scope_bias 0.3 — zero duplicated ranking/deadline logic), and injects one bounded `<relevant-memories>` block (≤ `LCM_PROACTIVE_RECALL_BUDGET_TOKENS`, default 500) with 1-3 labeled memory hints + `lcm_expand` handles. Pull-based memory tools can't deliver "remembers without being asked" — agents don't call memory tools when they don't know a memory exists; assembly-time injection is the mechanism the current top LongMemEval systems share.

Safety posture: block placed between the cache-stable summary prefix and the volatile fresh tail (summary-prefix caching intact); wrapped in an `_INJECTED_CONTEXT_TAGS` tag so `strip_injected_context_blocks` removes it before ingest — injected memory never re-enters the lossless store (tested); relevance floor + dedupe vs active context; any failure or timeout injects nothing and never blocks assembly; telemetry counters in `lcm_status`. `LCM_PROACTIVE_RECALL_PROVIDER` allows a cheap/local embedder for the injection path independent of the search provider.

One reviewer-worthy judgment call: `LCM_PROACTIVE_RECALL_MIN_SCORE` defaults to 0.01 on the RRF scale (single-arm RRF scores sit ~0.014-0.016); with rerank enabled scores become [0,1] relevance and the operator guide documents raising it (~0.3).

+14 fixture tests over the real recall pipeline; full-suite failure set byte-identical to base; ruff clean.

Externalization completing successfully, empty error logs

```
hermes_plugins.hermes_lcm.externalize: Large payload externalization skipped (non-blocking) [Errno 13] Permission denied: 'C:\\Users\\<username>\\AppData\\Local\\hermes\\lcm-large-outputs'
```

```yaml
LCM_LARGE_OUTPUT_EXTERNALIZATION_ENABLED=true

context:
  engine: lcm
plugins:
  enabled:
    - hermes-lcm
```

```text
hermes_plugins.hermes_lcm.externalize: Large payload externalization skipped (non-blocking) [Errno 13] Permission denied: 'C:\\Users\\jakub\\AppData\\Local\\hermes\\lcm-large-outputs'

Large payload externalization skipped (non-blocking): [Errno 13] Permission denied: 'C:\\Users\\jakub\\AppData\\Local\\hermes\\plugins\\hermes-lcm\\scripts\\tests\\sandbox\\lifecycle_soak_and_profile_rebinds\\primary-home\\lcm-large-outputs'

```

- ✅ Directory exists at target path
- ✅ User has FullControl permissions on directory
- ✅ Directory is empty (no files inside)

```powershell
Test-Path 'C:\Users\jakub\AppData\Local\hermes\lcm-large-outputs'  # True
```

title: feat: context_threshold_tokens for absolute token-count threshold
body:
## Problem

`context_threshold` in the `lcm:` config section is always treated as a **fraction** of the model context window:

```python
context_threshold_tokens = int(effective_context_length * self.context_threshold)
```

This makes compression triggering depend on whatever context length the current model reports. If the model or provider changes (e.g. 64k → 128k context), the same `0.4` fires at very different absolute token counts. Users who want a **fixed** trigger threshold (e.g. "always compress at 20k tokens regardless of model") have no way to express that.

## Request

Add a new config key `context_threshold_tokens` under `lcm:` that accepts an **absolute integer token count**, bypassing the `effective_context_length * threshold_percent` formula entirely.

### Semantics

- When `context_threshold_tokens` is **set** (positive int): use this absolute value directly as `threshold_tokens`. `context_threshold` (fraction) is ignored.
- When `context_threshold_tokens` is **unset** (default, 0): fall back to existing behaviour (`context_threshold * context_length`).

### Example

```yaml
lcm:
  context_threshold: 0.4           # used when context_threshold_tokens is 0 (default)
  context_threshold_tokens: 20000  # overrides fraction — always compress at ~20k tokens
```

### Why

- Users running mixed provider/model setups get consistent compression behaviour.
- Avoids subtle regressions when a model update changes the reported context window.
- Clear intent in config: "compress at N tokens" vs "compress at N% of model window".

title: codex_gpt_long_context preset should include a token-bounded fresh tail
body:
## Summary

I hit a compaction deadlock while using the exact runtime values from the `codex_gpt_long_context` preset:

```text
LCM_CONTEXT_THRESHOLD=0.75
LCM_FRESH_TAIL_COUNT=24
LCM_LEAF_CHUNK_TOKENS=8000
```

The preset does not currently set `LCM_FRESH_TAIL_MAX_TOKENS`. In a long-running, tool-heavy Telegram session, the active transcript had only 22 messages, but one synthetic preserved-objective message had grown to about 1.35 MB and contained 131 nested `[Session Arc Summary ...]` markers.

Because 22 messages was below `LCM_FRESH_TAIL_COUNT=24`, the entire active transcript was protected. LCM attempted compression three times and each attempt was a no-op:

```text
LCM compression no-op: no eligible raw backlog outside fresh tail
```

The request remained around 397K tokens against a 372K effective model context window and ended with:

```text
Context length exceeded: max compression attempts (3) reached.
```

## Workaround and validation

I added:

```text
LCM_FRESH_TAIL_MAX_TOKENS=64000
```

After restarting, LCM reduced the same session from approximately 368,921 tokens to 82,665 tokens. I then ran a tool-heavy benchmark:

1. Asked the agent to inspect gateway status using tools and summarize it.
2. Followed up by asking what I had requested and what it found.

The first turn completed across four successful model calls with multiple tool calls, and the follow-up accurately recalled the exchange. The oversized preserved-objective scaffold was no longer active.

## Why this appears to be a preset gap

PR #381 correctly makes the token cap opt-in and default-off for backward compatibility. However, the PR rationale also notes that a count-only tail makes compaction effectiveness depend on message-size luck. That is exactly what happened here.

The model-family preset is the place where a safe token bound can be enabled without changing default behavior for users who do not select the preset.

## Suggested direction

Please consider:

- adding `fresh_tail_max_tokens` to the preset-managed fields;
- benchmarking an appropriate value for `codex_gpt_long_context`;
- including the resulting value in the preset's `runtime_env`;
- adding a regression fixture where the active transcript is below the message-count limit but above the token limit because of one oversized recent or synthetic message.

The validated 64K value above is useful field evidence, but I am not assuming it is universally correct. A context-relative cap or another benchmark-backed fixed value may be better.

title: feat: add bounded answer-ready evidence detail to lcm_recall
body:
# feat: add bounded answer-ready evidence detail to `lcm_recall`

Intended tracker: `stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm` after the V1/V2/V3 merge surface is ready for the proposal.

Dependency note: upstream `main` is still receiving the V1/V2/V3 train. This proposal is mapped to the company integration snapshot `34490c80…` where `lcm_recall`, summary/chunk vector profiles, weighted RRF, temporal rollups, and exact recovery already coexist. It should be reviewed against that integrated shape (or its eventual upstream equivalent), not reimplemented against an earlier partial merge.

## Problem

At the company integration snapshot `34490c80a13bd4014e91a5ed8abd68f8db754be2`, `lcm_recall` successfully identifies relevant raw messages, summaries, and chunks across sessions. Its default response remains search-shaped: each hit contains a compact snippet and an expansion hint. A host answering a multi-evidence question must either answer from thin snippets or perform an unstructured sequence of `lcm_expand` / `lcm_load_session` calls.

This creates a gap between retrieval relevance and answer-ready evidence completeness:

- several top-ranked hits can come from one session while independently required sessions are omitted;
- the decisive statement may be outside the 300-character snippet even when the correct `store_id` or `node_id` was retrieved;
- a harness or host integration is tempted to open the LCM database directly, bypassing the production tool contract;
- payload growth is hard to reason about unless expansion, diversity, and truncation policies are first-class provenance.

The gap is general and user-facing: “the system found the right memory but still could not answer from the returned evidence.”

## User or operator impact

- Multi-session and temporal questions unnecessarily abstain despite high retrieval recall.
- Hosts implement product-specific follow-up logic or direct store access.
- Returning more hits can increase context while still repeating the same session.
- Operators cannot distinguish ranking failure, omitted evidence, expansion failure, or response truncation from the response itself.

## Current architecture

`tools.py::lcm_recall` currently:

1. runs a full-text message arm;
2. runs summary and chunk KNN arms using the task-scoped profiles in `vector_store.py`;
3. fuses ranks through `retrieval_core.py::rrf_fuse`;
4. applies current-conversation and recency priors;
5. optionally reorders a bounded window with the configured reranker;
6. serializes bounded snippets with stable `store_id` / `node_id` expansion handles.

`MessageStore.get_batch` and `SummaryDAG.get_node` already provide exact, local reads after ranking. Chunk hits already carry the character span needed to center an evidence window. No additional semantic search is necessary to hydrate a selected exact reference.

## Proposed direction

Add an opt-in `detail` argument:

```json
{
  "query": "...",
  "include": "all",
  "detail": "answer_ready",
  "limit": 25
}
```

Contract:

- `detail="snippets"` remains the default and preserves existing serialized behavior.
- `detail="answer_ready"` runs only after the existing rank/fusion/rerank sequence.
- Select hits in stable rank order with no more than five hits per `session_id`.
- Treat missing session identities independently; do not collapse all unknown identities into one synthetic session.
- Hydrate at most the first eight selected exact references.
- For a message/chunk hit, batch-read by `store_id` and return a window centered on the selected chunk span.
- For a summary hit, read the exact `node_id` and return a bounded summary window.
- Each hydrated content window is at most 2,400 characters.
- Remaining selected hits keep the compact 300-character snippet shape.
- The complete JSON response is at most 64,000 characters and drops only whole trailing hits when enforcing the cap.
- Echo the selected policy and observed counts under response provenance, including expanded-hit count, per-session limit, per-hit cap, response cap, query truncation, and response truncation.
- Hydration performs no additional embedding, FTS, rerank, or provider call.

## Invariants

- Ranking is complete before diversity or hydration; expansion cannot influence relevance scores.
- Exact refs are the sole source of hydrated content.
- `store_id`, `node_id`, session, role, timestamp, source, chunk span, and score provenance survive hydration.
- The default path remains backwards-compatible.
- No unbounded transcript is returned.
- This feature claims richer product evidence only; it does not claim answer accuracy.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

### Always return full turns

Rejected because it changes default payload size, penalizes simple lookups, and makes worst-case context growth difficult to bound.

### Have the host call `lcm_expand` repeatedly

Still useful for interactive drill-down, but inefficient for the common “hydrate these already-selected refs” path and encourages N-round-trip logic in every host.

### Add a second semantic query for every result

Rejected because the ranker has already selected exact refs. Another search adds cost and variance without guaranteeing evidence continuity.

### Implement expansion only in the benchmark bridge

Useful as an agentic experiment but cannot support a Hermes-LCM product claim. The production tool response must own the behavior.

## Backward compatibility

- New field is optional.
- Default stays `snippets`.
- Existing arguments, ranking, hit identity, and expansion hints remain unchanged.
- No database migration.
- No new dependency or provider call.
- Hosts that ignore new fields continue to work.

## Validation and evidence

Prototype: company isolated worktree head `dc855191f231d7bb3fe3d2475337d0584b4fbb22`, based on integrated snapshot `34490c80…`.

Required focused tests:

- implicit and explicit `snippets` outputs remain identical;
- invalid detail value fails clearly;
- stable per-session selection, including missing session identities;
- exact chunk-span-centered message hydration;
- exact summary-node hydration;
- only the first eight selected refs expand;
- every content window respects 2,400 characters;
- complete response respects 64,000 characters and records truncation;
- query truncation is explicit;
- hydration uses exact batch reads and does not invoke another search;
- role/source/session/date/provenance survive expansion.

Preliminary paired product-search evidence on the frozen 94 failures:

- answer-session R@25: 0.9326 to 0.9719;
- all required answer sessions represented: 79/94 to 85/94;
- average unique sessions: 7.95 to 9.60;
- average returned content: 14,718 to 10,650 characters;
- mean search latency: 1,505 ms to 1,795 ms.

These are retrieval/evidence results only. The corresponding end-to-end run is not a valid headline because an independent answer-stage protocol defect was later found.

## Acceptance criteria

- Focused product tests pass.
- Default output compatibility is demonstrated.
- Search-only paired A/B preserves or improves answer-session R@25 and all-required-session coverage.
- Average answer context stays within the 7,500-token benchmark budget.
- No response exceeds its declared cap.
- Actual expansion/diversity/truncation policy is persisted through the consuming bridge or host provenance.
- No claim of product answer-quality lift is made without a valid end-to-end held-out evaluation.

## Implementation status

Prototype exists. No upstream PR is opened by this issue.

## Existing issue relationship

- Complements semantic/hybrid retrieval design #386; it operates after ranking and is provider-independent.
- Complements natural-time retrieval #385; it does not create rollups or interpret temporal validity.
- Reuses the exact recovery contracts delivered by the cross-session recall and session-load work.

title: feat: Add native openai embedding provider option
body:
### Problem

With the rollout of the vector store and the addition of the Ollama provider, the infrastructure for handling external embedding HTTP payloads is already in place. It would be a massive workflow improvement to add an official openai provider option to target standard, openai-compatible local servers (such as llama.cpp server instances running specialized local embedding models).






### User or operator impact

This is resource saving for local inference users who also have local embedding models already deployed on local workstation or server. For example if someone is already running llama.cpp or vllm hosting an embedding model natively on a specific port (e.g. localhost:8081/v1/embeddings) for RAG or any other vector database they could use that instead of needing a completely separate instance of Ollama or background python environments just for embedding tasks for hermes_lcm.


Because hermes-lcm elegantly handles provider switching and vector store backfilling (/lcm embed backfill), allowing the plugin to natively communicate with the industry-standard openaI specification opens up immediate compatibility for a vast array of high-performance local inference backends.

### Proposed direction

Since the networking code and polling loops are already written to handle Ollama's HTTP layer, bridging to the OpenAI spec is architectural low-hanging fruit:

It simply requires routing payloads to the conventional /v1/embeddings endpoint instead of /api/embeddings.

Adjusting the POST body map from Ollama's "prompt" string key to the standard openai "input" string/array key.

### Alternatives and tradeoffs

Running all of the other options does not take advantage of resources available for cases where local openai embedding is available, while requiring maintenance and compute/memory for another embedding model of lower quality that what can be running via local openai instance (e.g. one of the Qwen3 embedding models), or even cloud OpenAI embedder.

### Backward compatibility

There is no compatibility issue as it is specifically provided within hermes_lcm backfill function.

### Validation or evidence

Rough config schema for this option:

export LCM_EMBEDDINGS_ENABLED=true
export LCM_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=openai
export LCM_EMBEDDING_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8081/v1
export LCM_EMBEDDING_MODEL=your-chosen-embedding-model

### Implementation status

Idea only

### Additional notes

While not a developer I'm happy to help with the testing.

title: Port Lossless Claw bundled recall skill and active recall policy
body:
## Problem

Hermes-LCM was inspired by and ported from Lossless Claw, but the port currently omits two model-facing layers that canonical Lossless Claw ships:

1. the bundled skills/lossless-claw skill and its progressive-disclosure recall-tool guidance;
2. the active LOSSLESS_RECALL_POLICY_PROMPT injected on every prompt build.

Hermes-LCM currently relies on tool schemas, README documentation, and a short compaction-time note. That leaves no normally discoverable Hermes skill and no active plugin-owned policy teaching evidence precedence, conflict verification, bounded query construction, scope selection, and the full recall escalation path.

## Relationship to #38 / #47

#38 was valid and PR #47 improved the schemas and README to distinguish current-session LCM tools from session_search. This issue is the remaining port-parity layer, not a request to undo that work:

- #47 changed README.md, schemas.py, and a schema test;
- it did not bundle/register/install a skill;
- it did not add an active plugin-owned recall policy.

## Canonical source

Verified against Martian-Engineering/lossless-claw@8ead658e536e99444586bbf78ceedcc0b6f16acf:

- skills/lossless-claw/SKILL.md
- skills/lossless-claw/references/recall-tools.md
- docs/agent-tools.md
- src/plugin/index.ts LOSSLESS_RECALL_POLICY_PROMPT
- openclaw.plugin.json skills declaration

## Proposed plugin-local approach

- Add a Hermes-specific bundled skill with references adapted to current Hermes-LCM tools and arguments.
- Register it through Hermes plugin skill registration where supported.
- Update scripts/install.sh so the same skill is discoverable in the active global/profile Hermes skills directory; plugin skill registration alone is explicit-only in current Hermes Agent.
- Add one concise static recall policy through the existing pre_llm_call plugin hook only while LCM is the active context engine. This uses ephemeral user-context injection and preserves the system-prompt cache prefix.
- Keep schemas as the source of exact argument truth, with tests ensuring skill/policy tool names remain aligned.
- Degrade gracefully on older hosts without skill or hook registration.

Suggested routing:

- current compacted conversation: lcm_grep -> lcm_describe -> lcm_expand_query;
- cross-conversation semantic recall: lcm_recall -> lcm_load_session or exact-handle lcm_expand;
- recent/time-bounded recall: lcm_recent or time-bounded lcm_grep;
- use lcm_expand as a known-handle drill-down, not broad first-step discovery.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Bundled skill and references contain no stale OpenClaw-only arguments or behavior.
- [ ] Install is profile-aware, idempotent, and refuses conflicting plugin/skill paths before partial installation.
- [ ] Active policy is deterministic and injected only for active LCM sessions.
- [ ] Inactive/disabled/older-host behavior remains unchanged and nonfatal.
- [ ] Focused tests cover registration, discovery, hook gating, byte stability, tool-name alignment, and generic host-equivalent dispatch.
- [ ] README/operator/retrieval documentation explains the skill and policy.
- [ ] No Hermes Agent core change is required.

## Non-goals

No new memory service, retrieval controller, provider call, database, or forced tool call on every turn. This issue is instruction/distribution parity and bounded tool-use correctness.

title: fix: sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked during context compression when vector store is active
body: ### Expected behavior Compaction events should trigger at the defined threshold and be successfully indexed into the vector database without interfering with the main conversation thread's ability to write to lcm.db. ### Actual behavior When hermes-lcm has vector embeddings enabled, concurrent background database reads/writes from the embedding/indexing pipeline trigger a thread deadlock with the main conversation engine during compaction events. When the active context hits the threshold and calls agent._compress_context(), the main thread attempts to write a node to the DAG database via self._dag.add_node(node). If the background embedding thread is concurrently interacting with lcm.db, the transaction times out, crashing the entire conversation step with an OperationalError. Error screenshot: ### Minimal reproduction 1. Run longer session in Hermes with hermes_lcm and vector index enabled 2. Watch logs live and see errors pop up on 2-3rd compaction 3. At one of subsequent compactions Hermes stops with "database locked" error. ### Version and branch hermes-lcm (with vector features enabled) 0.19.0; plugin_git_commit: ad3376607196039744ab7f03d5d1bf282a8dec75 ### Environment Windows, Hermes Agent v0.18.2 (2026.7.7.2) · upstream 3d7e1c5f), local OpenAI provider ### Relevant config ```yaml LCM_ENABLE_SLASH_COMMAND=1 LCM_CONTEXT_THRESHOLD=0.6 LCM_FRESH_TAIL_COUNT=10 LCM_LEAF_CHUNK_TOKENS=4000 LCM_DYNAMIC_LEAF_CHUNK_ENABLED=true LCM_LARGE_OUTPUT_EXTERNALIZATION_ENABLED=false LCM_SUMMARY_TIMEOUT_MS=2000000 LCM_EXPANSION_TIMEOUT_MS=1000000 LCM_SUMMARY_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_FAILURE_THRESHOLD=3 LCM_EMBEDDINGS_ENABLED=true LCM_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=fastembed LCM_EMBEDDING_MODEL=BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 LCM_PROACTIVE_RECALL_ENABLED=true LCM_TEMPORAL_ROLLUPS_ENABLED=true ``` ### Logs, traceback, or failing test ```text File "...\agent\conversation_compression.py", line 1060, in compress_context compressed = compress_fn(messages, **compress_kwargs) File "...\plugins\hermes-lcm\compaction.py", line 771, in compress self._dag.add_node(node) File "...\plugins\hermes-lcm\dag.py", line 249, in add_node cur = self._conn.execute( sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked ``` ### Validation attempted According to limited testing so far it is partially fixed by: sqlite3 lcm.db "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;" But some turns get stuck when run from Hermes Desktop with red 'database locked' warning and silent logs.

title: feat: add LCM_ABSOLUTE_THRESHOLD_TOKENS for absolute compaction threshold
body:
## Summary
- Add `LCM_ABSOLUTE_THRESHOLD_TOKENS` env var. When `> 0`, pin `threshold_tokens` to that absolute prompt-token count after ratio math in `_set_context_length()`.
- Suppress Codex GPT-5.5 ratio auto-raise while the absolute override is active so the setpoint cannot climb back.
- Document the knob in `README.md` and `docs/operator-guide.md` as a cross-model **context-health** control (common coding default: `130000`).
- Add focused unit tests for cross-window pinning, ratio fallback, invalid env, and auto-raise suppression.

## Why
LCM's compaction trigger is currently ratio-only:

```text
threshold_tokens = context_threshold × context_length
```

Switching models silently moves the compaction point even when the task and quality target have not changed:

| Model window | Ratio 0.35 | Ratio 0.50 |
|---|---:|---:|
| 262K | ~91K | ~131K |
| 500K | ~175K | ~250K |
| 1M | ~350K | ~500K |

For coding agents this is the wrong coupling. Compaction should keep the **working context inside a healthy band**, not maximize window utilization:

1. **Recall stays high** — the model can still find the right file, API, constraint, and prior decision.
2. **Context corruption stays low** — long multi-file sessions accumulate noise; past a point more tokens reduce reasoning quality ("lost in the middle", instruction dilution, contradictory mid-session state).
3. **Coding quality stays stable across models** — the same repo/task should get comparable context hygiene on a 262K or 500K/1M backend.

~130K active tokens is a strong default **context-health setpoint for highest-quality programming effect**: enough room for system prompt, skills, multi-file diffs, tool results, and a useful fresh tail; early enough that LCM can still summarize while session structure is recoverable; independent of which model is selected.

Existing knobs are insufficient:
- `LCM_CONTEXT_THRESHOLD` drifts with `context_length`.
- `LCM_MAX_ASSEMBLY_TOKENS` / `LCM_RESERVE_TOKENS_FLOOR` limit assembly cap, not the compaction trigger.

## Proposed behavior
```python
# end of _set_context_length(), after ratio-derived threshold_tokens
_abs = int(os.environ.get("LCM_ABSOLUTE_THRESHOLD_TOKENS", "0") or 0)
if _abs > 0:
    self.threshold_tokens = _abs
    self._config.codex_gpt55_autoraise_enabled = False
```

- Unset / `0` → identical to today (ratio-based).
- No API or config-schema break; follows existing `LCM_*` env pattern.

## Validation
- [x] Focused validation: `pytest tests/test_absolute_threshold.py -q` → `4 passed`
- [x] Related command surface: `pytest tests/test_absolute_threshold.py tests/test_lcm_command.py -q` → `81 passed`
- [x] `git diff --check` clean on committed files
- [ ] Default full suite (optional CI): `pytest -q`
- [ ] Release script (optional CI): `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going ...`

## Test plan
- [x] `LCM_ABSOLUTE_THRESHOLD_TOKENS=130000` → `threshold_tokens == 130000` for windows 262K / 500K / 1M
- [x] unset env → ratio behavior unchanged
- [x] absolute set on Codex GPT-5.5 route → auto-raise disabled, absolute still wins
- [x] invalid env value → falls back to ratio
- [ ] CI green on this PR

## Alternatives considered
1. Companion plugin monkey-patch via `resolve_active_lcm_engine()` — works locally, not discoverable.
2. Config-file key — viable later; env matches other operational LCM knobs for v1.
3. Per-model threshold map — over-engineered for "one health setpoint across models".
4. Only lowering the global ratio — still model-dependent (1M × 0.25 ≈ 250K, already past the coding-health band).

title: feat: add grounded answer-ready recall foundation
body:
## Summary

- Add opt-in `lcm_recall(detail="answer_ready")` output that hydrates bounded exact-source windows for raw-message hits. Omitted `detail` and explicit `detail="snippets"` retain the existing response bytes.
- Add immutable exact references binding session, message, source span, and content digest. References fail closed after deletion, source drift, or content mismatch.
- Keep observation time, event occurrence time, write time, and explicit question/as-of time separate in storage and tool output.
- Add dependency-free `lcm_compute` operations for grounded date, count, compatible-unit arithmetic, difference, and ordering questions. Ambiguous, incomplete, stale, or ungrounded input returns evidence-only fallback instead of a computed claim.

## Why

The ordinary recall path can retrieve useful evidence, but it does not currently offer a bounded, immutable grounding contract for deterministic downstream reasoning. This change adds that contract as an explicit opt-in while preserving the existing default recall API and bytes.

## Compatibility and safety

- Default `lcm_recall` output has a byte-for-byte regression test.
- Invalid detail modes and stale, deleted, or content-mismatched references fail closed.
- Relative dates are anchored only to persisted observation time. Caller-supplied anchors must match, and unavailable observation time remains `null` rather than becoming an invented epoch.
- Host-supplied candidate answers are accepted only when they exactly equal the canonical deterministic answer, preventing extra narrative claims from entering a verified result.
- Database migration is additive: nullable observation-time columns are added, legacy rows keep their write timestamp, and no observation time is invented.
- Synthetic tests cover legacy migration, backup/restore, source deletion and invalidation, profile rebinding, rotation, and schema-stamp remediation without using a live database.
- Secret-redacted content cannot be reconstructed through exact references.

## Review guide

1. `tools.py` and `schemas.py`: opt-in recall contract and unchanged default response path.
2. `exact_refs.py`: immutable source binding and fail-closed validation.
3. `occurrence_time.py` plus storage changes: separation of observed, occurred, ingested, and question/as-of time.
4. `reasoning.py`: dependency-free grounded computation and ambiguity fallback.
5. `tests/test_v1_upstream_foundation.py`: compatibility, provenance, migration, invalidation, secret-safety, and computation contracts.

## Validation

title: feat: configurable embedding backfill batch size (LCM_EMBEDDING_BACKFILL_BATCH_SIZE)
body:
## Problem

`_EMBEDDING_BACKFILL_BATCH_SIZE` is hardcoded to `32` in `command.py`. This value is sent as a single `input` array to the embedding provider in one HTTP request. When using the Ollama provider with `nomic-embed-text` (which has `num_ctx: 8192`), the Ollama `/api/embed` endpoint concatenates all items in the `input` array into a single context window. A batch of 32 summaries (~38k tokens combined) exceeds the 8192-token context limit, causing an HTTP 400 error:

```
{"error":"the input length exceeds the context length"}
```

This results in all batched summaries being marked as `uncertain` with `provider_error:Ollama embedding request failed (400)`, and the entire backfill fails with `embedded: 0`.

## User or operator impact

Any operator using the Ollama embedding provider with a model that has a limited context window (e.g. `nomic-embed-text` at 8192 tokens, `bge-small-en` at 512 tokens) will hit this failure. The backfill is unusable without patching the source code. There is currently no environment variable or configuration option to adjust the batch size.

The Voyage and fastembed providers handle this differently (Voyage batches by token budget with an item cap; fastembed runs in-process), so the hardcoded `32` is only safe for providers that can accept arbitrary batch token counts — which Ollama cannot.

## Proposed direction

Make `_EMBEDDING_BACKFILL_BATCH_SIZE` configurable via an environment variable:

```python
_EMBEDDING_BACKFILL_BATCH_SIZE = int(os.environ.get("LCM_EMBEDDING_BACKFILL_BATCH_SIZE", "32"))
```

This preserves the default of `32` (no behavior change for existing users) while allowing operators with context-limited embedding models to reduce the batch size. With `LCM_EMBEDDING_BACKFILL_BATCH_SIZE=1`, each summary is embedded individually, staying well within any model context limit.

### Alternatives and tradeoffs

- **A. Token-budget-aware batching** (more robust): Instead of a fixed item count, estimate the combined token count of the batch and split so each request stays under the provider model context limit. This is what Voyage already does with `_VOYAGE_MAX_BATCH_TOKENS`. However, this requires knowing the model context limit per provider, which adds complexity.
- **B. `truncate: true` for Ollama**: Changing `truncate` from `false` to `true` in the Ollama request would avoid the 400 but silently truncate input, producing misleading embeddings. The current `truncate: false` behavior is correct — failing loudly is better than silently truncating.
- **C. Env var override only** (this proposal): Simplest fix. Operators who know their model limits can set the batch size. Combines well with the existing `LCM_EMBEDDING_BACKFILL_TIMEOUT_S` and `LCM_EMBEDDING_BACKFILL_BUDGET_S` env vars that already control backfill behavior.

Option C is the minimal viable fix. Option A is the ideal long-term solution but can be a follow-up.

## Reproduction

1. Configure Ollama provider: `LCM_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=ollama`, `LCM_EMBEDDING_MODEL=nomic-embed-text`
2. Run `/lcm embed warmup` (succeeds — single short text)
3. Run `/lcm embed backfill --apply` with 24+ pending summaries
4. All fail with `provider_error:Ollama embedding request failed (400)`
5. With batch size reduced to 1 (via local patch), the same backfill succeeds

## Environment

- Plugin: hermes-lcm v0.19.0
- Provider: Ollama
- Model: nomic-embed-text (8192 token context)

---

*This issue was drafted by an AI assistant (GLaDOS, Hermes Agent) at the direction of a human operator. No environment-specific details, credentials, or private infrastructure information are disclosed in this report.*

title: fix: release SQLite TEMP staging snapshots before compaction writes
body:
## Summary
- Wrap rc1 temporal-rollup and recent-fallback TEMP staging in transaction-preserving SQLite savepoints.
- Release helper-created read snapshots before later DAG writes while preserving caller-owned outer transactions.
- Mark escaped compaction failures as terminal `error` instead of leaving status stuck on `running`.

## Why
`v0.20.0-rc1` introduced TEMP-table staging on the shared DAG connection for temporal rollups and recent fallback. Those helper writes could leave an implicit transaction open. If another connection committed afterwards, the next DAG publication on the stale snapshot could fail with `SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT`, surfaced by Python as `sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked`, and abort the conversation compression turn.

This was reproduced from the exact rc1 base (`ad337660`) and then observed on a real rc1 Hermes runtime. After loading this exact patch and restarting the gateway, the affected older conversations became usable again and the direct stale-snapshot regression stayed green.

This is intended as a focused candidate for rc2. It fixes one concrete rc1 regression; it is not a broad cross-process locking redesign.

Refs #421

## Validation
- [x] Regression tests confirmed the rc1 staging-snapshot failure before the fix.
- [x] Affected surface: `pytest -q tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_lcm_recent.py tests/test_rollup_builder.py` -> `847 passed`
- [x] Full suite: `pytest -q` -> `2297 passed, 12 xfailed`

title: fix(backfill): skip empty summaries

Skip null, empty, and Unicode-whitespace-only leaf summaries during embedding backfill discovery.

## Why

This came from an rc1 production finding. A summary-only Voyage backfill admitted a blank leaf summary into a mixed provider batch. Voyage rejected the batch with HTTP 400, so valid neighboring summaries were marked failed alongside the blank row.
