title: feat: expose a provider-neutral management connector for opt-in Teams mode
body:
## Problem

An opt-in Hermes Teams mode needs an authenticated management plane that can provision and operate tenants, principals, grants, shared collections, review scopes, migration, and rollback without exposing administrative authority as model-visible tools or hard-coding one vendor dashboard into Hermes-LCM.

The product decision is explicit: Teams ships inside the canonical Hermes-LCM repository/distribution as an optional mode/module. External systems are replaceable connector clients.

## Proposed direction

Add a provider-neutral management connector contract to the in-repository Teams module.

The trusted connector boundary accepts canonical authenticated management requests and maps them to Teams lifecycle operations. Vendor-specific identity, database, billing, and UI concepts stay in connector adapters.

Supported capability families:

```text
teams.status / teams.doctor
teams.enable / teams.disable / teams.preflight
principals.provision / suspend / delete
memberships.grant / revoke / inspect
collections.create / retire / inspect
shared_memory.seed_import
review_scope.open / close / revoke
audit.query / export
migration.plan / apply / verify / rollback
backup.plan / verify / restore
```

Each operation has an explicit capability, request ID/idempotency key, actor/audience, target tenant/deployment, validation result, audit record, and typed failure taxonomy.

## Security and lifecycle contract

- Authenticate the external control plane independently of the model/session.
- Resolve deployment/tenant identity from trusted host configuration; callers never select filesystem/database paths.
- Administrative operations are absent from ordinary model-visible tool schemas.
- Missing/stale/revoked authority fails closed with no ambient-profile fallback.
- Grant/revoke and review-scope operations advance policy/membership/revocation revisions consumed by `AccessContextV1`.
- Enable is explicit and versioned; package upgrade never silently enables Teams.
- Disable stops Teams routing and connector authority while preserving auditable reversible state.
- Standard single-user mode creates no Teams catalog/policy/storage side effects.
- Equivalent local/operator recovery remains possible if the external connector is unavailable.

## First reference connector

Implement ElectricSheep Dashboard + Supabase as the first external client/adapter:

- map authenticated ElectricSheep tenant/user/membership records to canonical Teams requests;
- do not make Hermes-LCM import or depend on ElectricSheep/Supabase internals;
- keep credentials and administrative responses outside model-visible context;
- test replay, retry, stale membership, partial failure, and connector unavailability.

This reference connector proves replaceability; it is not the authority model.

## Dependencies

- Architecture/milestone tracker: #481
- Authority contract: #482
- Neutral fail-closed authorization seam: #473
- In-repository Teams policy adapter: #483
- Pilot acceptance: #498
- Hermes Agent host context carrier: NousResearch/hermes-agent#78802
- Routed-profile isolation prerequisite: NousResearch/hermes-agent#68559 / PR NousResearch/hermes-agent#78030

## Acceptance criteria

- A fake connector and the ElectricSheep/Supabase connector pass the same conformance suite.
- Provision/grant/revoke/status/disable operations are authenticated, idempotent, audited, and non-model-visible.
- Revocation affects the next Teams memory operation through updated context revisions.
- Duplicate request ID with same digest produces one effect; same ID with different digest is a conflict.
- Connector loss does not prevent bounded local doctor/disable/rollback recovery.
- Standard mode remains unchanged before enable and after a verified disable/rollback.
- No vendor-specific identity or storage schema leaks into the core Teams policy interface.

## Non-goals

- Billing or subscription enforcement inside Hermes-LCM.
- A mandatory ElectricSheep control plane.
- General cross-company federation.
- Employee-facing shared-memory publication UI in the first security/operations pilot.

## Implementation status

Issue/contract handoff ready; implementation not started.

title: test: accept the opt-in LCM Teams MVP with two principals
body:
## Problem

Hermes Teams should not be called complete when only architecture, profile isolation, or prerequisite hardening exists. The MVP needs one production-shaped acceptance lane proving that two principals, one opt-in Teams deployment, the external management connector, and all fail-closed boundaries work together.

This is the goal-bearing handoff gate for the first security/operations pilot. It is not a claim that full collaboration, cross-company federation, or employee-facing publication UI is complete.

## Pilot shape

- one isolated tenant deployment;
- two employee principals plus one operator/admin principal;
- one Hermes profile per employee;
- private employee collections;
- one operator-seeded shared collection;
- read-only bounded federation;
- ElectricSheep Dashboard/Supabase reference connector;
- standard single-user mode verified before enable and after disable/rollback.

## Required acceptance matrix

### Setup and compatibility

- Standard Hermes-LCM setup creates no Teams policy/catalog/storage side effects.
- Explicit preflight and enable create/adopt versioned Teams state without silently rewriting the legacy database.
- Package upgrade does not silently enable Teams.
- Disable and rollback are auditable and reversible.

### Identity and isolation

- Principal A can read/write A-private memory and cannot enumerate B-private memory.
- Principal B receives the symmetric guarantee.
- Both can read only explicitly authorized shared collections.
- Session, conversation, profile, collection, cursor, and reference IDs are not accepted as authority.
- Missing/malformed/stale context denies before existence/count/ranking/hydration disclosure.

### Delegation, cron, and callbacks

- A delegated subagent receives a strict subset of parent authority.
- Profile-owned cron uses the correct tenant/principal/profile scope.
- Post-turn/background callbacks cannot retain authority after revocation or ownership-generation change.
- Concurrent A/B turns do not exchange context, cache state, process visibility, credentials, CWD, or terminal backend.

### Revocation and administration

- Membership/grant revocation blocks the next operation.
- Stale leases, references, cursors, and review handles fail closed.
- Admin review is explicit-target, time-bounded, read-only, visibly scoped, and audited.
- Admin review does not imply export, edit, delete, publish, or membership authority.

### Connector and operations

- ElectricSheep/Supabase connector passes the provider-neutral conformance suite.
- Duplicate/retried management operations are idempotent; conflicting reuse is rejected.
- Connector unavailability leaves local doctor/disable/rollback recovery available.
- Audit records actor, target, operation, policy revision, result class, and request ID without plaintext memory content.

### Data lifecycle

- Operator seed/import is authorized, idempotent, provenance-preserving, and unavailable as a model tool.
- Migration uses backup/archive-first parity checks and never deletes the original database automatically.
- Export/delete/retention behavior is explicit per collection class.
- Abrupt failure at defined enable/import/disable boundaries leaves a diagnosable resumable or rolled-back state.

### Non-enumeration and hostile tests

- Guessed/replayed store, node, session, collection, reference, cursor, and review-handle identifiers do not disclose cross-principal existence.
- Authorization precedes database open and result disclosure in every retrieval arm.
- Model-authored tool arguments cannot widen tenant/principal/grant scope or invoke management capabilities.
- Unsafe local execution/mount/config fallback in a managed Teams profile fails closed.

## Dependencies

- Architecture/milestone tracker: #481
- `AccessContextV1`: #482
- Neutral fail-closed authorization seam: #473
- In-repository Teams policy adapter/setup lifecycle: #483
- Hermes Agent host context carrier: NousResearch/hermes-agent#78802
- Provider-neutral management connector: #497
- Retrieval authority prerequisites: #476 / PR #487 and message adapter PR #489
- Routed-profile execution prerequisite: NousResearch/hermes-agent#68559 / PR NousResearch/hermes-agent#78030

## Exit criteria

The pilot closes only when:

1. every matrix row has an automated or explicitly witnessed artifact;
2. exact code/config/package versions are pinned;
3. rollback is exercised, not merely documented;
4. no P0/P1 isolation finding remains;
5. standard mode compatibility is verified;
6. the external connector and local recovery path both pass;
7. remaining federation/encryption/backup/product-UX work is explicitly classified as post-MVP rather than silently waived.

## Non-goals

- Cross-company query federation.
- Full employee publication/collaboration UX.
- Proven 100-employee capacity.
- Billing integration.
- General availability or customer rollout.

## Implementation status

Acceptance contract handoff ready; pilot not started.

title: feat: freeze the AccessContextV1 identity, delegation, lease and revocation contract
body:
Closes #482. Part of the opt-in LCM Teams chain tracked by #481.

## What this is

A frozen, machine-checkable contract for the authenticated host context that opt-in LCM Teams mode will
consume — identity, delegation, lease and revocation — plus a shared fixture corpus and the
authority-path inventory.

**This PR is deliberately inert.** It adds an `access_context/` subpackage, a JSON fixture corpus, tests
and one doc. It **edits no existing file, and nothing in the repository imports it.** A reviewer should be
able to conclude "this cannot change behaviour" by inspection, then confirm it from the diff: every path
in the first commit is a new path.

The intent is that the contract lands and stops moving *before* anything enforces it, so the authorization
seam (#473) and the policy adapter (#483) implement against a fixed target instead of co-evolving with it.

## Why the fixtures are JSON rather than Python

The contract has two sides. `NousResearch/hermes-agent#78802` is the *producer* of the host context; LCM
is the *consumer*. Shipping the corpus as JSON lets the producer validate against the same vectors without
importing this package. It also keeps the PR dependency-free — **stdlib only** (PyYAML is not a dependency
here, so the inventory is JSON too).

## Fail-closed degradation is a 2×2, and the cells are kept distinct

| | Teams off | Teams on |
|---|---|---|
| **carrier absent** | standard mode; contract not consulted | **fail closed** — `context_missing`, no unscoped fallback |
| **carrier present** | **ignored** — carrying context must not by itself enable Teams | validate |

The third cell is worth calling out: a host that happens to propagate context must never self-enable
Teams. Enabling stays explicit and configuration-driven. This is also what keeps the chain safe if #78802
never lands — Teams simply stays off.

## The authority-path inventory, and why it is machine-checked

#473 asks that the inventory be machine-readable or test-enumerated **so new memory paths cannot silently
omit the hook**. That property is only real if a test fails when someone forgets. So:

- The inventory's `lcm_*` entries must equal `plugin.yaml`'s `provides_tools` **by set equality in both
  directions** — adding a tool without classifying it fails the suite.
- Every module referenced must exist on disk, and every non-tool `entry_point` must be **found in its
  module's source**, which is what stops the inventory drifting into fiction.
- The fixture-kind set is asserted **closed**, so a count assertion cannot quietly go stale.

The inventory covers **38 entries across 19 modules**: the 15 public `lcm_*` tool handlers plus **23
non-tool authority paths** — `store.py`, `compaction.py`, `rollup_store.py`, `rollup_builder.py`,
`externalize.py`, `placeholder_ledger.py`, `maintenance.py`, `reset_state.py`, `db_bootstrap.py`,
`diagnostics.py`, `scripts/import_lossless_claw.py`, `retrieval_core.py`, `vector_store.py`, `dag.py`,
`aux_session.py`, `lifecycle_state.py`, `engine_registry.py`, `engine.py`. An inventory listing only the
front door would not serve the purpose, since the point is precisely the paths that can bypass public tool
handlers.

On `cron`: this repo has **no separate OS-cron entry point**. The only cron-like path is `engine.py`'s
rollup maintenance scheduler, so that is what the inventory records, with a `notes` field saying exactly
that. Naming the absence seemed more useful than inventing an entry or leaving the category silently empty.

## Denials disclose nothing — including through the detail side-channel

Denials carry an exact **internal** reason and a blurred **public** result. `SCOPE_FORBIDDEN`,
`SCOPE_MISMATCH`, `OWNERSHIP_CHANGED` and `LEASE_STALE` all project to a single public
`TARGET_NOT_FOUND_OR_FORBIDDEN`, so a caller cannot tell "not found" from "forbidden".

Blurring the reason is not sufficient on its own, and this is worth stating because it is easy to get
wrong: if the accompanying `detail` map varies by reason, the **shape** of its keys re-identifies what the
reason field just hid. So the public projection emits a **fixed key set** (`context_id`, `request_id` —
both values the caller itself supplied), always present, carrying `None` when absent internally. Varying
*presence* leaks just as effectively as varying values.

The test asserts the public key set is identical for every `DenialReason`, that no discriminating internal
key survives, and that all reasons sharing a public bucket project to **literally equal** objects —
indistinguishable rather than merely similar.

## A note on the ordering test

`test_protocol_order_authorize_precedes_every_disclosure_primitive` freezes #473's six steps: authorize
operation → resolve authorized targets → open collection → re-authorize stored scope → count/rank →
hydrate → issue handle → audit. In particular **target resolution precedes counting and ranking**, because
counting or ranking over unresolved candidates discloses existence and count for targets the principal may
not be entitled to.

To be straightforward about what this proves: it is a **contract freeze against a reference fake, not a
behavioural proof** — nothing implements the protocol yet, by design of this inert PR. Enforcement, and
the tests binding real retrieval arms to this order, are #473.

## Naming note for reviewers

There is a `bypass.py` at the repository root; it is **LCM-bypass compaction** (sessions opting out of
context management) and is unrelated to authorization bypass. It is untouched here. To avoid the
collision, the artifact in this PR is called the **authority-path inventory** rather than a "bypass map".

## Verification

- **CI is green on this branch across 3.11 / 3.12 / 3.13 / 3.14**, plus lint and workflow-lint.
- Contract tests: `pytest tests/test_access_context_v1_{model,validation,fixtures,inventory}.py -q` →
  **77 passed**.
- Locally this checkout shows 35 failures in `test_packaging_install.py`, `test_host_capability.py` and
  `test_auto_focus_topic.py`. Those are **environment artifacts of my checkout**, not repository defects —
  they are the host-integration surface that needs a hermes-agent stub CI provides, they reproduce on
  pristine `main` @ `6b7dbb1` before any change here, and the before/after failure sets are compared by
  diff rather than by eye: **identical, no new failures**. CI is the authoritative signal, and it is clean.
- Additivity: every path in the first commit is an addition; grep for `access_context` outside its own
  tree returns only its own tests; no `pyproject.toml` change.
- The 23 non-tool entry points were each checked to exist in their module's source, so the inventory
  describes the repository rather than an aspiration.

## Review

This branch was reviewed across two different models before being opened, on the principle that a model
reviewing its own output finds less than a different one does. Four defects were found and fixed that way,
including two in the denial projection. The full review trail is in a comment below.

## What is deliberately not here

Enforcement (#473) and policy (#483). This PR freezes the shape only. It creates no Teams config, no
storage, and no behaviour change in standard single-user mode.

title: fix: share SQLite storage across LCM engine clones
body:
## Summary

LCM engine clones currently construct a fresh set of SQLite-backed helpers. A clone therefore pays database initialization cost again and retains another set of SQLite file descriptors even though it is serving the same logical database as its prototype.

This change gives each clone family one reference-counted storage bundle while keeping mutable engine/session/model state clone-local. Independently constructed engines still own separate bundles, but bundles resolving to the same canonical database path share one in-process reentrant lock for helper construction, operations, backup/commit, and final teardown.

Fixes #463.

## Why this is needed

Hermes creates engine clones for child agents. Before this change, ten retained clones added 60 file descriptors on the measured macOS checkout and spent roughly 100 ms constructing duplicate SQLite helper sets. That multiplication raises the risk of descriptor exhaustion and repeated schema/WAL setup under parallel child-agent workloads.

The ownership boundary is the important part of the fix:

- clones share only the storage helpers;
- session IDs, cursors, runtime counters, model/provider metadata, adaptive retrieval state, and assertion extractors remain engine-local;
- every engine owns exactly one idempotent lease;
- owner-first shutdown releases one lease without closing storage still used by clones;
- final release attempts every helper close and reports combined failures;
- abandoned clones release their lease through finalization;
- failed clone construction rolls its acquired lease back.

This is complementary to #470's cleanup work. It does not replace #486's cross-process FTS bootstrap locking; the lock introduced here is process-local.

## Implementation

- Add a reference-counted `_SharedStorage` bundle for message store, summary DAG, lifecycle state, optional assertion store, and optional query-view store.
- Pass the bundle into `clone_for_agent()` and preserve clone-local runtime/model state.
- Use a weak canonical-path lock registry so independently constructed bundles for the same database serialize helper initialization, operations, backup/commit, and teardown without sharing mutable bundle ownership.
- Allow each SQLite helper to adopt the shared reentrant lock.
- Synchronize every touched store/DAG operation, lifecycle debt cleanup, backup, close, and commit path that uses a shared connection.
- Add lifecycle, concurrency, rollback, finalization, profile-rebinding, aggregate-cleanup, and descriptor-regression tests.
- Add `scripts/measure_clone_storage.py` for reproducible before/after measurements against a selected checkout.

## Reproduced benchmark

Environment: macOS, Python from the active Hermes environment, 25 samples, 10 retained clones. The benchmark imports each selected checkout using `LCM_BENCH_REPO_ROOT`.

Commands:

```bash
LCM_BENCH_REPO_ROOT=/private/tmp/hermes-lcm-baseline-check-20260804 \
  python scripts/measure_clone_storage.py --samples 25 --clones 10 --json

LCM_BENCH_REPO_ROOT=/private/tmp/hermes-lcm-shared-storage-impl-20260804 \
  python scripts/measure_clone_storage.py --samples 25 --clones 10 --json
```

Commits:

- Base: `6b7dbb1`
- Feature: `1708241c1ce9c759348509f9148b60e0f9fc02ff`

Results:

- Retained-clone file-descriptor delta: `+60` → `0`
- Median clone setup: `5.877985 ms` → `0.198782 ms`
- Ten-clone setup: `100.084453 ms` → `2.203067 ms`
- Median initial startup: `6.731055 ms` → `7.368695 ms`

Raw local receipts:

- `/private/tmp/lcm-storage-benchmark-final-base-20260804.json`
  - SHA-256 `2bcd2a9430f2d63a5b4f7ef00a9386157a9475e27825d935c44e03d3d3c09c06`
- `/private/tmp/lcm-storage-benchmark-final-feature-20260804.json`
  - SHA-256 `ba969980fa6087ded140a811b1bcf91a2b725e9f64aae536f1484f7cc84a7626`

## Verification

Green feature/affected gates:

- `tests/test_lcm_core.py::TestLCMEngineSharedStorage`: 9 passed
- `tests/test_lcm_engine.py`: 751 passed, 1 skipped
- `tests/test_lcm_core.py` excluding one independently reproduced upstream failure: 316 passed
- `tests/test_packaging_install.py`: 38 passed in the grouped run before the known isolated baseline failure was reproduced
- `tests/test_assertion_lifecycle_tools.py tests/test_assertion_store.py tests/test_query_view_store.py`: 49 passed
- `tests/test_lcm_core.py::TestLifecycleStateStore`: 19 passed
- `tests/test_assertion_store.py`: 20 passed
- `tests/test_query_view_store.py`: 21 passed
- Ruff on every changed Python file: passed
- Python compilation on changed production/benchmark files: passed
- `git diff --check`: passed
- Independent adversarial concurrency/lifecycle review: PASS after two repair rounds

Full-suite result:

- The suite remains red on current `main` for pre-existing or load-sensitive tests. The observed failures were reproduced against pristine `6b7dbb1`, including strict wall-clock embedding deadlines, macOS `/var` versus `/private/var` containment assertions, trajectory token/chunk expectations, provider-routing behavior, and an isolated packaging registration test.
- Three doctor failures initially exposed an incompatible post-shutdown alias-clearing change. That change was reverted; all three doctor tests pass on the final feature commit.
- No remaining full-suite failure was unique to this feature branch in the bounded base comparison.

## Scope

This PR intentionally does not:

- share one bundle across independently constructed engines;
- provide cross-process locking;
- change session/runtime/model ownership;
- change public configuration;
- include the separate reasoning-control or preflight-maintenance features.

title: feat: add separate summary and expansion reasoning controls
body:
## Summary

LCM currently lets operators choose different models for summary and expansion tasks, but it cannot independently tune the reasoning effort for those tasks. This adds strict `summary_reasoning_effort` and `expansion_reasoning_effort` settings and carries them through the real summary and expansion request paths.

Refs #495.

Hermes-Session: `20260804_101014_c509f5f7`

## Why

Routine context summaries and explicit expansion answers have different cost and quality profiles:

- summaries run frequently and usually benefit from lower-cost reasoning;
- expansions are user-requested retrieval/synthesis operations where stronger reasoning can be worth extra latency and cost.

Model selection alone cannot express that difference. Hermes also has one authoritative per-call `reasoning_config` contract. Sending a provider-specific reasoning alias alongside it can conflict with host routing.

## Implementation

- Add independent YAML/environment settings for summary and expansion reasoning effort.
- Validate supported values strictly while preserving the existing default when a setting is empty.
- Pass the summary value through both real summary call paths.
- Pass the expansion value through the real expansion synthesis path.
- Translate the requested effort only into Hermes `reasoning_config`; do not inject a provider-specific `extra_body.reasoning` alias.
- Report both effective settings in diagnostics.
- Document the new settings.

## Behavioral contract

- Summary and expansion efforts can differ.
- `none` explicitly disables reasoning through Hermes `reasoning_config`.
- Empty values preserve the normal task/provider default.
- Unsupported nonempty values fail during configuration validation.
- Both configured settings reach real outbound Hermes request boundaries.
- Provider-specific reasoning fields remain absent.

## Verification

Final clean branch `a79dea9df4070e509e26f7d66ed09fcb3492b63e`:

- `python -m ruff check README.md config.py engine.py escalation.py model_routing.py tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_reasoning_routing.py tools.py` — passed
- `python -m pytest -q tests/test_reasoning_routing.py` — 9 passed
- focused engine reasoning tests — 4 passed
- rollup reasoning propagation and affected reasoning paths — 14 passed locally
- final independent closure review — PASS
- grouped implementation gate before clean replay — 751 engine tests passed with 1 skipped, plus reasoning/config/property checks
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — passed

The repository's broad suite has known failures on pristine `6b7dbb1`; none of the bounded failures was unique to this feature branch.

## Scope

This PR does not change model selection, global provider defaults, or unrelated auxiliary tasks. It includes only the separate reasoning controls, their real consumption paths, diagnostics, documentation, and behavioral tests.

title: perf: defer noncritical LCM preflight maintenance
body:
## Summary

LCM can currently enter synchronous maintenance compaction before the first model call even when the prompt remains below the configured threshold and there is no critical pressure. This change keeps that routine debt recorded but defers the model work until an existing required trigger makes compression necessary.

Refs #496.

Hermes-Session: `20260804_101014_c509f5f7`

## Why

Pre-model latency is user-visible. Eligible raw backlog should remain tracked, but ordinary under-threshold maintenance should not block the live turn merely because debt exists.

This is intentionally narrower than asynchronous compaction. It changes only the preflight decision for noncritical, under-threshold maintenance and preserves synchronous behavior where capacity or an explicit request requires it.

## Implementation

- Continue recording and refreshing maintenance debt for eligible raw backlog.
- Return from real preflight without starting compression when the prompt is below threshold and configured pressure is noncritical.
- Preserve synchronous compression for threshold, overflow, cleanup, ignored-backlog, explicit-required, and critical-pressure paths.
- Exercise the real preflight path and prove the deferred branch makes no summary-model call.

## Behavioral contract

- Noncritical under-threshold backlog records debt and returns without synchronous compression.
- Required sibling branches remain synchronous.
- Deferred debt remains available for a later required trigger.
- If the critical-pressure ratio is disabled, debt may wait until threshold, overflow, cleanup, ignored-backlog, or an explicit required trigger.

## Verification

Final clean branch `3ece8ce19d540f95a53728d04ad9d821f460ee82`:

- `python -m ruff check compaction.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py` — passed
- focused real-preflight maintenance/threshold/pressure tests — 7 passed
- grouped implementation gate before clean replay — affected engine and API/package tests passed
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — passed

The repository's broad suite has known failures on pristine `6b7dbb1`; none of the bounded failures was unique to this feature branch.

## Relationship to existing work

- This preserves maintenance-debt accounting rather than replacing it.
- It preserves critical-pressure escape behavior.
- It is separate from session-start rollup deferral.
- It does not implement the broader asynchronous compaction proposal.

## Scope

This PR contains only the preflight decision change and its behavioral tests. It does not add a worker, queue, timer, configuration surface, or background-maintenance architecture.

title: LCM Teams v1: let several people share one LCM without seeing each other's memory
body:
# LCM Teams v1 — let several people share one LCM install without seeing each other's memory

## The problem, in one paragraph

LCM remembers everything an agent has seen. Today that assumes **one person per install**: any code that
can reach the database can read every message, summary and session in it. That is fine for a single user,
and it is why nothing here changes for one.

It stops being fine the moment two people share a deployment. A five-person company running one LCM has
no way to say "Ana's agent may read Ana's history, not Ben's." This PR adds that ability, **switched off
by default**, so nothing changes until someone turns it on.

## What it looks like

**Today — one owner, no checks:**

```
  request ──► retrieve / write / load session ──► SQLite
             (whoever asks, gets)
```

**With Teams enabled:**

```
  request ──► WHO is asking?  ──► MAY they touch THIS thing? ──► only their rows ──► SQLite
              (identity)          (policy decides)               (nothing else is opened)
                  │                     │
                  └── absent + Teams on ┴──► refuse, don't guess
```

**With Teams off — the default, and every install today:**

```
  request ──► retrieve / write / load session ──► SQLite
             (identical to before; the checks are present but always answer "yes")
```

## The bug worth understanding, because it is subtle

Early in this work the permission check asked the wrong question. Ben calls
`lcm_load_session(session_id = <Ana's session>)`:

```
  Ben ──► "may Ben read in BEN'S session?" ──► yes, obviously ──► loads ANA'S session
                   ▲
                   └── the code checked who was asking, never what they asked FOR
```

No permission policy could fix that, however well written — it was being handed the wrong question. The
fix passes the thing you asked for, not the thing you own:

```
  Ben ──► "may Ben read ANA'S session?" ──► no ──► refused
```

Two more of the same family, all found and fixed here: a check that could never fail because it compared
a value to itself, and a check that reported "all good" on rows it had structurally never looked at.

## What "off by default" actually means

Three independent things must all be true before any behaviour changes:

1. Teams is explicitly switched on in config.
2. The host tells LCM who is asking.
3. A policy exists that says no to something.

Miss any one and you get today's behaviour exactly. Switch on Teams but fail to supply an identity and it
**refuses rather than guessing** — the one place we chose to fail loudly instead of quietly.

## Remembering who owns what

Permission checks need to know which rows belong to whom, and LCM never recorded that. So each row now
carries an owner column, added as a **nullable** column — empty means "from before Teams", which reads
exactly as it does today.

When someone switches Teams on, existing history is stamped with its original owner (every row already
records its session, and sessions belong to people). A health check reports how many rows are stamped and
how many are not, as **numbers, not a thumbs-up** — and it says *"nothing to verify"* rather than
*"everything is fine"* on an empty database, because "all rows are correct" is trivially true when there
are no rows.

## Reviewing the 14 commits

They are in build order and each stands alone. Roughly:

| Commits | What |
|---|---|
| 1–3 | The vocabulary: who someone is, what they may do, and how a refusal is worded so it never leaks whether a thing exists. |
| 4 | The permission layer itself. Nothing calls it yet. |
| 5–7 | Wiring it into reads, writes, and background work. |
| 8 | A test that fails the build if someone adds a new way to reach memory and forgets to protect it. |
| 9 | The "wrong question" fix above. |
| 10–11 | An import bug found by running against a real database, plus its lint fallout. |
| 12–14 | The owner column, a performance fix, and a file-handle leak fix. |

## What we checked

- **Every existing test passes with Teams off**, which is the claim that matters most for anyone running
  LCM today. CI is green on Python 3.11–3.14.
- **Run against a copy of a real 136 MB production database** (24,765 messages, 129 sessions), not just
  fixtures. Reads returned byte-identical results to current `main`, apart from one added health-check
  line. Two people were then set up on that real data: the second could not reach the first's sessions,
  while the first still read all of their own — because a run where *everything* is denied proves nothing.
- **Every safety check was verified by deliberately breaking it** and confirming it failed. A test that
  cannot fail is worse than no test, since it reads as coverage.
- 4,804 lines added, 2 lines replaced, across commits 1–11. Commit 12 necessarily rewrites the `INSERT`
  statements of the tables gaining a column, so it is not additions-only, and saying otherwise would be
  untrue.

## What this deliberately does not do

- **It does not decide who may see what.** This is the mechanism; the actual rules — roles, membership —
  are the next piece. With Teams on today the mechanism runs and permits everything, which is why the
  tests for that path are marked expected-to-fail until the rules land.
- **Summaries built from several people's data** are not yet split per person. That needs summaries to be
  built per owner, which changes behaviour for multi-person installs and belongs in its own change.
- **Code that bypasses the engine** and opens the database directly is outside this. Closing that means
  changing constructor signatures across the storage layer — again, its own change.

## Release note

The current release, v0.20.0, predates this work, so anyone pinning releases gets none of it. Cutting a
v0.21 after this lands gives fleets a Teams-era line to pin. Nothing depends on it — Teams is off by
default and this changes nothing for existing installs either way.

title: Stable references to remembered things, plus a startup race fix (rolls up #486, #487, #489)
body:
# Stable references to remembered things, plus a startup race fix

Rolls up **#486 → #487 → #489**. These were never three independent changes — each is built directly on
the one before, so #489 already contains all three commits. This branch *is* their tip; nothing is
dropped or rewritten.

## What it gives you

When LCM hands back a search result or a message today, there is no reliable way to say *"that exact
thing, again, later"*. You can note an ID, but nothing guarantees the thing behind it is still the same
thing — it may have been re-summarised, re-chunked, or replaced.

These commits add a **durable reference**: a handle you can keep and hand back, which either returns the
same content it pointed at or tells you it no longer can.

```
  search ──► result #3
              │
              └── keep a reference ─────────────► later ──► same content
                                                     │       (or an honest "this changed")
                                                     └── not "some row that now has that id"
```

Plus a fix for a startup collision: two processes launching at once could both try to repair the
full-text search index and trip over each other.

```
  before:  process A ──┐
                       ├──► both repair the FTS index ──► one of them errors
           process B ──┘

  after:   process A ──┐
                       ├──► first one repairs, the other waits ──► both continue
           process B ──┘
```

## The three commits, in order

| # | Commit | In plain terms |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `fix: serialize concurrent FTS bootstrap repair` (#486) | Stops two processes repairing the search index simultaneously. Adds the lock handling the other two rely on. |
| 2 | `feat: add provenance-bound retrieval reference foundation` (#487) | A reference records *where its content came from*, so it cannot silently start pointing at something else. |
| 3 | `feat: add durable message reference adapter` (#489) | Applies that to messages specifically, so a saved pointer to a message stays a pointer to *that* message. |

## Why one PR rather than three

Commit 1 adds the lock handling that 2 and 3 both depend on. Merging them separately means either landing
1 on its own — leaving the thing it exists to support unmerged — or reading the same corner of

`git bisect` work exactly as they would have.

title: fix: share LCM storage across runtime clones
body:
## Summary
- Add a reference-counted `_StorageBundle` holding the SQLite helpers (`MessageStore`, `SummaryDAG`, `LifecycleStateStore`, `AssertionStore`, `QueryViewStore`) that `clone_for_agent()` runtimes now share, instead of each clone opening its own connection set.
- Each runtime releases its reference once on `close()` / `shutdown()`; a repeated close is a no-op, so it cannot close helpers a live prototype or sibling still uses. The last release closes every helper, attempting all of them even if one `close()` raises (first error re-raised, the rest logged).
- If an optional helper constructor (`AdaptiveRetrievalRegistry`, `ModelAssertionExtractor`) fails while a clone is being built, the clone gives back its bundle reference before the error propagates.
- Per-agent session, cursor and lifecycle state stays independent; only storage is shared. The helpers were already thread-safe (`check_same_thread=False` plus per-helper locks).
- `tests/conftest.py` no longer searches parent directories for a hermes-agent checkout: it uses the CI stub in this checkout, or `HERMES_AGENT_ROOT` when set.

## Why
- Hermes core calls `clone_for_agent()` for every `AIAgent` it builds with the LCM engine. Before this change, each clone opened a new set of `lcm.db` / WAL descriptors, so a long-running gateway kept accumulating them (hermes-agent#79537, parent hermes-agent#72782). This is the LCM half of that work. It is separate from the generic `SessionDB` fix in hermes-agent#72822.
- No change to Hermes core is needed. An earlier revision also added a `create_runtime()` alias for a proposed core contract (hermes-agent#79575). That PR was closed without merging, so the alias has been dropped.

## Validation
- [x] Focused validation: `pytest tests/test_fd_hygiene.py tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py -q` -> 1072 passed, 2 skipped (the FD-hygiene test skips on macOS because it has no `/proc/self/fd`. It ran green on Linux at the previous head.)

  - [x] `python -m compileall -q .`
  - [x] `python -m py_compile scripts/import_lossless_claw.py`
  - [x] `bash -n scripts/install.sh scripts/update.sh`
  - [x] `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD && git diff --check`
  - [x] `ruff check .`, `python scripts/validate_dependency_contract.py`
- [ ] `scripts/validate_release.sh --full`: not run locally. CI covers the Linux matrix once the workflow is approved for this fork.

## Notes

title: fix(reconcile): normalize Hermes-generated replay scaffolding
body:
## Problem

Hermes-generated transient wrappers can change between active-context
replays even when the durable message is unchanged. This breaks replay
identity matching and can cause previously stored messages to be appended
again.

Affected representations:
- volatile TODO annotations
- model-switch wrappers
- standalone model-switch notes
- out-of-band user blocks
- tool messages misclassified as generated scaffold

## Root cause

Replay identity currently compares host-generated presentation layers as
if they were durable message content.

## Minimal fix

Normalize only the recognized Hermes-generated replay layers while
building replay identity. Raw stored content, provider-visible content,
the scalar cursor algorithm, and the database schema remain unchanged.

## Regression tests

- TODO annotation replay
- model-switch wrapper replay
- standalone model-switch note
- OOB block replay
- real tool output versus generated scaffold
- negative tests preserving ordinary user content
- normalization idempotency and tool-call metadata

Focused result: 27 passed.

## Relationship

Supersedes #462, #465, #490, and #494.

Includes only the narrowly scoped tool-scaffold correction from #471.

Complements #437, which handles partial tool-tail replay after restart.
The PRs apply and test independently; the complete tested production
stack uses both.

title: fix(reconcile): reject forked replay snapshots without tail continuity
body:
## Problem

A shorter fork or side-channel snapshot that has no continuity with the
current durable tail can be interpreted as new session content and
appended to the canonical store.

## Root cause

The existing scalar-cursor reconciliation path lacks a narrow rejection
case for disconnected shorter snapshots.

## Minimal fix

Reject only snapshots matching the demonstrated fork signature: shorter
than the durable session and without tail continuity. The scalar cursor,
store schema, and engine/reconcile contract remain unchanged.

## Regression tests

- disconnected fork snapshots of multiple sizes are rejected
- the minimum guard boundary is covered
- ordinary short continuations remain accepted

Focused result: 11 passed.

## Relationship

Supersedes #464.

This PR applies and tests independently from #437 and the replay-identity
normalization PR.

title: fix(reconcile): tolerate compacted-out tool rows in suffix matching
body:
## Problem

After the real compression path removes tool rows from the active replay,
the remaining user/assistant suffix can fail to match the durable store.
The scalar cursor can then treat the replayed history as new and append it
again.

## Root cause

Suffix matching currently requires tool rows that may legitimately be
absent after compression.

## Minimal fix

Allow suffix reconciliation to tolerate tool rows omitted by the real
compression path while preserving the existing scalar-cursor and storage
architecture.

## Regression tests

The regression fixture uses the real compress() path rather than manually
deleting tool rows.

Focused result: 3 passed.

## Relationship

Contains only the compacted-tool portion split from #471.

Complements #437, which handles tool-call-anchored partial restart replay.
The two patches apply and test independently.

title: fix(lcm): make request pressure fresh-tail aware
body:
## Summary
- make LCM request-pressure decisions aware of protected/fresh-tail compressibility
- enable an automatic assembly reserve for real large context windows by default (`reserve_tokens_floor=-1`; explicit `0` still disables it)
- keep small-context tests uncapped while preventing large provider requests from assembling up to the exact model limit
- add regression coverage for protected-tail-only overflows and auto-reserve behavior

## Why
Hermes Agent can ask the context engine whether request pressure is actually compressible before retrying compression. LCM protects the latest user/fresh tail, so when pressure is caused only by protected recent messages, another compression pass is a no-op. This PR lets LCM decline that no-op path and caps assembly by default with headroom for provider overhead.

Related Hermes Agent draft PR: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/79717
Related Hermes issue: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/64382

## Test Plan
- `PYTHONPATH=/tmp/hermes-lcm-protected-tail-upstream:/tmp/hermes-context-overflow-upstream python3 -m pytest tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_lcm_core.py::TestConfig -q`

title: [compaction] DAG summaries persisted to state.db as role=user rows can replace the real latest user message
body:
## Summary

Compaction writes DAG summaries into the host state.db as **role=user** messages (`engine.py` forces `summary_role = "user"` at the assembly boundary, and the reconcile path persists `[Current user objective preserved from compacted history]` rows). When the persisted summary row's timestamp coincides with a real inbound user message, the summary **replaces** the real user message as the latest user input from the model's perspective — the agent answers the old summary instead of the new user message.

## Reproduction

1. Long-running chat session with LCM as context engine (`context.engine: lcm`).
2. User sends a new message while/before compaction triggers.
3. Compaction runs, and a `[Session Arc Summary (dN, node X)]` (or `[Current user objective preserved ...]`) row is written into the host `state.db` `messages` table with `role='user'` and a timestamp at/near the real message's arrival.
4. On the next turn, the assembled context presents the summary as the latest user turn. The model replies about the summary's content, completely ignoring the actual user message (verified: state.db has no record of the real user message; the only `role=user` row at that timestamp is the summary row).

## Impact

- "Model stops understanding the user" / non-sequitur replies after compaction.
- 64 such pseudo-user rows accumulated across 51 sessions in one deployment (7/19–8/6).
- The synthetic rows also pollute host-side session search and any logic that treats `role=user` rows as genuine user turns (e.g. `_is_synthetic_compression_user_turn` in the host compressor does NOT recognize these LCM formats).

## Suggested fix

- Persisted summary rows should not be written as `role=user`, or should carry a marker the host can recognize as synthetic (align with the host's `_is_synthetic_compression_user_turn` recognition), or the real inbound user message must always be persisted ahead of / instead of the synthetic summary at the same timestamp.
- Related upstream work: #355, #370 (preserve the sole real user prompt through compaction).

## Environment

- hermes-lcm v0.20.0
- Host: Hermes Agent, context.engine=lcm, Feishu gateway

title: reconcile: post-compression replay can re-append an already persisted turn
body:
## Summary

`reconcile: post-compression replay can re-append an already persisted turn`

## Description

### Bug

When the host compresses the active context **in the middle of a turn** and then re-sends the same turn (replayed tail segment plus newly produced rows), the reconcile layer fails to recognize the already-persisted portion and appends it again.

The incoming batch is a **mixed NEW/REPLAY ordering**:

```
N0a (tool)      — genuinely new row produced during compression
N0b (assistant) — genuinely new row produced during compression
T1  (tool)      — already persisted (replay)
N1  (assistant) — genuinely new
N2  (tool)      — genuinely new
A1  (assistant) — already persisted (replay)
U1  (user)      — already persisted (replay)
U2  (user)      — already persisted (replay)
```

### Reproduction (clean upstream main)

- Repo: `stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm`
- Upstream SHA: `e1977c68503d8a862da20b6cf12d054977dcc1c2` (`origin/main` after `git fetch origin --prune`)
- Test: `tests/test_reconcile_f14_compress_partial_turn.py::TestPostCompressionPartialTurnReplay::test_partial_turn_replay_after_compress_no_duplicate`
- The test uses the **real `compress()` path** (not a simulated compaction): ingest batch A → `engine.compress(...)` → `on_session_start(boundary_reason="compression")` → ingest batch B (mixed NEW/REPLAY + 2 new rows).
- Result: **FAILS** on clean upstream main. The 4 already-persisted rows (`T1, A1, U1, U2`) are re-appended; expected only the 4 genuinely new rows (`N0a, N0b, N1, N2`) to be written.

### Evidence points

- **Clean upstream main reproduces** (test above FAILS).
- **PR #437 still reproduces** — same test FAILS on `main` + #437 (branch `fix/m2-main-437`, SHA `ff3450f`).
- **PRs #507/#508/#509 did not introduce the issue** — the same FAIL profile exists on clean `main` (M0) and on the full minimal stack (S3 = `main` + R1 + #437 + R4 + R5, SHA `ae175ad`); the duplication count is identical on every branch.
- **Real compress() path is used** — no manual message deletion or compaction simulation.
- **Current scalar cursor cannot represent mixed NEW/REPLAY ordering.** The engine semantics are `messages[:cursor]` = replayed (skipped) and `messages[cursor:]` = written to the canonical store. With ordering `NEW, NEW, REPLAY, NEW, NEW, REPLAY, REPLAY, REPLAY`, every possible cursor value either re-writes a replayed row or drops a genuinely new row (full enumeration in the test file comments; e.g. cursor=2 skips `N0a,N0b` but re-writes `T1`; cursor=3 re-writes `A1,U1,U2`; cursor=8 drops all 4 new rows).

### Expected behavior

- Replayed rows (`T1, A1, U1, U2`) are not appended again.
- Genuinely new rows (`N0a, N0b, N1, N2`) are appended exactly once.
- No data loss, no duplication.

### Request

No fix is imposed in this issue. The scalar-cursor contract cannot express the mixed ordering, so a maintainer decision is requested on the reconciliation contract before a minimal fix is attempted (e.g. per-row disposition vs. a narrow cursor extension).

### Test file (mock only — no production data)

All identifiers are synthetic (`N0a, N0b, T1, N1, N2, A1, U1, U2`). No real session IDs, store IDs, timestamps, message content, database paths, or user/project names are referenced.

title: AAAK compression provider — WITHDRAWN / DECLINED on measurement (0.9729× cl100k_base = net expansion; the ~30× claim was unverified)
body:
> **STATUS — WITHDRAWN / DECLINED (2026-10-09).** The "~30× token reduction" figure in this proposal was **unverified**, and it has since been **measured and rejected**: `tiktoken:cl100k_base` aggregate **0.9729×** (215 → 221 tokens — a *net expansion*), only **1 of 9** cases above 1.00×. AAAK is declined (not deferred); **no PR will follow and nothing will be published**. Every "~30×" claim below is struck through accordingly. Full evidence and reasoning: `ether-btc/hermes-lcm-aak-contribution` → `DECISIONS.md` (2026-10-09 entry) and the home-wiki audit `aaak-declined-2026-10-09`.
>
> _A journal is an **evidence artifact**: compressing it at rest trades greppability for a measured loss. If journal efficiency is wanted, the order is: (1) cut **volume** (rollup/prune), then (2) compress only **derived views** — gated on a real measurement._

---

## Problem

hermes-lcm currently relies on LLM-based summarization (expensive, high latency) or the Caveman rust_cave_001 provider (~2-4x reduction, output needs decoder). There's a gap for a **deterministic, high-compression, AI-native provider** that:
- Requires zero LLM calls (sub-millisecond latency)
- ~~Achieves ~30x token reduction on prose~~ — **measured and rejected**: 0.9729× on `cl100k_base` (a net expansion)
- Output is natively readable by LLMs without a decoder
- Has zero external dependencies (stdlib only)

## User or operator impact

Operators running local LLMs with tight context windows (7B-13B models) face context pressure during long sessions. Current options:
- **LLM summarization**: 500ms-5s per compaction, requires provider availability
- **Caveman**: Only 2-4x reduction, compressed output requires decoding logic
- **No compression**: Context overflow, truncated history

## Proposed direction

Add **AAAK (AI-readable Algorithmic Abbreviation & Keyword) compression** as a new provider option for hermes-lcm, adapted from Lumina MemPalace (Bino5150/lumina, Apache-2.0).

### What this provides:

1. **AAAK Compression Engine** — Deterministic abbreviation map (longest-match-first), filler word stripping, label-prefixed output (PREF:, PROJ:, SESS:, etc.), ~~~30x reduction on prose~~ — **measured-rejected**
2. **4-Layer Tier Manager** — Explicit token budgets (identity:50, critical:120, recent:300, nightstand:200, deep:∞), rolling summary pattern (pipe-separated AAAK facts per topic), budget enforcement with temporal decay sorting
3. **Temporal Decay Engine** — Exponential forgetting: w(t) = e^(-λ × t) with configurable λ (default 0.05/day), sort-by-recency for recent/nightstand tiers
4. **Context Builder** — Builds injection-ready ContextBlock compatible with hermes-lcm context assembly, respects tier order, budgets, focus topics, overrides
5. **Comprehensive Test Suite** — 26 tests covering all components + full pipeline integration

### Integration approach (recommended: Option A - Standalone Provider Package)

Publish `aaak-provider` to PyPI. hermes-lcm detects and uses it via a provider registry pattern or optional import. Users install:
```bash
pip install aaak-provider
```

### Config schema proposal:

```yaml
# ~/.config/hermes/hermes-lcm/config.yaml
lcm:
  compression:
    provider: "aaak"  # or "caveman", "llm", "none"
    aaak:
      abbreviation_map_path: "~/.config/hermes/hermes-lcm/aaak_abbrev.json"
      tier_budgets:
        identity: 50
        critical: 120
        recent: 300
        nightstand: 200
        deep: null
      lambda_rate: 0.05
      nightstand_enabled: true
      nightstand_min_tokens: 800
      rolling_summary_enabled: true
```

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|--------|------|------|
| **A: Standalone PyPI package** | Zero coupling, independent versioning, users opt-in | Requires provider detection mechanism |
| **B: Built-in provider** | Tight integration, no extra install | Increases repo size, tied to hermes-lcm release cycle |
| **C: Config-driven plugin interface** | Extensible, follows Mnemosyne pattern | More architectural work upfront |

**Recommended: Option A** — Lowest risk, validates demand, can evolve to B/C later.

## Backward compatibility

- Default compression provider remains unchanged (current LLM summarization)
- AAAK is opt-in via config or explicit import
- No changes to existing compression APIs
- Apache-2.0 license compatible with hermes-lcm

## Validation or evidence

- **Package**: `/home/hermes-pi/projects/hermes-lcm-aak-contribution/` — 5 modules, 26 tests
- **All tests pass**: `pytest tests/ -v` → 26 passed in 0.14s
- **Install test**: `pip install -e .` → clean install, imports work
- **Compression demo**: `"The user prefers dark mode and vim keybindings for coding"` → `"PREF: USR prefers dark-mode + vim-bindings for coding"`
- **Zero dependencies**: stdlib only (Python ≥3.11)
- **Source**: Lumina (Bino5150/lumina) — Apache-2.0, 101★, tested on 4GB GPU

## Implementation status

**Prototype exists** — Full implementation at https://github.com/ether-btc/hermes-lcm-aak-contribution

## Additional notes

This originated from the Lumina MemPalace hardware assessment project. The AAAK provider was extracted as a standalone, hermes-lcm-targeted package. Key architectural decisions:

- **Rolling summaries** replace per-consolidation DAG nodes (bounds complexity)
- **Nightstand tier** isolates auto-generated content with promotion gates
- **Deterministic compression** enables reproducible testing and debugging
- **AI-readable output** means no decoder logic needed in retrieval path

Questions for maintainer:
1. Preferred integration path (A/B/C)?
2. Does hermes-lcm have or plan a provider registry for compression backends?
3. Where should AAAK config live? (hermes-lcm config, separate file, env vars)
4. Should rolling summaries persist in hermes-lcm DB (new node type) or externalized payloads?
5. Is a nightstand tier for auto-writes desirable, or should this map to existing episodic/working?

title: fix: log hermes_cli import failure instead of silently swallowing it
body:
## Problem

The `register()` function in `__init__.py` used a bare `except Exception:` with no logging when importing `get_hermes_home` from `hermes_cli.config`. This silently swallowed import errors, making it impossible to debug profile-scoped storage issues — if the import failed, the plugin fell back to the `HERMES_HOME` env var with zero indication of why.

## Fix

Capture the exception and log a warning with the exception details before falling back to the environment:

```python
except Exception as exc:
    logger.warning("hermes-lcm: could not import get_hermes_home (%s); falling back to env", exc)
    hermes_home = os.environ.get("HERMES_HOME", os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes"))
```

## Scope

One file changed, 2 lines. No behavioral change on the happy path; only adds observability on the error path.

title: fix: gate opportunistic maintenance compaction on token pressure
body:
## Summary
- Gate the two OPPORTUNISTIC maintenance-compaction arms on the divergent-replay path behind a token floor, so a media-heavy session stops requesting compaction at any size.
- Add `maintenance_min_pressure_ratio` (`LCM_MAINTENANCE_MIN_PRESSURE_RATIO`), a fraction of `threshold_tokens`. **Default `0.0` preserves current behavior exactly.**

## Why

`should_compress_preflight` reaches the leaf-candidate check two ways, and only one is gated.

Non-divergent path — gated:

```python
if self.threshold_tokens > 0 and rough >= self.threshold_tokens:
    eligible, reason = self._leaf_compaction_candidate_status(messages, ...)
    if eligible:
        return self._mark_preflight_compression_requested()
```

Divergent-replay path — the identical check, no token gate:

```python
eligible, reason = self._leaf_compaction_candidate_status(replay_messages, ...)
if eligible:
    return self._mark_preflight_compression_requested()
if self._has_ignored_backlog_outside_fresh_tail(replay_messages):
    return self._mark_preflight_compression_requested()
```

That path is entered whenever ingest rewrote the replay view — in practice an externalized payload: inline media, base64, a large tool result. A session that traffics in those requests an opportunistic maintenance compaction however small it is.

Observed against a 750,000-token threshold:

| observed tokens | % of threshold |
|---|---|
| 129,088 | 17% |
| 158,262 | 21% |
| 175,730 | 23% |
| 239,896 | 32% |

Three of those landed inside eight minutes, one on a session that had just been compacted. Those passes freed **27–47%**, where pressure-driven compactions on the same deployment freed **84–86%** — and each still costs a summarizer call plus the conversation's prompt cache.

Deliberately **not** gated: deterministic ingest-cleanup adoption returns earlier and stays available at any size (already durable, no summarizer work). Overflow recovery is checked before the floor on every path.

## Validation
- [x] Focused validation: `pytest tests/test_maintenance_pressure_floor.py -q` -> `11 passed`
- [x] RED proof: reverting both call sites -> `2 failed, 9 passed` (`test_both_opportunistic_arms_are_gated`, `test_cleanup_adoption_is_not_gated`)
- [x] Default validation:
  - [x] `pytest tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q` -> `1108 passed, 1 skipped` (incl. the new file)
  - [x] `pytest -q` -> `7 failed, 2797 passed, 2 skipped, 12 xfailed` — see Notes
  - [x] `bash -lc 'ulimit -n 1024 && pytest -q'` -> same 7, all environmental
  - [x] `python -m compileall -q .` -> exit 0
  - [ ] `python -m py_compile scripts/import_lossless_claw.py` — not run, no scripts touched
  - [ ] `bash -n scripts/install.sh scripts/update.sh` — not run, no shell scripts touched
  - [x] `git diff --check` -> clean
  - [x] `ruff check .` (pinned 0.15.13) -> `All checks passed!`
- [x] Workflow validation: n/a, no workflows changed

## Notes

**The 7 remaining failures are environmental on macOS + Python 3.14 and are not caused by this change.** Verified against a pristine `upstream/main` worktree, which fails **10** in the same two families — a superset, with shifting membership run to run:

- **Wall-clock deadline assertions** — `test_embedding_provider.py`, `test_embedding_search_modes.py` assert real elapsed time (e.g. `assert elapsed < 0.06`). Membership varies between runs, so this is a flake family rather than a fixed list.
- **macOS `/private` symlink** — `test_path_containment.py`, `test_path_security.py`. `TemporaryDirectory()` returns `/var/...` while the resolved path is `/private/var/...`, so a `startswith` containment check fails. Linux CI is unaffected.

Neither family touches compaction. Claiming *their-suite-minus-known-environmental-reds*, not full green.

Two of the 11 tests exist specifically to stop the fix going half-inert: gating only one of the two arms leaves the other free to request compaction at any size, and the cleanup-adoption ordering assertion pins that deterministic cleanup keeps working below the floor. Both fail if the change is reverted.

The floor ships **off**. Operators who want it set `LCM_MAINTENANCE_MIN_PRESSURE_RATIO=0.5` (or whatever fraction suits their workload).

All values above are from synthetic/local runs — no transcripts, credentials, or `lcm.db` contents are included.

title: test: compare against the resolved temp base so path tests pass on macOS
body:
## Summary
- Resolve the temp-directory base before the containment prefix check in two path tests, so they pass on macOS as well as Linux.

## Why

Both assertions compare a **resolved** path against an **unresolved** tempfile base:

```python
assert str(path).startswith(tmpdir)
```

On macOS `TemporaryDirectory()` returns `/var/folders/...`, while `_state_db_path_for_engine` and `get_large_output_storage_dir` both resolve symlinks and return `/private/var/folders/...` (`/var` is a symlink to `/private/var`). The prefix check fails there and passes on Linux, where `/var` is a real directory.

The implementations are correct — resolving before a containment check is exactly right, since comparing unresolved paths is how traversal bugs slip through. Only the assertions are unportable, so this resolves the expected side too rather than relaxing what is being asserted.

Noticed while validating an unrelated change on macOS: these two show up in every local `pytest -q` run and are easy to mistake for damage caused by the branch under test.

title: fix: tolerate None tool_calls in _serialize_messages
body:
## Summary
- Treat `tool_calls=None` on an assistant message as an empty list in `LCMEngine._serialize_messages`, instead of letting the list comprehension raise `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable`.
- Add two regression tests under `TestExtraction` covering the standalone and matched-tool-result cases.

## Why
Reproduction stack from v0.21.0-rc2 (engine.py:5061):

```
File ".../hermes_lcm/engine.py", line 5061, in _serialize_messages
    matched_tool_calls = [
        tc for tc in tool_calls
        if not _tool_call_id(tc) or _tool_call_id(tc) in matched_tool_ids
    ]
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable
```

Triggered when a stored assistant row is reconstructed with `tool_calls=None` (e.g. an empty value that round-tripped as SQL NULL). The default `msg.get("tool_calls", [])` only handles the missing-key case, not the null value case. The same safe pattern (`msg.get("tool_calls") or []`) is already used elsewhere in the module — `message_analysis._assistant_tool_call_ids` (line 31), `engine.py` lines 4019 and 5357 — so this aligns the buggy site with the surrounding convention.

Repro recipe (deterministic):

```python
from hermes_lcm.config import LCMConfig
from hermes_lcm.engine import LCMEngine

engine = LCMEngine(config=LCMConfig(database_path=":memory:"))
engine._serialize_messages([
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Hello.", "tool_calls": None},
])
# TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable
```

The two new tests in `TestExtraction` lock this down: one with the bare None case, one with the same assistant followed by a matched tool result.

title: feat: add OpenAI-compatible embedding provider
body:
## Summary

Adds an `OpenAICompatibleProvider` to the embedding stack, alongside the existing `voyage` / `ollama` / `fastembed` providers. It targets any OpenAI-format `/v1/embeddings` endpoint — llama.cpp server, vLLM, SiliconFlow, or a private gateway — so operators who already run an embedding service can point LCM at it instead of running a second embedding stack.

## Motivation

Issue #419 asks for exactly this: with the vector store and the Ollama provider in place, the HTTP embedding infrastructure already exists; a provider-neutral OpenAI-compatible option closes the gap for everyone with a local or cloud OpenAI-format embeddings endpoint.

## Implementation

- `embedding_provider.py`: new `OpenAICompatibleProvider(_ResilientProvider)` modeled on `OllamaProvider` — `_request` / `_embed` / `embed_documents` / `embed_document_batches` / `embed_query` / `embed_query_interactive`, dimension tracking, deadline budgets, and the same spend-guard / circuit-breaker semantics as the other remote providers.
- `resolve_provider()` accepts `openai-compatible` (aliases `openai`, `siliconflow`); unsupported-provider error text updated.
- `config.py`: two new env fields — `LCM_EMBEDDING_BASE_URL` (API root; trailing slash stripped, `/embeddings` appended) and `LCM_EMBEDDING_API_KEY` (falls back to `SILICONFLOW_API_KEY`).

## Env contract

```bash
LCM_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=openai-compatible
LCM_EMBEDDING_MODEL=BAAI/bge-m3     # any model id your endpoint serves
LCM_EMBEDDING_BASE_URL=https://api.siliconflow.cn/v1
LCM_EMBEDDING_API_KEY=sk-...        # falls back to SILICONFLOW_API_KEY
```

Request shape is the standard OpenAI one (`{"model": ..., "input": [...]}` with a `Bearer` header). Deadline and identity semantics match the other remote providers: `LCM_EMBEDDING_QUERY_TIMEOUT_S` bounds interactive queries, `LCM_EMBEDDING_BACKFILL_TIMEOUT_S` bounds backfill batches, and vectors are stored under the full `(provider, model, ...)` identity so switching back reactivates existing vectors without re-backfilling.

## Tests & docs

- 9 new unit tests in `tests/test_embedding_provider.py` (request shape, auth header, trailing-slash handling, query/interactive paths, missing-key and fallback behavior, base-url/model validation, network-error non-retry, response-count mismatch, `resolve_provider` wiring).
- `docs/embeddings-setup.md`: new "Option 4 — OpenAI-compatible API" section plus TL;DR row.

Closes #419

title: feat: add LCM_DISABLED_TOOLS env filter for context-engine tools
body:
## Summary

Adds an opt-in `LCM_DISABLED_TOOLS` environment variable that removes named `lcm_*` tools from the model-facing surface, so their full JSON schemas are not injected into every turn. This is a surgical, reversible alternative to disabling the whole context-engine toolset.

## Motivation

All 15 context-engine tool schemas are injected every turn, including heavy advanced tools (`lcm_compute`, `lcm_compile_evidence`, `lcm_evidence_pack`, `lcm_retrieve`, `lcm_query_state`) that many operators never call. On small-context routes those schemas are a meaningful fixed per-turn cost (~3-4k tokens for the advanced set). Operators who want the compression engine but not the evidence/assertion surface now have a per-tool switch instead of all-or-nothing.

## Implementation

One env var, three enforcement points, all reversible:

- `engine.get_tool_schemas()` — disabled tools are excluded from the injected schema list (zero tokens per turn).
- `engine.handle_tool_call()` — disabled tools are refused **before** message ingest, returning a clear error: `LCM tool <name> is disabled via LCM_DISABLED_TOOLS`.
- plugin `register()` — disabled tools are filtered from Path A plugin-registry registration, mirroring the engine so they cost nothing on every host path.

```bash
LCM_DISABLED_TOOLS=lcm_compute,lcm_compile_evidence,lcm_evidence_pack,lcm_retrieve,lcm_query_state
```

Unset the variable to restore all 15 tools. Unknown/whitespace entries are ignored; no tool names are hardcoded into the filter itself.

## Tests & docs

- New `tests/test_disabled_tools.py` (5 tests): full 15-tool baseline without env, 10-tool filtered set with env, refusal in `handle_tool_call` before ingest, enabled tools still dispatch, and env parsing (trimming, empties, unset).
- README environment-variable table row for `LCM_DISABLED_TOOLS`.

title: fix: recall policy accumulates in replayed user api_content and can be misattributed
body:
## Expected behavior

The Hermes-LCM recall policy should remain product-owned guidance and must not be attributable to the user.

For one model request, the canonical policy should appear at most once, regardless of how many prior user turns are replayed. Historical replay should not multiply the policy once per user message.

The behavior should preserve clean stored user content and clean LCM ingest. A supported opt-out should exist; issue #420's maintainer follow-up explicitly requested that the policy default off.

Any fix should preserve prompt-cache stability. This report does not assume that moving the policy into a mutable system prompt is the right solution.

## Actual behavior

With Hermes-LCM active, the plugin's `pre_llm_call` hook returns:

```python
{"context": recall_policy}
```

Hermes appends this context to the current user message's API copy and persists that copy as `api_content`. On later turns, the host substitutes each historical `api_content` back into the corresponding message sent to the provider.

As a result:

- every eligible historical user message can carry its own copy of the 2,230-byte policy;
- all copies are sent under role `user`;
- the model can interpret product-owned instructions as text authored or pasted by the user;
- policy overhead grows with the number of replayed user turns until compaction removes those turns from active context;
- there is no dedicated supported switch to disable only recall-policy injection.

This caused a real attribution failure: the assistant stated that the user had pasted the `Hermes-LCM Recall Policy`, although the block had been added by the runtime.

The clean transcript remains correct, but that alone does not prevent model-facing misattribution because the provider receives `api_content`.

## Minimal reproduction

1. Install and activate Hermes-LCM:

```yaml
plugins:
  enabled:
    - hermes-lcm

context:
  engine: lcm
```

2. Start a text session and send two ordinary user messages.
3. For each user turn, let the active Hermes-LCM `pre_llm_call` hook return the canonical recall policy.
4. Build the next provider request from the persisted messages, applying Hermes' historical `api_content` substitution.
5. Inspect the provider-bound messages.

A minimal host-level reproduction using the current Hermes helpers produces:

```text
clean_policy_occurrences=0
wire_policy_occurrences=2
wire_user_messages=2
each_wire_role_user=True
```

The relevant host behavior is:

- `agent/turn_context.py::compose_user_api_content()` appends plugin context to the user API copy and documents that the result is persisted as `api_content`;
- `agent/turn_context.py::substitute_api_content()` replaces historical message content with that sidecar for provider replay;
- `hermes_cli/plugins.py` documents `pre_llm_call` context as user-message injection.

The relevant plugin behavior is:

- `__init__.py::_pre_llm_context()` returns the policy even when pre-answer evidence mode is `off`;
- `register()` installs the hook whenever an active LCM engine is resolved.

## Version and branch

- hermes-lcm: `v0.21.0-rc2`, commit `10cbb78347ec86f3004153b24767324ded9e37b4`
- The same injection path is still present on current `main` at the time of filing.

## Environment

- Ubuntu 26.04
- Hermes Agent v0.20.0 (2026.8.3)
- Hermes runtime Python 3.11.15
- Hermes WebUI session

## Relevant config

```yaml
plugins:
  enabled:
    - hermes-lcm

context:
  engine: lcm
```

No dedicated recall-policy enable/disable setting is configured because none is currently exposed.

## Logs, traceback, or failing test

Read-only inspection of one real session showed:

```text
policy_bytes=2230
user_rows=26
user_rows_api_with_policy=22
user_rows_clean_content_with_policy=0
per_api_content_policy_occurrences_min=1
per_api_content_policy_occurrences_max=1
replayed_policy_bytes_if_all_rows_active=49060
```

The final byte count is the upper bound if all 22 affected rows are included in one active request; compaction may reduce the active subset.

Issue #420 introduced the active policy through the user-context seam. Its maintainer follow-up requested deterministic tests proving that the policy defaults off, appears exactly once per turn, preserves clean transcript/LCM ingest, and leaves inactive paths byte-identical. The current implementation tests the hook result, but does not appear to cover multi-turn host replay or user-authorship ambiguity.

Related: #420

## Validation attempted

- Searched all repository issues and pull requests for recall-policy attribution, `api_content`, and `pre_llm_call` duplicates; no matching bug was found.
- Verified current `main` still returns `{"context": recall_policy}`.
- Verified clean `content` does not contain the policy while historical `api_content` does.
- Reproduced two policy copies across two provider-bound user messages with the current Hermes composition/substitution helpers.
- Confirmed the behavior is not caused by pre-answer evidence: `_pre_llm_context()` returns the policy when that mode is `off`.

## Suggested acceptance criteria

- Product-owned policy cannot be mistaken for user-authored content.
- At most one canonical policy copy is present in a complete provider request.
- Multi-turn replay does not grow policy copies linearly with user turns.
- Clean stored user content and LCM ingest remain unchanged.
- Prompt-cache behavior is measured and preserved or any trade-off is explicit.
- A supported policy-only opt-out exists; default behavior is reconciled with the maintainer direction in #420.
- An integration test covers at least two user turns, persisted `api_content`, historical replay, exact copy count, and role/attribution boundaries.
