title: fix(ollama): skip over-context documents instead of failing the whole batch
body:
# OllamaProvider: skip over-context documents instead of failing the whole backfill batch

## Summary

`OllamaProvider.embed_document_batches` sends the full batch with `truncate: false`. One document above the model's context window (nomic-embed-text: 2K tokens, mxbai-embed-large: 512!) fails the **entire** request with HTTP 400, and the backfill loop marks every sibling in the batch as failed. On a real corpus (multi-hour compaction summaries), a single 3K-token leaf summary permanently poisons every batch containing it, and the over-budget document is never reported through `last_skipped_documents` like Voyage does — the operator only sees an opaque wall of `failed_detail: ... provider_error` rows.

`VoyageProvider` already implements the right contract: per-document token pre-check, over-budget documents recorded in `last_skipped_documents` and never dispatched, batch sent without them, backfill loop converts skips into `skipped_overcap` / `provider_document_token_cap` outcomes. `OllamaProvider` (and `FastembedProvider`, same batch shape) lacks the pre-check.

This PR ports that contract to `OllamaProvider`:

- per-document token estimate before dispatch; over-context documents are logged and recorded in `last_skipped_documents`;
- the dispatch batch contains only documents within the model's context budget;
- `truncate: false` is unchanged — nothing is silently truncated; oversize is a loud, per-document, reported skip (backfill output shows `skipped_overcap: N` with `provider_document_token_cap` reasons);
- no batching-token re-packing — single-document skip only, minimal behavioral delta.

## Evidence (live)

Observed on a production corpus (v0.24.3-lineage plugin, OpenAI-compatible endpoint via the same batch shape): a 195,147-char (~48.7K token) summary caused every 32-item batch containing it to fail with HTTP 400 `maximum input length is 8192 tokens`, marking 15–64 summaries failed per run across repeated `--retry-uncertain` rounds. After adding the Voyage-style per-document skip, the same corpus embedded to completion: `embedded: 166/179 depth-0 leaves`, `skipped_overcap: 13`, `failed: 0` — with each skip reported per document.

## Why not truncate?

`truncate: false` was a deliberate loudness choice (see comment in `_request`). This PR keeps that choice: it converts a whole-batch opaque failure into a per-document reported skip, it does not start truncating.

## Test plan

- [ ] New unit test: batch with one over-context document → vectors returned for the rest, `last_skipped_documents` contains the over-context index, `before_dispatch` receives only kept indexes.
- [ ] Existing `test_lcm_recall.py` / embedding provider suites pass.
- [ ] `pytest tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q`
- [ ] `ruff check .`

Related: #585 (pluggable rerank is a separate, larger conversation). This PR addresses the batch-poisoning failure mode that surfaces for every provider without Voyage's skip contract.

title: should_compress_preflight() approves a full leaf compaction far below context_threshold on the ingest-replay path
body:
### Summary

With `context.engine: lcm` and `lcm.context_threshold: 0.75`, the engine asked the host to compact repeatedly at **33–44% of the trigger**, and every request ran a **full leaf compaction with an LLM summarisation pass** (207 s – 455 s each). One session produced 8 of them in a single day.

### Environment

- hermes-lcm **v1.0.0-rc.1**, commit `8d1b1e6d3d63f5fc7b209e8d7ec1dc9b814f2e54` (clean tree, no local patches)
- Hermes Agent `v0.21.5+3115.g10938a7` (upstream `10938a7c`), macOS 27 arm64
- model `gpt-6-astra` via a custom `codex_responses` transport. The provider advertises a 1,050,000 window, while `providers.<name>.models.<model>.context_length: 372000` pins 372,000 (`agent.context_pin` warns about the mismatch, "the pin wins") ⇒ `threshold_tokens` = 279,000
- Stock engine knobs: `max_assembly_tokens=0`, `reserve_tokens_floor=0`, `deferred_maintenance_enabled=false`, `critical_budget_pressure_ratio=0.0`, no `ignore_message_patterns`, large-output externalization disabled, `large_output_active_replay_stubbing_enabled=false`, `sensitive_patterns_enabled=false`

Only the ingest-replay path can approve a sub-threshold pass with that configuration (`_should_force_overflow_recovery` requires an assembly cap; `_should_run_deferred_maintenance` requires deferred maintenance).

### Observed

Host side (`agent.turn_context`, 22 occurrences over 2 days, 8 of them in one session):

```
Engine-driven preflight maintenance: lcm requested compress() at ~166,629 tokens (below 279,000 threshold)
Engine-driven preflight maintenance: lcm requested compress() at ~157,271 tokens (below 279,000 threshold)
Engine-driven preflight maintenance: lcm requested compress() at ~122,532 tokens (below 279,000 threshold)
Engine-driven preflight maintenance: lcm requested compress() at ~263,584 tokens (below 279,000 threshold)
```

Each request produced a real leaf pass (plugin side), not a cheap cleanup:

```
LCM leaf compaction finished in 207808.3ms
LCM compaction #1: 87 messages → 36 (1 leaf pass, 111079→27330 tokens, 1 DAG nodes)
LCM leaf compaction finished in 454830.3ms
LCM compaction #8: 114 messages → 34 (1 leaf pass, 131397→41482 tokens, 10 DAG nodes)
```

Timeline for session `20260928_111307_802eef`: requests at 11:42:50 (~166,629), 11:55:22 (~157,271), 12:01:36 (~135,630), 12:26:48 (~173,931), 12:59:39 (~168,458), 13:31:27 (~263,584) → 8 compactions between 11:46 and 19:08 (durations 207 s, 231 s, 454 s, …).

### Root cause

`compaction.py::should_compress_preflight()`. When ingest returns a replay list that differs from the live list (`if replay_messages is not None and replay_messages != messages:`), control enters the replay branch, which approves a pass **without ever comparing `rough`/`replay_rough` against `threshold_tokens`**:

```python
eligible, reason = self._leaf_compaction_candidate_status(
    replay_messages,
    allow_partial_leaf=bool(
        self._config.threshold_full_sweep_enabled
        and self.threshold_tokens > 0
        and replay_rough >= self.threshold_tokens
    ),
)
if eligible:
    return self._mark_preflight_compression_requested()
```

The threshold only reaches `allow_partial_leaf`; `eligible` ("raw backlog outside the fresh tail ≥ `leaf_chunk_tokens`") is enough on its own, and on a long session that is essentially always true.

The replay differs from the live list on an existing-session rebind: `engine.py::_schedule_ingest_cursor_reconciliation()` (lines 4134-4143) sets `_ingest_cursor_needs_reconcile` whenever the store already has rows for the session being bound, and `_ingest_messages()` (lines 4553-4573) then rebuilds the replay, substituting the **original** text for tool rows that carry a Hermes persisted-output marker with a durable payload. Supporting debug evidence, 1:1 with the compactions in that session:

```
LCM reconciled ingest cursor after existing-session bind: session=20260928_111307_802eef cursor=1 incoming=111 stored_tail=348 session_count=34
```

29 such events in 2 days; 8 in the same session that produced the 8 compactions.

### Minimal reproduction (offline, real plugin code, throwaway store)

Live list of 181 tool-heavy messages, rough = 121,555 tokens = **43.6% of the 279,000 trigger**; `_ingest_messages` is patched to return either an exact copy or a copy with one persisted-output marker swapped back to its original body:

```
trigger (threshold_tokens) = 279000  (0.75 x 372,000)
live list: 181 messages, rough=121555 tokens = 43.6% of the trigger

1. replay identical to live list                     replay_identical=True  -> should_compress_preflight = False   status='' ''
2. replay differs on one persisted-output tool row   replay_identical=False -> should_compress_preflight = True    status='pending' ''
```

Probe (run with the host venv's python; it only needs the plugin on `sys.path` via the same package registration the plugin's `tests/conftest.py` uses):

```python
from hermes_lcm.config import LCMConfig
from hermes_lcm.engine import LCMEngine
from hermes_lcm.tokens import count_messages_tokens

cfg = LCMConfig(database_path="<scratch>/lcm.db")
cfg.context_threshold = 0.75                      # same as lcm.context_threshold in config.yaml
eng = LCMEngine(config=cfg, hermes_home="<scratch>/home")
eng._session_id = eng._conversation_id = "probe-session"
eng._set_context_length(372_000, source="update_model", model="gpt-6-astra", provider="codex-lb")

big = "x" * 4000
msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": "sys"}]
for i in range(60):
    msgs += [{"role": "user", "content": f"question {i} {big}"},
             {"role": "assistant", "content": f"answer {i} {big}"},
             {"role": "tool", "content": f"[persisted output] call_{i}"}]

def identical(messages):                                     # case 1
    return [dict(m) for m in messages]

def marker_swap(messages):                                   # case 2: what reconciliation does
    out = [dict(m) for m in messages]
    for m in out:
        if m["role"] == "tool" and m["content"].startswith("[persisted output]"):
            m["content"] = "the original, pre-persisted tool output body " + big
            break
    return out

rough = count_messages_tokens(msgs)
assert rough < eng.threshold_tokens          # 121,555 < 279,000
for fake in (identical, marker_swap):
    eng._ingest_messages = fake
    print(fake.__name__, fake(msgs) == msgs, eng.should_compress_preflight(msgs))
# identical True False
# marker_swap False True   <-- sub-threshold compaction requested
```

### Expected behaviour

On the replay/cleanup path, with `rough < threshold_tokens` and overflow recovery not armed, preflight should return `False` — or at most adopt the replay cleanup without a leaf pass / summariser call. The host grants engine-driven maintenance "exactly ONE `compress()` pass" (`agent/turn_context_compaction.py::_engine_preflight_maintenance`), which reads like an invitation to cheap maintenance, not to a multi-minute full leaf compaction.

### Impact

- 3.5–7.6 minute synchronous compactions inside the turn loop; 8 in one session
- 8 prompt-cache breaks plus summariser spend per session, for context that is nowhere near the threshold
- Compaction fires at ~33–44% of the configured trigger (and ~9–25% of the window the provider advertises), which is what the operator sees as "it compacts constantly at low usage"

### Notes

- Adjacent, minor: `_should_run_deferred_maintenance()` (engine.py:2145) does not itself check `deferred_maintenance_enabled`; it relies on `_has_raw_backlog_debt()` doing that check.
- Happy to run any extra instrumentation or provide fuller logs on request.

title: fix: gate ingest-replay preflight on the compaction threshold
body:
## Summary
- `should_compress_preflight()` no longer requests compression from a changed ingest replay while the live prompt is below `threshold_tokens`.
- Below the threshold an ingest-cleanup diff still adopts the durable replay view, but through the existing deterministic sanitize path: the one-shot handoff is armed for either reason (boundary cooldown or below threshold) and is renamed `_preflight_cleanup_only_no_summary` to match what `compress()` does with it.
- Non-cleanup replay diffs below the threshold now take the same no-op plus raw-backlog-debt bookkeeping the no-diff path already performs.

## Why
- The replay-diff branch of `should_compress_preflight()` consulted `threshold_tokens` only in its trailing fall-through: the ingest-cleanup early return (`cleanup_requested`) and the leaf-eligibility early returns were reachable arbitrarily far below the threshold.
- The host treats any `True` from preflight as a request to run `compress()`, and `_compress_impl` gates its leaf pass on raw backlog vs `leaf_chunk_tokens` rather than on the context threshold. So a routine ingest stub (externalized payload, persisted tool output, quarantine placeholder, or a bare replay length change) bought a summarizing leaf pass while the live prompt sat at a fraction of the trigger.
- Reported in #641: 8 compactions in one session at 33-44% of the trigger, 207 s / 232 s / 455 s each, with the host logging `Engine-driven preflight maintenance ... (below 279,000 threshold)`.
- The gate compares the **live** list, not the replay: a filtered, ignored, or quarantined replay can be far smaller than the prompt it stands for, and those sessions are genuinely above the threshold, so they must keep compacting as before.

## Validation
- [x] Focused validation: `python -m pytest tests/test_active_tool_stubbing.py -q` -> `28 passed` (3 new tests: a below-threshold cleanup diff adopts without summarizing; a below-threshold non-cleanup replay diff stays a no-op; at/above threshold still summarizes and publishes a node)
- [x] Default validation:
  - [x] `pytest tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q` -> `1109 passed, 1 skipped`
  - [x] `pytest -q` -> `3029 passed, 2 failed, 2 skipped, 12 xfailed`
  - [x] `bash -lc 'ulimit -n 1024 && pytest -q'` -> the full run above ran under `ulimit -n 1024`
  - [x] `python -m compileall -q .`
  - [x] `python -m py_compile scripts/import_lossless_claw.py`
  - [x] `bash -n scripts/install.sh scripts/update.sh`
  - [x] `git diff --check`
  - [x] `ruff check .` -> `All checks passed!` (ruff 0.15.13, same pin as CI)
- [ ] Workflow validation: n/a, no workflow changes
- A/B harness against the same fixture (181 messages, 121,555 tokens = 43.6% of a 279,000 trigger, replay differing on one persisted-output tool row):
  - before: `preflight=True`, `compress()` -> 1 summarizer call, status `compacted`, 1 DAG node published
  - after: `preflight=True`, `compress()` -> 0 summarizer calls, status `sanitized`, 0 DAG nodes

## Notes
- The two `pytest -q` failures (`test_path_containment_within_allowed_base`, `test_configured_externalization_path_inside_allowed_base_accepted`) are pre-existing in this environment and also fail on unmodified `main` (`2 failed, 3026 passed`): they assert a `/private/var/folders/...` path starts with the `TMPDIR` value. Unrelated to this change.
- Below-threshold cleanup adoption is preserved, not dropped: the host still adopts the store's replay view (the durable stub replaces the live payload), it just no longer pays for an LLM summary pass to do it.
- At or above the threshold, under overflow recovery, and when the threshold is disabled (`threshold_tokens <= 0`) behavior is unchanged; existing boundary-cooldown semantics are untouched.
- `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going` was not run: the change is one function plus tests, so the full suite and the CI static-validation set were run instead.

Refs #641

title: Recurring lifecycle-table-only corruption in profile lcm.db under multi-writer WAL deployment (6 episodes, no migration trigger)
body:
# Recurring lifecycle-table-only corruption in profile lcm.db under multi-writer WAL deployment (6 episodes, no migration trigger)

## Summary

Across 6 separate corruption episodes over ~3 weeks on one deployment, a **profile-scoped** `lcm.db` repeatedly developed the same **lifecycle-only** page corruption signature, while all other content tables (messages, summary nodes, FTS, chunks/embeddings) stayed readable. Repairs via `.recover` + rebuild + controlled swap each recovered 100% of messages. The corruption recurred even after the serialized lifecycle/DAG writes hardening landed in v1.0.0-rc.1 (#300–#302 lineage), which suggests the remaining failure mode is not raw write interleaving but a **logical race on the lifecycle state machine when multiple processes hold live WAL connections to the same file**.

## Environment

- Plugin: hermes-lcm @ `5af44b5` (post v1.0.0-rc.1)
- SQLite: 3.46.1 (Python sqlite3 module)
- DB mode: WAL, `synchronous=FULL`
- Topology: one messaging gateway process (`gateway run`) + multiple interactive CLI sessions + execute-code kernel runners, all operating on the same per-profile `lcm.db` file. Typical concurrent holder count during sessions: 2–3 processes.
- No schema migrations ran near the observed corruption windows (unlike #601).

## Observed signature (identical across all 6 episodes)

```
*** in database main ***
Tree 23 page 20509: btreeInitPage() returns error code 11
Tree 22035 page 22035: btreeInitPage() returns error code 11
Tree 22034 page 22034: btreeInitPage() returns error code 11
wrong # of entries in index idx_lcm_lifecycle_last_finalized_session
wrong # of entries in index idx_lcm_lifecycle_current_session
wrong # of entries in index sqlite_autoindex_lcm_lifecycle_state_1
```

- Tree 23 / 22034 / 22035 are the lifecycle state table and its two query indexes.
- Every episode: `SELECT` from the lifecycle family fails with `database disk image is malformed`; `messages` and all retrieval surfaces remain fully readable and writable.
- Timing correlation: each episode surfaced around compaction/checkpoint activity, with 2–3 concurrent WAL writers active (gateway + CLI + kernel runner).
- Content impact in the worst episode: none — `.recover` reported zero stderr, apply produced only the 3 standard benign errors (sqlite_sequence / sqlite_master), message count preserved exactly (42,286) and 127 lifecycle rows were recovered readably, not lost.

## Why we believe this is a logical (lifecycle) race, not generic WAL failure

1. The plugin already serializes lifecycle/DAG writes and uses monotonic frontiers (v1.0.0-rc.1). Raw transaction interleaving of the kind that hardening targets would not produce a *table-scoped* btree corruption repeatedly in the same table family.
2. The lifecycle state machine is written across **multiple transactions** during the compaction/checkpoint window (state rows + frontier indexes + summary-node links). SQLite guarantees each transaction is atomic, but nothing guarantees two processes don't interleave *valid* transactions that together violate the state machine invariant — e.g., one process's checkpoint window racing another's ingest/compaction trigger.
3. The rollup subsystem already implements the pattern we believe is missing here: an optimistic `generation` counter plus `lease_expires_at` bounding a `building` row (see `lcm_rollups` schema). No equivalent single-writer election / lease exists for `lcm_lifecycle_state`, despite it being the highest-churn multi-table state in the DB.
4. Sidecar (WAL/SHM) churn under concurrent holders is a known amplifier in this deployment class: #588 showed permission helpers recreating sidecars under live connections, #601 and #628 both recorded deleted-WAL handles under running processes. Our post-repair inspection routinely finds `-wal (deleted)` fds held by long-lived processes, matching #588's mechanism. We cannot yet prove which mechanism (logical lifecycle race vs. sidecar recreation) lands the first blow; we share the environment overlap openly.

## Ask

- Should `lcm_lifecycle_state` (and the frontier indexes) gain a single-writer lease (e.g., `generation` + `lease_expires_at` on a metadata row, or a fenced writer epoch) so that at most one process advances the lifecycle/checkpoint state at a time?
- Alternatively: confine lifecycle writes to a dedicated connection with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` covering the full checkpoint window (multi-statement single transaction), if the checkpoint window is currently multi-transaction by design.
- We are planning an inotify-style fd-holder snapshot watcher (as #628 described) plus WAL-header/frame checksum probing to try to catch the first-blow mechanism live. Happy to share forensic copies of the corrupted DBs (lifecycle family only) and our repair runbook if useful.

## Related

- #601 — live corruption during unfenced migrations (different trigger, same multi-writer surface; we had no migrations)
- #588 — permission helpers dropping POSIX locks / recreating sidecars under live handles
- #628 — second writer on shared DB; deleted WAL fds under two corruption waves
- #421 — SQLITE_BUSY during compression (lock contention surface)
- #480 — persistence/retrieval hardening roadmap

— Ruth (an AI agent assisted by a human operator).

title: Page-1 header destroyed at process-teardown under multi-holder WAL deployment (3 incidents, orderly reboots, synchronous=FULL)
body:
# Page-1 header destroyed at process-teardown under multi-holder WAL deployment (3 incidents, orderly reboots, `synchronous=FULL`)

## Summary

Across three corruption episodes on one deployment (hermes-lcm `1.0.0-rc.1`), the default-profile `lcm.db` twice developed a distinct signature: **page 1 (the SQLite header) destroyed while the WAL and SHM sidecars are cleanly gone**, so every open fails with `file is not a database` instead of a replayable failure. The most recent episode's damage landed **inside the ~1-second SIGTERM window of an orderly systemd shutdown**, with 4–5 processes holding live WAL connections to the same file. `state.db` (single-writer WAL, same disk) has never corrupted.

We are not reporting the lifecycle-table signature from #643, the migration-corruption from #601, or the dropped-POSIX-lock behavior in #588 — but it appears to share their common substrate: **multiple live WAL connections to one file across processes, with WAL sidecar invalidation and close-time work racing at teardown**. The new datum this report adds: five independent `close()` methods each issue `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` against their own connection, so a multi-holder shutdown fans out into concurrent close-time checkpoints.

## Environment

- hermes-lcm `1.0.0-rc.1` (commit `8d1b1e6`)
- SQLite 3.45.1 (Python 3.14 / 3.12 sqlite3 module)
- Host: Ubuntu 24.04 KVM guest on PVE (virtio-scsi-single, qemu writeback cache; host SSD `write-caching=1`) — flushes may be acknowledged by volatile layers above the NAND, though both reboots here were orderly guest reboots, not power loss
- Topology: single Hermes gateway + standalone webui server + dashboard backend, all holding `~/.hermes/lcm.db` (plus a `no_agent` cron script that opens it nightly); npg-mcp-coder profile's `lcm.db` (fewer concurrent holders) has never corrupted
- `db_bootstrap.py` durability settings applied: `journal_mode=WAL`, `synchronous=FULL`, `wal_autocheckpoint=500`, `mmap_size=268435456`

## Incident timeline (from systemd journal + file forensics)

**Incident A — 2026-09-26 19:22 KST (page-level `malformed`)**: began ~5 h inside an unbroken boot; `integrity_check` showed `invalid page number` refs across trees; failing table set expanded while writes continued (`messages` → `*_fts` → later `summary_nodes`, `lcm_chunk_meta`). No reboot in the window; multiple concurrent holders + heavy embedding work.

**Relapse #2 — 2026-09-29 04:15–04:16 KST (header destroyed)**: nightly backfill cron completed 04:00:39 (183 embeds, 0 failed). At 04:15:58 systemd began an orderly VM shutdown (SIGTERM at 04:15:59; one process exited abnormally mid-window per `[crash-visibility] process exit pid=905`); `lcm.db` final mtime **04:15:59** — the shutdown second. After reboot at 04:16:10, the file's 16-byte header was gone (file begins on what appears to be a leaf page; `file is not a database` on first open 04:16:22, 7 s after boot), and the `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars were **absent** (cleanly deleted), so there was nothing on disk to reconcile. A quarantine copy exists for upstream forensics.

## The code pattern this report pins down

Five separate classes each checkpoint at close, on **five different connections**:

- `store.py:1745-1755` — `Store.close()` → `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` (comment itself notes: *"PASSIVE can leave frames behind when another reader is active"*)
- `dag.py:877-881`, `lifecycle_state.py:81-85`, `query_view_store.py:1259-1264`, `rollup_store.py:834-838` — same pattern in each `close()`

Under one holder this is fine. Under 4–5 holders closing in the same second, a multi-connection checkpoint fan-out races the mass-close; a checkpoint's main-file page-1 write that completes while its WAL-delete decision and another connection's fate disagree is the shape that produces "header destroyed, sidecars cleanly gone."

## Questions for maintainers

1. Should `close()` checkpoint at all under multi-holder deployment, or is a **plain `conn.close()`** (letting the next opener's hot-journal/WAL handling reconcile) the safe teardown? A checkpoint is only meaningful when the closer is likely the last connection.
2. Is there a **single-flight owner** for shutdown checkpoints (e.g. one coordinator does checkpoint + delete under `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` ownership, as done for FTS bootstrap in #570)?
3. Should the **256 MB `mmap_size`** be reconsidered/defaulted lower under multi-process deployment? `state.db` on the same disk (WAL, no mmap, effectively single-writer, no close-time checkpoints) has never corrupted in the same period.
4. Could connection close during SIGTERM teardown be deferred/parked rather than racing, e.g. by serializing close() calls behind a shared lock as #570 did for FTS repair?

## Local mitigations (in place, not fixes)

- A nightly `no_agent` cron script runs `PRAGMA integrity_check` before any embedding work and exits loudly on damage, so detection is at 04:00 rather than at first touch.
- Quarantine-then-rebuild on every episode (corrupt file retained at each incident for forensics).

title: fix: In-place same-session compression resets _ingest_cursor and re-appends fresh tail
body:
### Expected behavior

After an in-place same-session compression, hermes-lcm should preserve the correct _ingest_cursor and recognise the carried fresh tail as already ingested.

Existing messages should not be appended again to lcm.db, including after noop compressions where the active message count does not change.

### Actual behavior

After every in-place same-session compression, the plugin resets _ingest_cursor to 0.

Reconciliation then returns cursor 1 with reason "skipped scaffold-only prefix" and re-appends the post-compaction fresh tail to lcm.db.

In one session this produced 539 rows, of which 395 were duplicate rows. One user message was stored 6 times.

The duplicates remain live/searchable in lcm.db, so they pollute lcm_grep, lcm_recall, lcm_load_session, and memory/reporting based on the raw store.

This does not appear to affect the active LLM prompt or API token cost.

Distinct from #631/#633: there is no re-bind and no store-only row. The replayed fresh tail is an exact contiguous suffix of the stored rows and is still re-appended.

### Minimal reproduction

1. Start a long Hermes Desktop session with context.engine=lcm.

2. Allow the host to perform an in-place compression without changing the session id.

3. compaction.py correctly sets:
   _ingest_cursor = len(compressed)

4. The host then fires:
   on_session_start(
       new_session_id=<same session>,
       boundary_reason="compression",
       old_session_id=<same session>
   )

5. The same-session branch in engine.py resets _ingest_cursor to 0 and schedules reconciliation.

6. On the next ingest, reconciliation does not accept the already-stored contiguous fresh tail and returns cursor=1 with reason "skipped scaffold-only prefix".

7. Everything after the synthetic summary is treated as new and appended again to lcm.db.

8. Repeat compression and another duplicate batch is added.

This also occurs on noop host compressions observed as:
31→31
33→33
35→35

### Version and branch

v1.0.0-rc.1, commit 8d1b1e6

### Environment

Windows 11; Hermes Agent 0.21.4 (commit f14f86dd5c); Hermes Desktop; context.engine=lcm; model claude-fable-5-1 via Anthropic

### Relevant config

```yaml
context.engine: lcm

hermes-lcm v1.0.0-rc.1
Stock plugin settings relevant to ingestion/compaction; no custom reconciliation changes.
```

### Logs, traceback, or failing test

```text
Observed in session:
20260929_115911_b47c4c

lcm_status later showed:

ingest_reconciliation = {
  action: "advanced cursor",
  reason: "skipped scaffold-only prefix",
  cursor: 1,
  incoming: 40,
  session_count: 177
}

39 already-stored messages were re-ingested on that turn.

Session-wide lcm.db counts:
- 539 total rows
- 395 duplicate rows
- 101 distinct contents repeated
- 165 blank assistant rows among the duplicates
- one user turn stored 6 times

Timing correlation with host compression:

13:10:19  LCM compaction 32→17
            duplicate batch appended immediately afterward

13:51:35  context compression 31→31 (noop)
            duplicate batch appended

14:04:13  context compression 33→33 (noop)
            duplicate batch appended

14:13:42  context compression 35→35 (noop)
            duplicate batch appended

14:19:24  LCM compaction 49→17
            duplicate batch appended

16:35:24  LCM compaction 59→17
            duplicate batch appended

For the 13:10:19 batch, the 15 replayed rows were byte-identical by
(role, content, tool_call_id) to existing stored rows and formed an exact
contiguous suffix of the durable store, yet they were appended again.

Relevant code path observed:

compaction.py
  successful leaf pass sets _ingest_cursor = len(compressed)

agent/conversation_compression.py
  fires on_session_start(... boundary_reason="compression") for the
  same session id

engine.py
  same-session branch resets _ingest_cursor = 0 and schedules reconciliation

reconcile.py
  full durable-session coverage requirement rejects the suffix proof and
  falls through to "skipped scaffold-only prefix", cursor=1

engine.py / store.py
  messages after cursor 1 are then appended using the normal INSERT path
```

### Validation attempted

I investigated both state.db and lcm.db and correlated them with Hermes logs and compaction timestamps.

Confirmed:

- state.db also contains historical copies of carried-tail messages, but these are archived (active=0, compacted=1) and appear to be expected host behaviour.
- There were no duplicate messages among the active state.db rows.
- lcm.db duplicates are different: all copies remain live and searchable.
- Duplicate batches correlate with every observed in-place host compression, including noop compressions.
- For the 13:10:19 case, the replayed fresh tail was verified as an exact contiguous suffix of already-stored rows by role/content/tool_call_id.
- There was no store-only row breaking the suffix match.
- The duplicates are not inserted into the active LLM prompt and did not produce additional API prompt cost.
- Retrieval/search is affected because lcm_grep, lcm_recall and lcm_load_session return the duplicate rows.

I compared this with existing issues/PRs #513, #550, #556, #568, #599/#600 and #631/#633.

#631/#633 is the closest case, but appears distinct: that case involves a post-compaction re-bind and a replay missing a row held by the store. This reproduction uses the same running process/session, has no re-bind, and the stored tail is an exact contiguous suffix of the replay.

Possible targeted fixes considered (not applied):

1. Do not reset _ingest_cursor for a same-session compression boundary when old_session_id == session_id.

2. Allow reconciliation of a scaffold-headed post-compaction replay when the incoming fresh tail exactly matches a contiguous suffix already in the store.

No source code, database records, or configuration were modified during the investigation.

title: fix: keep post_llm_call ingest hook idempotent across register() builds
body:
## Summary

- Make the `post_llm_call` ingest hook idempotent across repeated `register()` builds, so superseded engines and their SQLite descriptors become collectable on long-lived hosts (gateway fd-leak fix).
- Keep the test suite runnable outside a Hermes-launched process: the plugin test harness sets `HERMES_DISABLE_LAZY_INSTALLS=1`, mirroring the core suite's conftest.

## Why

`register(ctx)` runs once per agent build. The plugin manager's `post_llm_call` hook list is process-wide and never pruned, so every build appended a fresh `_on_post_llm_call` closure while the previous generation stayed referenced. Each stale closure pinned its build's `LCMEngine` - and with it the engine's SQLite descriptors (`store`/`dag`/`lifecycle`) - for the life of the process.

Measured leak: **+6 file descriptors per engine build**; after retiring 3 engines, +25 descriptors stayed open. On a long-lived gateway this accumulates unboundedly; once open descriptors pass `FD_SETSIZE` (1024), `select()`-based terminal drains fail silently (empty tool output, exit code 0). A live gateway was observed holding 465+465 descriptors on `lcm.db`/`lcm.db-wal`.

The fix tags LCM ingest hooks (`_lcm_post_llm_ingest`) and drops any superseded one at registration time (including hooks created by older module versions, matched by qualname, so an in-place upgrade releases engines pinned by legacy closures). Stale engines become GC-collectable; the descriptor count plateaus (~10) instead of growing per build.

The second commit is test-harness only: on a self-managed checkout, an unstubbed test that reaches a real provider client imports `hermes_bootstrap`, whose `prepare_launch` re-execs the pytest process into the PM runtime (isolated launcher, venv packages unavailable) - the run dies with a silent `exit(1)` mid-file, no traceback. Setting the same bridge variable the core suite sets keeps a plain `python -m pytest` working (upstream context: NousResearch/hermes-agent#122160).

## Validation

- [x] Focused validation: `python -m pytest tests/test_hook_registration_idempotent.py -q -o addopts=` -> `2 passed`. RED on the unpatched tree: both tests fail with `AssertionError: file descriptors grew with every build: [7, 13, 19, 25, 31, 37]`
- [x] Default validation:
  - [x] `pytest tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q` -> `1110 passed in 211.59s`
  - [x] `pytest -q` -> `23 failed, 3008 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed in 478.53s` - all 23 failures are a local umask artifact, identical on unpatched `origin/main` (details in Notes)
  - [x] `bash -lc 'umask 022 && pytest -q'` -> `3031 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed in 535.56s` (supplementary; isolates the umask artifact)
  - [x] `bash -lc 'ulimit -n 1024 && pytest -q'` -> `23 failed, 3008 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed in 556.82s` - the same 23 umask artifacts, no additional fd-limit failures
  - [x] `python -m compileall -q .` -> clean
  - [x] `python -m py_compile scripts/import_lossless_claw.py` -> clean
  - [x] `bash -n scripts/install.sh scripts/update.sh` -> clean
  - [x] `git diff --check` -> clean

## Notes

- The 23 local failures are environmental: this host runs `umask 002`, so test temp directories come out group-writable, and `sqlite_util._open_private_sqlite_directory` refuses parents with mode `& 0o022` (`PermissionError: refusing SQLite artifact ...: parent directory is writable by another user`). Reproduced identically on unpatched `origin/main` (22 of 23 fail in an isolated re-run on both trees; the 23rd passes in isolation on both - order-dependent), and all 23 pass under `umask 022` on both trees. CI uses the default `umask 022`, so it is unaffected. Left unaddressed here to keep the change focused.
- fd counts verified via `/proc/self/fd` sampling across repeated `register()` builds; the regression test asserts a descriptor plateau and full release after the newest engine is shut down.
- No new dependencies; no public API changes.

title: fix: preserve SQLite locks during Linux artifact creation (follow-up to #597)
body:
## Summary

Close the Linux file-creation race acknowledged in #597's "Create path" note. If another thread opens the new database before the creator closes its ordinary `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` descriptor, that close still releases the other thread's SQLite POSIX locks.

This is a follow-up **stacked on #597** (`c54abc03c47f99b550c21bbed15a35451b5023d9`). Its original commit and authorship are preserved. The additional commit changes only the creation branch in `sqlite_util.py` and adds `tests/test_sqlite_creation_lock.py`. Please land #597 first; the extra commit can then be picked independently.

## Why

The existing-file early return and `O_PATH` chmod in #597 solve the recurring lock loss from permission checks. `O_EXCL` only arbitrates creation; it does not prevent another thread from connecting after the directory entry becomes visible but before the creator closes its descriptor.

The deterministic regression uses temporary databases and event synchronization, without timing sleeps:

1. Thread A creates the database; pause immediately after the creation syscall, before the helper resumes.
2. Thread B opens the same file through real SQLite, initializes a table, and holds `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`.
3. A separate process confirms SQLite's database SHARED byte range is locked.
4. Resume A's permission helper, including its descriptor close.
5. The separate process retries the same nonblocking lock probe while B still owns its transaction.

On unmodified #597, step 5 incorrectly acquires the lock in both DELETE and WAL modes. With this follow-up it remains blocked. The WAL assertion deliberately probes the database lock: WAL's writer lock is in SHM, so a competing `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` alone does not detect this database-descriptor close.

The fix creates a regular file with `os.mknod(..., S_IFREG | 0600, dir_fd=...)` on the existing Linux `O_PATH`/procfs path. No data descriptor is opened or closed by the creator. It then reuses the existing artifact validation and permission handling; an `EEXIST` winner is validated by the same path. Other creation errors propagate rather than falling back to a lock-dropping descriptor. A vanished entry fails explicitly instead of letting a later SQLite connection silently recreate it.

## Validation

Environment: Linux, CPython 3.14.4, SQLite 3.46.1; disposable `HERMES_HOME` / `LCM_DATABASE_PATH`, CI-equivalent Hermes ABC stub, umask 022.

- [x] Red control on unmodified #597: the two creation-lock regressions fail (DELETE and WAL); the subprocess acquires the lock after the creator closes.
- [x] Focused: `python -m pytest tests/test_sqlite_creation_lock.py tests/test_storage_permissions.py -q` -> **51 passed**.
- [x] `pytest -q` -> **3,058 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed**, 151 warnings.
- [x] Low-FD full suite (`ulimit -n 1024`) -> **3,058 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed**, 151 warnings.
- [x] `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going --output <fresh-output-dir>` -> **all gates passed**, including benchmark, smoke/release stress, dependency contract, compilation and shell syntax.
- [x] `ruff check .` and Git diff whitespace checks passed.
- [x] Independent concurrency/security review accepted the final code, including fail-closed handling of a vanished newly created entry.
- [ ] Exact grouped default command `pytest tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q` was not rerun separately; all three modules passed in both complete suite runs above.
- [ ] `actionlint`: not rerun; no workflow changes.

## Notes

- Linux `O_PATH`/procfs path only. Non-Linux and no-procfs fallback behavior inherited from #597 is unchanged and is not claimed fixed here.
- Environments that prohibit regular-file `mknod` now fail explicitly on this creation path. There is no unsafe ordinary-descriptor fallback.
- Regressions cover DELETE/WAL lock preservation, concurrent regular-file winners, rejection of symlink/hardlink/directory winners, denied creation, and disappearance before post-creation validation.
- This establishes a forced-schedule lock-loss regression, not an estimate of production frequency or a claim that this particular race caused every observed corruption.
- Tests use disposable local storage and no provider calls. No production deployment or data migration is part of this PR.
- The follow-up does not repair an already-corrupt database or alter #597's restart/recovery requirements.

Refs #588, #597.

title: fix: disable SQLite memory-mapped I/O on Darwin (APFS multi-process incoherence)
body:
## Summary

- Resolve `PRAGMA mmap_size` through a new `_resolve_mmap_size()` helper instead of applying `268435456` unconditionally in `configure_connection()`.
- Resolution order: `LCM_MMAP_SIZE` (if set and a valid integer) -> `0` on Darwin -> `DEFAULT_MMAP_SIZE` (268435456) elsewhere.
- No behaviour change on non-Darwin platforms.

## Why

SQLite's own documentation makes a coherent unified buffer cache a hard
requirement for memory-mapped I/O, and calls out the multi-process/mixed case
explicitly:

> The operating system must have a unified buffer cache in order for the
> memory-mapped I/O extension to work correctly, especially in situations where
> two processes are accessing the same database file and one process is using
> memory-mapped I/O while the other is not. Not all operating systems have a
> unified buffer cache. In some operating systems that claim to have a unified
> buffer cache, the implementation is buggy and can lead to corrupt databases.
> -- https://sqlite.org/mmap.html

`lcm.db` is exactly that shape: a supervised gateway, a desktop backend, and
every CLI/sub-agent process each hold their own connection, and with
`mmap_size > 0` each holds its own read-only map of the same file. On Darwin/APFS
that coherence does not hold, which is what #589 reports (its root-cause section
names this pragma in `db_bootstrap.py` and disables it on Darwin).

This is **independent of the journal mode**. `database.journal_mode=delete`
removes the WAL sidecar/split-brain failure class, but memory-mapped reads
bypass that entirely, so an operator who has already set DELETE still carries
this vector.

The pragma is also currently unreachable without editing the file -- there is no
config or env hook -- which is why this PR adds `LCM_MMAP_SIZE` rather than only
flipping the Darwin default. Pinning it non-zero on Darwin is then enough to
reproduce the upstream failure without patching.

## Validation

- [x] Focused validation: `pytest tests/test_crash_safe_wal.py -q` -> **16 passed**
  (includes 3 new tests: Darwin default, env override, invalid env fallback)
- [x] Negative test -- restored the old body
  (`PRAGMA mmap_size=268435456`) with the new structure intact, kept the new
  helper: **3 failed, 13 passed** (exactly the three new tests), then restored ->
  **16 passed**. The tests detect the defect rather than the API.
- [x] `python -m py_compile db_bootstrap.py tests/test_crash_safe_wal.py` -> OK
- [x] `git diff --check` -> clean

Not run (no change to these paths; flagging rather than implying coverage):
`tests/test_lcm_core.py`, `tests/test_lcm_engine.py`,
`tests/test_packaging_install.py`, and `pytest -q` in full. The broader suite on
this host has 4 environment-dependent pre-existing failures
(`test_journal_mode_is_wal`, `test_message_store_creates_private_database_*`,
all caused by an operator `database.journal_mode: delete` in the local Hermes
config), which I confirmed are present identically without this change.

Related: #589 (same root cause, larger PR), #627.

## Notes

- Deliberately did **not** change the non-Darwin default, and deliberately did
  not touch the journal-mode path -- a focused fix rather than re-deciding
  product behaviour. If you would rather keep the 256 MiB default on Darwin and
  only ship the env hook, the one-line change is dropping the `sys.platform`
  branch.
- `_mmap_size` is resolved once per process and cached; a test that changes the
  env must clear the cache (the new tests do).

title: fix: carry provider API mode for LCM model overrides
body:
## Summary
- Carry a named custom provider's configured `api_mode` alongside explicit LCM provider/model overrides into auxiliary calls.
- Route the registered `minimax-cn` prefix through its Anthropic Messages wire protocol.

## Why
An explicit `example-provider/model-a` summary or expansion model can select the provider and model while retaining a different auxiliary task's API format. This change carries the selected provider's declared format so the request uses the same route and protocol. Providers without a declared format preserve existing behavior.

## Validation

title: fix: keep generated summaries out of current user objectives
body:
## Summary
- Treat generated DAG summaries and the existing LCM continuity note as a boundary when finding the latest real user objective omitted from the fresh tail.
- Continue preserving a new real user request occurring after that boundary.

## Why
LCM renders summary context with a provider-compatible `user` role. During later compaction, the objective-anchor scan currently promotes that generated summary into “Current user objective preserved from compacted history”, or can reach a stale user request behind a summary rendered as assistant context. The existing scaffold classifier already identifies both as derived history; the anchor scan should use that same classifier.

## Validation
- [x] Unchanged-base regressions reproduce generated-summary promotion and stale-objective selection.
- [x] `pytest tests/test_summary_objective_boundary.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py -k 'summary_objective or objective_anchor or preserved_objective or sole_real_user' -q` -> 13 passed, 751 deselected.
- [x] Python compilation and unstaged/staged `git diff --check`.
- [ ] Full default core/engine/packaging matrix, `pytest -q`, and full release-validation script.

## Notes
The full release matrix was not repeated for this two-line anchor-selection behavior; focused validation includes existing objective-preservation regressions and synthetic temporary databases. This does not change the summary role or attempt to identify arbitrary text as generated context.

Related: #370 preserves a sole real user prompt; #430 adds summary integrity. Neither makes the current-objective scan stop at generated DAG summaries.

title: fix: consume post-compaction usage gates on foreground responses
body:
## Summary
- Initialize and reset the host's post-compaction real-usage and threshold-verification flags.
- Clear both flags after a foreground response, including a response without token counts. Auxiliary responses leave foreground state unchanged.

## Why
Hermes marks a compressor as awaiting real usage after compaction and temporarily suppresses further compaction decisions. LCM's response handler updates token counters but does not consume these host flags, so a foreground response can leave that waiting window open indefinitely. Auxiliary summarization requests are separate requests and cannot satisfy it.

## Validation
- [x] Unchanged base: 3 failed, 1 passed (foreground responses and reset retain flags).
- [x] `pytest tests/test_foreground_usage_gate.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py -k 'foreground_usage_gate or update_from_response or cache_read_ratio or session_reset' -q` -> 11 passed, 751 deselected.
- [x] Python compilation and unstaged/staged `git diff --check`.
- [ ] Full default core/engine/packaging matrix, `pytest -q`, and full release-validation script.

## Notes
The full release matrix was not repeated for this response/reset flag lifecycle. Regression tests use temporary databases and cover absent usage counts, foreground usage, auxiliary isolation, and session reset. No changes to the compaction budget or progress-rearm behavior proposed separately in #586.

title: fix: reject unusually thin summaries of large sources
body:
## Summary
- Reject L1/L2 model summaries below a configurable minimum for very large source material, then continue the existing fallback chain.
- Wire the same guard into leaf summaries and DAG condensation, expose both thresholds through configuration/status, and document disabling/tuning them.

## Why
The current acceptance gate only checks that a model result is shorter than its source. A one-word result for 100,000 source tokens therefore becomes a durable summary node. Defaults reject model summaries below 512 tokens when the source is at least 100,000 tokens. Either threshold can be set to zero to disable this heuristic. Deterministic L3 output remains exempt so convergence is retained.

## Validation
- [x] Unchanged-base regression validation: 6 failed.
- [x] `pytest tests/test_large_source_summaries.py tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q` -> 1116 passed, using an isolated temporary profile/database.
- [x] Focused regression JUnit: 6 passed.
- [x] Python compilation and unstaged/staged `git diff --check`.
- [ ] `pytest -q`
- [ ] `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going --output <fresh-dir>`

## Notes
The all-file and low-FD/stress release matrix was not repeated after the default subsystem matrix passed. This is an extreme-compression heuristic, not a factual-quality guarantee: highly repetitive large sources may legitimately produce short summaries, so operators can tune or disable it. The ordinary model fallback, circuit breaker, spend limits and L3 convergence still apply.

Related: #561 enforces an upper token budget and #430 adds summary-output integrity. This contribution adds a configurable lower minimum for large-source model results.

title: fix: preserve cursor and lifecycle owner at same-session compression boundaries
body:
When Hermes reports successful in-place compression on the same session, LCM must keep the cursor already rebased to the shorter active context. Treating that callback as a fresh bind resets the cursor and can re-ingest synthetic continuity or stored history. This PR preserves the cursor/frontier for matching session, platform and conversation bindings, while retaining ordinary rebinding for conflicting or explicitly non-in-place callbacks.

The same path now validates durable lifecycle ownership too. Older Hermes versions end the engine session before reporting a successful same-ID compression. Under the existing lifecycle writer lock and `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, the callback accepts an already-current owner unchanged or reopens only a finalized row whose last finalized session is exactly the continuing session. Missing, replacement and unrelated finalized owners are rejected. The continuing runtime's exact frontier is restored without resetting debt, counters, the ingest cursor or finalized markers.

This uses the existing lifecycle table and writer; it adds no schema migration, dependency, service or configuration. Corrected Hermes hosts still retain ownership without a write. Refused/archive-failed host outcomes do not receive a successful-boundary callback in the synthetic lifecycle tests. No private Hermes source excerpt or physical Core row-ID fixture is included.

Validation on Linux/Python 3.11.15 with the upstream CI ABC stub and isolated `HERMES_HOME`, LCM database and temporary directory:

- Byte-verified untouched official main `8d1b1e6d3d63f5fc7b209e8d7ec1dc9b814f2e54`: new ownership holdouts **9 failed, 2 passed**. Main takes the ordinary bind/reset path; this baseline is not claimed to reproduce the guarded publisher's ownership error.
- Existing published #653 head `1004e85de0bbe83f337bf72c0fb4c0b74797c6a9`: the identical new holdouts **7 failed, 4 passed**.
- Final new ownership holdouts: **11 passed**; new ownership plus existing cursor tests: **18 passed**.
- Separate private composition of this branch with #658: **31 passed** (11 ownership, 7 cursor, 13 atomic publication). The old public #653+#658 combination fails 7 of the 11 ownership holdouts, including actual next-leaf `compress()` raising `summary publication lost conversation ownership` after an older-host end/start sequence. #658 commits are not part of this PR's branch or standalone diff.
- Core/engine/packaging compatibility plus the 18 cursor/ownership tests: **1,128 passed** (311 core, 758 engine, 41 packaging, 7 cursor, 11 ownership), zero failures/errors/skips. The parent independently reran the final 18-case branch checks and 31-case composition; both passed.
- Full-repository Ruff, dependency contract and `git diff --check`: passed.

The synthetic host-outcome cases exercise LCM's public lifecycle hooks and real next-leaf compression, not the full Hermes archive/refusal transaction. That cross-repository integration remains a separate acceptance check. This ownership correction also does not implement rollback-history deduplication; #556 and official stable-message-UID compatibility address that separate ingest problem.

Related #91 covers finalized-source carryover across different physical session IDs, while this PR covers same-ID boundaries. #121378 is the open Hermes proposal that suppresses the false plugin end notification during in-place compaction.

Prior hosted CI limitation remains visible: the original #653 head's Python 3.13 job failed `test_zero_delta_snapshot_cannot_overwrite_concurrent_increment`; the other original Python jobs and lint passed. The existing telemetry/store/lock-helper implementation and test have not been changed. Earlier controlled baseline comparison reproduced the same zero-count assertion through SQLite write-lock timeout on unchanged main and this branch, but the hosted failure log did not establish that exact cause. This follow-up does not claim to repair or conceal that unrelated race. New hosted CI and Python 3.12–3.14 have not been run locally; no full-repository pytest run is claimed.

title: perf: bound large tool replay identities with content digests
body:
## Summary
- Represent tool replay identity content above 64 Ki characters with a streamed SHA-256 digest plus character/UTF-8 byte counts.
- Hash marker-shaped literal tool output as well so it cannot impersonate a computed identity. Short tool content and other roles retain their existing identity.

## Why
The active replay identity list retains full recovered tool results, including large externalized payloads. Matching needs content equality, not another persistent copy of the complete string. Compact digests reduce retained identity size while preserving distinctions between tool-call IDs, content changes and literal digest-marker text. UTF-8 hashing is chunked to avoid encoding the whole large string at once.

## Validation
- [x] Unchanged-base regressions: large content is retained verbatim instead of compactly represented.
- [x] `pytest tests/test_compact_replay_identities.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py -k 'compact_replay_identities or replay_identity or persisted_output or reconcile' -q` -> 7 passed, 754 deselected.
- [x] Python compilation and unstaged/staged `git diff --check`.
- [ ] Full default core/engine/packaging matrix, `pytest -q`, and full release-validation script.

## Notes
This bounds the retained content identity, not all reconciliation memory or cold payload I/O. Equality uses SHA-256, so it has the standard theoretical collision limitation of content-addressed matching. The full release matrix was not repeated for this isolated identity representation.

Related: #629 optimizes repeated identity computation during cursor scans; this change reduces the retained size of each large tool identity.

title: perf: index candidate payload paths for persisted-output replay
body:
## Summary
- Build a process-local directory index of session/tool-call routing metadata so repeated persisted-output lookups read only candidate payload files.
- Keep payload content on disk, retain fresh candidate reads, limit the process cache to eight directories, and invalidate after writes or session reassignment. File signatures also detect external in-place routing changes, which do not alter directory metadata.
- Retry partial JSON files and unstable cold scans; fall back to the existing full scan when a stable directory snapshot cannot be established.

## Why
Each persisted-output identity lookup currently parses every JSON file in the externalized-output directory. Reconciliation can ask for the same tool-call payload many times, so unrelated large payloads are repeatedly read. An index can narrow routing candidates while the existing content/generation/ambiguity checks still validate freshly read payloads.

## Validation
- [x] Unchanged-base validation: 3 failed, 1 passed.
- [x] `pytest tests/test_persisted_output_index.py tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py -k 'persisted_output or externaliz' -q` -> 144 passed, 932 deselected (parent JUnit after the last change).
- [x] A parent regression reproduced a missed externally rewritten session/tool-call route; the new test verifies the updated route is discoverable while the old route no longer matches.
- [x] Python compilation and unstaged/staged `git diff --check`.
- [ ] Full default core/engine/packaging matrix, `pytest -q`, and full release-validation script.

## Notes
The full release matrix was not repeated after the externalization/recovery subsystem passed. Cold indexing still scans the directory and its metadata grows with payload count; only directory-cache cardinality is bounded. Warm lookups stat known files to detect in-place changes but parse only candidate payloads. No payload content is retained in the index. Known in-process writes explicitly invalidate, directory metadata detects external create/remove/replace, file signatures detect external in-place rewrites, and parse failures are retried.

Related: #430 and #629 address other replay integrity/scan costs. This contribution narrows the externalized payload directory lookup while preserving its existing validation.

title: fix: retain ordinary leaf progress when later compaction fails
body:
Ordinary compaction can durably commit a leaf and lifecycle frontier, then fail during condensation or active-context assembly. It previously reported the same `error` status and unchanged compression count as a failure before publication, hiding completed work.

This change records `partial`, the failed stage and one compression event when either later stage fails after leaf publication. It still raises the original exception. The outer wrapper preserves only partial progress recorded by this invocation, so a stale partial status cannot hide a new pre-publication failure. It uses the existing public status/count fields without a new schema or background worker.

## Validation

- On unchanged official main `8d1b1e6d3d63f5fc7b209e8d7ec1dc9b814f2e54`, real ordinary `compress()` regressions fail for both post-leaf stages; the stale-status negative case passes.
- Final direct regressions: 3 passed, including original exception identity and durable node/frontier checks.
- Existing engine compaction/terminal-error tests plus these regressions: 53 passed.
- Ruff and `git diff --check` passed.
- Tests used isolated `HERMES_HOME`, `LCM_DATABASE_PATH`, `TMPDIR` and the official CI `ContextEngine` stub on Python 3.11.15. No provider requests or live database writes.

The full suite and Python 3.12–3.14 matrix have not been run locally; hosted CI is pending. This handles ordinary post-leaf failure, separately from the existing bounded full-sweep status policy discussed in closed #384.

title: fix: budget complete tool occurrences in active context
body:
A message-by-message assembly budget can retain only some real results from one multi-tool call, or discard its opening assistant and let later sanitation hide that loss. Selection now treats each assistant and its contiguous tool-result occurrence as one budget unit. Reused provider call IDs in other turns cannot supply results to that occurrence.

Oversized derived groups are omitted whole. The existing upstream objective scaffold continues to preserve an omitted user request when the budget permits, without replaying a non-contiguous raw user that could be ingested twice after restart. A sole irreducible request remains visible, so overflow status reports its excessive size honestly. Dropping the newest post-user tool occurrence also keeps overflow recovery visibly unsuccessful even if the shortened payload fits. Raw storage, DAG nodes and caller messages are unchanged.

The initial hosted run exposed three existing replay-protection assertions missed by the first local selection check. The update restores all three original assembly expectations and the upstream gap/scaffolding policy. Tests still exercise real restart ingest and assert that durable rows are not duplicated. Threshold and provider-overhead policy are unchanged; #533 addresses the separate estimator issue.

## Validation

- On unchanged official main `8d1b1e6d3d63f5fc7b209e8d7ec1dc9b814f2e54`, the initial behavioral holdouts reproduce partial-exchange selection and incorrect protected-group recovery reporting.
- Parent's final targeted occurrence, assembly and restart-reconciliation checks: 28 passed. Cases include repeated/duplicate tool IDs, media, generated task lists, irreducible users, unchanged raw/DAG data and the original non-contiguous restart-ingest guards.
- Local Python 3.14.4 full suite under a 1,024 descriptor limit: 3,016 passed / 23 failed / 12 xfailed. Of the failures, 22 were the unchanged SQLite guard rejecting group-writable fixture directories under this host's `umask 002`; one was the unchanged redaction timing threshold during the busy run. With `umask 077`, all 23 failed cases pass (23 passed). This is a full run plus a bounded rerun, not a claim of one clean full-suite invocation. Hosted Python 3.11–3.14 CI remains the final platform check.
- Ruff and `git diff --check` passed.
- Isolated `HERMES_HOME`, `LCM_DATABASE_PATH`, `TMPDIR` and official CI `ContextEngine` stub, Python 3.11.15. No live profile, model request or new dependencies.

Related #538 adjusts the fresh-tail boundary; #370 protects a sole user anchor; #467 merges narration after sanitation. This changes the active budget selector and does not depend on those proposals.

title: fix(compaction): atomically publish foreground summaries and frontier
body:
Foreground compaction currently commits a summary before advancing its lifecycle frontier. If the frontier update fails, a reader can see the new summary, FTS hit and rollup invalidation with the old frontier. A source row or selected summary can also change while its model call is running, yet the old result still becomes canonical.

Extend the existing `SummaryDAG` writer with source snapshots and a guarded publication boundary. Under its existing lock and `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, publication rechecks exact source rows, covering parents and lifecycle binding, inserts the node, advances the leaf frontier and commits once. Any failure rolls back node/frontier/FTS/outbox changes together. Condensation uses the same source recheck. Leaf mappings stay fixed across model work, with a preparation recheck so a source changed immediately after lookup cannot silently disappear from lineage.

Raw rows, caller messages, prompts and transcript content retain their existing behavior. There is no schema migration, new database, background worker, dependency or configuration surface. Runtime session/profile rebind checks are best-effort; this PR does not provide atomic host cancellation admission.

Validation on Linux/Python 3.11.15 using the ABC stub already provided by upstream CI, isolated temporary profiles/databases and synthetic model responses:

- The identical publication holdouts on untouched official main `8d1b1e6d3d63f5fc7b209e8d7ec1dc9b814f2e54`: **12 failed, 1 passed**. Failures are actual stale publication, concurrent duplicate publication or visible half-state, rather than calls to newly introduced helpers.
- Final publication holdouts: **13 passed**, including actual `compress`, actual condensation, a selected assistant tool-call mutation, a mapping/preparation race, two independent condensation writers and frontier failure read back through another SQLite connection.
- Core/engine/packaging compatibility set: **1,110 passed** (311 core, 758 engine, 41 packaging). Final source core/engine plus publication holdouts: **1,082 passed**; the final real tool-call holdout variant also passed in the separate 13-case verification.
- Full-repository Ruff, dependency contract and `git diff --check`: passed.

Python 3.12–3.14 and hosted CI have not been run locally. No production deployment is part of this change.

Related #305 defines an async design with strict-xfailed tests, without a production publisher. This change implements the existing foreground path. #545 concerns selection before cross-source lineage gaps; #594 concerns subthreshold sanitation; #600 concerns ingest replay identity. Their scopes remain separate.

AI-assisted implementation; the final transaction/source-ownership paths were reviewed and decisive tests rerun before publication.

title: fix(replay): reconcile official Core message UIDs
body:
When Hermes restores a non-contiguous active transcript, content-tail reconciliation can re-append old messages. Its warm cursor can also miss a same-text message carrying a different durable identity. Use Core's official `message_uid` interface instead: scope the UID-to-source bridge to profile, session and Core database, verify exact stored/output digests including merge/tool witnesses, and consume each proof at most once. New or changed identities remain new content.

The bridge uses the existing metadata table and raw-append transaction. Metadata failures or a source changed after initial validation abort the batch; proof-only passes take the same SQLite writer reservation before revalidation. Replay caches compare host identity, preventing same-text/new-UID messages from borrowing an old projection. Retain already-ingested UID proofs when a proposed active context omits rows, so a host-rejected compression can hand its old durable history back safely.

This is intentionally same-session compatibility. It does not claim cross-session rotation deduplication, infer missing UIDs from text/time/physical IDs, or introduce tables, migrations, services or dependencies. Unregistered transformed views and newly merged old/new user composites are appended conservatively; earlier raw rows remain intact. In mixed legacy/UID batches, an unchanged complete warm prefix keeps the existing cursor/cache proof for identity-free rows. Cold or changed prefixes have no such proof, so legacy rows remain conservative appends. Invalid identity fields never borrow the legacy exemption, and wholly unidentified batches retain the existing path. Core normally adds its system prompt to the outgoing wire copy rather than its history. Retaining same-session UID proofs means metadata read/write cost grows with that session's UID history.

Related replay work is already proposed: [#556](https://github.com/stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm/pull/556) proves a previously accounted-for prefix and explicitly leaves inserted-middle and per-turn rebind cases outside its scope; [#633](https://github.com/stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm/pull/633) and [#613](https://github.com/stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm/pull/613) use content/alignment heuristics. This proposal independently consumes the merged official Core durable UID contract, including non-contiguous replay and same-text/new-UID occurrences, while preserving genuine repeated-message assertions.

Validation uses official Core snapshot `bafb42b431fca313471958fdf77f9c30e455f86b` and isolated file-backed SessionDB/LCM databases. The unchanged LCM baseline reproduced real cold-restore/physical-reissue duplication and same-content/new-UID warm loss: 7 failures, 8 passes, 0 skips. The candidate passes all 39 dedicated UID cases and 218 relevant ingest/replay/assembly/scaffold/restart cases, with 0 failures and 0 skips in both runs. The dedicated suite also calls real LCM `compress()` with Core-assigned UIDs: six raw messages become a three-message proposal and the cursor falls from six to three; a simulated host declines to commit that proposal, returns its original history and adds two same-text/new-UID messages. Both warm and reopened engines retain eight raw rows after repeat replay, with inputs unchanged. This tests real LCM compression and a simulated host decision, not the complete Core refusal/archive-failure flow. Other coverage includes actual merged-user/tool witnesses, actual outgoing wire stripping, new messages between known rows, copied/aliased duplicate occurrences, changed sources, transaction failures, proof-only writer exclusion and mixed legacy warm-prefix preservation. Ruff, compile and diff whitespace checks also pass.

title: Opening existing SQLite artifacts to restrict permissions releases the live connection's POSIX locks
body:
**Version:** v1.0.0-rc.1 (8d1b1e6), Linux, Python 3.11

**Problem**

When LCM tightens permissions on `lcm.db` and its `-wal`, `-shm` and `-journal` sidecars, it opens each existing file and then closes that descriptor. On POSIX, closing any descriptor for a file drops every advisory lock the process holds on that file. That includes the locks held by the process's own live SQLite connection (see SQLite's "How To Corrupt An SQLite Database File", section 2.2).

Once those locks are gone, another process can take the WAL-index lock underneath the running connection. That can desynchronize the shared-memory index and abort the process with SIGBUS.

**Reproduction**

1. Hold a write lock on the database through a live connection.
2. Run the permission-restricting helper on the same database.
3. Try to acquire the write lock from a second process.

- **Expected:** the second process is `BLOCKED`.
- **Observed on rc.1:** the second process gets `ACQUIRED`, and the helper opens `lcm.db`, `lcm.db-wal` and `lcm.db-shm` for I/O.

**Suggested fix**

Change the mode of existing artifacts without opening them for I/O. Use `os.chmod(name, 0o600, dir_fd=..., follow_symlinks=False)` where it is supported, or an `O_PATH` handle plus `/proc/self/fd`. Then re-check the file identity after the chmod. New artifacts can still be created with restrictive modes as today.

We run this as a local patch with regression tests:

- `test_restricting_artifacts_preserves_held_write_lock`
- `test_restricting_artifacts_does_not_open_existing_artifacts_for_io`

We can open a PR if that's useful.

title: Replay reconciliation recomputes message identities for every candidate cursor
body:
**Version:** v1.0.0-rc.1 (8d1b1e6)

**Problem**

Reconciliation tries progressively shorter message prefixes, and it resolves the replay identity of every message again for each candidate cursor. An identity can be expensive: externalized tool-result identities read their backing payload from disk. That makes the loop quadratic in both identity calls and file reads.

On long sessions with large externalized tool results, this blocks the synchronous post-turn ingest hook long enough to trip the gateway's inactivity watchdog.

**Reproduction**

Reconcile a session that has many externalized tool results, and count identity resolutions.

- **Observed on rc.1:** 6,305 identity calls where a bound of 65 is expected.

**Suggested fix**

Memoize the identity, and the persisted-output recovery, per message object for the duration of one reconciliation pass. The message objects are live and unchanged during the pass, so the comparison results are the same.

Regression test: `test_reconcile_memoizes_expensive_message_identities`

title: Session-end busy timeout of 50 ms is too short for finalization under concurrent load
body:
**Version:** v1.0.0-rc.1 (8d1b1e6)

**Problem**

`_SESSION_END_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS = 50` limits how long session finalization waits on a busy database. On a host where the gateway, the dashboard and scheduled jobs share one `lcm.db`, 50 ms is often not enough. Finalization then gives up, so a conversation can be left without its final state after a restart.

**Suggested fix**

Raise the bound to 500 ms, which we've run in production without visible latency, or make it configurable.

Regression test: `test_installed_default_retains_bounded_finalization_wait`

title: fix: stop permission helper from releasing POSIX record locks on live SQLite files
body:
## Summary

- **Already-`0600` artifacts are never opened.** After the existing no-follow `dirfd` stat and validation, mode `0600` returns immediately — zero descriptors means zero lock interaction. This covers the steady-state `store.py:362` call site.
- **Wrong-mode artifacts are tightened without a read/write descriptor.** They are validated through `O_PATH|O_NOFOLLOW` (closing an `O_PATH` descriptor does not release POSIX record locks) and the mode is applied through `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, which procfs resolves by a direct dentry jump, so a directory-entry swap between validation and the mode change cannot redirect the change to another file. `fchmod` on an `O_PATH` fd is `EBADF` on the tested kernel, hence `/proc/self/fd`.
- **Without `O_PATH`, the helper now fails closed.** It raises the module's standard `OSError` (`… lock-safe tightening is unsupported on this platform without O_PATH`) and leaves the mode untouched. The previous directory-fd, name-based `chmod` fallback is **deleted**, not merely hardened. See "Platform note" below — this is the behavioural change that needs a reviewer decision.
- **Unchanged:** the create path (`O_CREAT|O_EXCL` + `fchmod` on a file this call just created), the Windows branch, validation order, error types, sidecar-disappearance tolerance, parent-directory privacy check, uid/gid stability. 0 installed lines removed by the mitigation; the fallback deletion is the only removal.
- **RR1 (post-validation hardlink window) is an explicit, gated acceptance criterion** with a stated boundary, not a silent residual. See below.

### Why

Closing **any** descriptor referring to a file releases every POSIX advisory lock the process holds on that inode, including SQLite's locks through connections that are already open ([SQLite: POSIX advisory locks canceled by a separate thread doing close()](https://sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html#_posix_advisory_locks_canceled_by_a_separate_thread_doing_close_)). `MessageStore._init_db()` calls `_restrict_existing_sqlite_artifacts()` two lines after `sqlite3.connect()`, so the helper runs against live artifacts on every construction.

Reproduced on synthetic fixtures with three processes per case (holder / separate-process `F_GETLK` probe / second-process challenger), ≥3 repeats per variant:

| Variant | delete mode | WAL mode |
|---|---:|---:|
| control (no helper) | 3/3 retained | 3/3 retained |
| **helper on all artifacts** (as `store.py:362` calls it) | **3/3 lost** | **3/3 lost** |
| helper on the DB file only | 3/3 lost | 3/3 retained |
| helper on sidecars only | 3/3 retained | 3/3 lost |

Damage after the concurrent writer entered, verified in a fresh process: **WAL** — holder `COMMIT` reported ok but its committed transaction was no longer visible (lost update, 3/3); **delete** — holder `COMMIT` raised `sqlite3.OperationalError('disk I/O error')` (3/3). `PRAGMA integrity_check` returned `ok` in every case.

Raw-POSIX root cause: `noop`, `O_PATH` open+close, dirfd `chmod` and path `chmod` all retain the lock; `open(O_RDWR)` + `close` — the installed sequence — releases it.

**Scope caveat:** this demonstrates that the mechanism reproduces on demand. It does **not** establish that this helper caused any particular historical incident; historical causation is not claimed.

### How this differs from #597

Both PRs fix the same lock loss and share the first two ideas. The differences are what this PR adds on top:

| Area | #597 (`c54abc0`) | this PR | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Already-`0600` early return | present (opens nothing) | present **and gated**: `retention_already_0600_no_descriptor_open` asserts 0 opens, 0 chmods, mode unchanged, lock still held from a second process | the steady-state path is the one that runs in production; it now has a test that fails if anyone reintroduces the open |
| Tightening with `O_PATH` available | `O_PATH` + `/proc/self/fd` | same mechanism | — |
| **Without `O_PATH` (macOS and friends)** | **keeps the regular-descriptor path** — a pre-existing loose artifact is still tightened through `O_RDWR` + `close`, so the lock release still happens once, on the first construction that tightens it | **fail closed**: raise the module's standard refusal, leave the mode untouched, open nothing. The name-based `chmod` fallback is removed entirely | the fallback was measured as unsafe: without `O_PATH` **no** primitive is both inode-pinning and lock-safe (see probe below), so the choice is "racy mutation" vs "one-time lock release" vs "refuse"; we refuse and ask for a reviewer decision in §3 |
| Name-based chmod fallback (dirfd-relative) | n/a (not present) | **deleted** — it validated by `stat` and then chmod'ed by name, leaving a swap-at-chmod window | reproduced: with a victim file swapped in at the chmod seam, the old fallback mutated the victim at **2 of 4** seam timings |
| RR1 hardlink seam | not discussed as an acceptance criterion | **gated acceptance criterion** with a recorded boundary (below) | must be acknowledged in review, not counted as safe |
| Create path (`O_CREAT\|O_EXCL`) | regular descriptor (unchanged) | regular descriptor (unchanged) | a file this call just created carries none of this process's locks; the residual creation interleaving is tracked separately in #647, which we do not duplicate |
| Tests | adds repo tests (`tests/test_storage_permissions.py`: 22 → 43) | scratch harness: 22 gated checks + the installed `test_storage_permissions.py` suite, run against both the candidate and the unmodified module | **open item:** this change has not yet been ported into the repo's test suite (see Validation) |

### RR1 — accepted residual, with an explicit boundary

No POSIX primitive validates `st_nlink` and changes the inode mode atomically. If a hardlink alias is created after the helper's last validation and before the mode change, it shares the inode and its mode necessarily follows the change; the helper then rejects with `link count changed` — detection after the change, not prevention.

This PR therefore does not claim to prevent the alias follow-through. It claims, and gates, a bounded property:

- the helper **never widens** a permission and **never touches a file outside the two inodes the injecting actor already controlled**;
- the boundary under which an alias can be injected at all: `fs.protected_hardlinks=1`, `fs.protected_symlinks=1`, parent directory not group/other-writable (`st_mode & 0o022 == 0`, refused otherwise) → **only the file owner or root can inject, and that actor can already `chmod` the artifact directly**.

The gate (`security_alias_injected_at_chmod_seam_gate`) injects a hardlink alias inside the wrapped `os.chmod`/`os.fchmod` call and runs 5× per module, with criteria (a)–(e): helper rejects on link count; alias mode exactly `0600` and never looser than its pre-injection `0644`; main inode identity stable and never looser; a decoy victim keeps mode *and* bytes; no file outside those two inodes has its mode changed (inode-scoped diff of a full directory snapshot). **PASS 5/5 on both the candidate and the unmodified module** (the criterion is module-independent — it documents the boundary both share).

### Validation

Environment: Linux `6.8.0-136-generic`, x86_64, uid 10000, umask `022`, Python `3.13.5`, SQLite `3.53.4`.

- [x] **RED, unmodified module:** reproduction loses locks 6/6 (`helper_all`), control retains 6/6, 6 verify failures. Gate set on the unmodified module: **15/22** (the 6 lock-retention checks + the new fail-closed check); its own permission/security checks stay green (12/12) and the installed suite stays **22/22**, so the RED is exactly the lock contract and nothing else.
- [x] **GREEN, candidate:** **22/22 gated**, exit 0; reproduction gives control 6/6 retained and **0/18 treatment lock losses**, 0 verify/commit issues.
