- `command.py`'s backfill/cleanup helpers that own long-running write transactions are declared with `@_fenced_on_conn` / `@_fenced_on_engine_store` decorators rather than re-indenting their bodies.
- `_ensure_inflight_table` stays unfenced on purpose: its `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` schema creation is serialized by SQLite's own file locks, and the upstream concurrent-first-run behavior contract (`test_concurrent_first_run_inflight_schema_creation_is_idempotent`) requires both racers to reach the barrier unfenced.

Also included, as its own commit (predates the gate, from the same incident series):

- `mmap_size=0` pinned on LCM connections (was 256 MiB): mmap page invalidation while a 229 s compaction write transaction ran was the suspect in an earlier corruption incident; with mmap off every read is a normal page-cache read.

## Why

Field-verified on 2026-10-04 (corruption #6 of 6 since August): the `metadata` root page's rightmost child pointed at page 2753, an un-freed overflow page holding `messages.content` text, while the freelist held exactly 2847/2848/2855/2857. `synchronous=FULL`, `mmap_size=0`, and a fastdata relocation all predate that event and none prevent this class; hardware, power loss, and disk-full were ruled out with byte-level triage (header fields, zero-block scan, page-type histogram) now documented in `skills/hermes-lcm/references/diagnostics.md`.

## Validation

- [x] Focused validation: `python3 -m pytest tests/ -q` (with CI's hermes-agent ABC stub as in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`) -> 3032 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed at 19 min; the one failure seen mid-development was `test_concurrent_first_run_inflight_schema_creation_is_idempotent` and was fixed by un-fencing `_ensure_inflight_table` (see Why)
- [x] New regression suite `tests/test_cross_process_write_gate.py` (5 tests): the serialization test spawns two real OS processes and asserts their critical sections never overlap; with the gate disabled the same test fails (`gate failed to serialize writers: b held [...], a entered at [...]`), proving it detects unserialized writers rather than passing trivially
- [x] `python -m compileall -q .` -> clean
- [x] `python -m py_compile scripts/import_lossless_claw.py` -> clean
- [x] `bash -n scripts/install.sh scripts/update.sh` -> clean
- [x] `git diff --check` -> clean
- [x] `python scripts/validate_dependency_contract.py` -> `dependency contract valid: version 1.0.4`
- [x] `pytest tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q` -> 311 passed (plus test_host_capability.py reruns clean with the CI stub present)
- [ ] `ulimit -n 1024 && pytest -q` on the fixed branch and on clean `main` (both running; will post results as a comment)
- [ ] Workflow validation: `actionlint` (workflows unchanged, so not applicable)

## Notes

- Deployed and verified live on a 4-process deployment since 2026-10-16 ~20:40 CDT: `PRAGMA integrity_check` ok, zero DB errors, and the guard's hourly verified snapshots green since.
- A full-suite run under `ulimit -n 1024` showed 5 `test_host_capability.py` failures caused by a missing CI stub directory in my sandbox, not by the patch; re-running that file with the stub present passes 10/10. The two ulimit runs (branch vs clean main) are in flight and I'll comment the comparison.

Refs #681

title: fix(reconcile): memoize replay identities per pass; allow 500ms session-end busy wait
body:
## Summary

Two changes to session reconciliation and finalization:

1. **Memoize replay identities within one reconciliation pass** (`reconcile.py`). The prefix search evaluates progressively shorter candidate cursors and recomputed `_message_replay_identity()` and `recover_hermes_persisted_output_with_file_stat()` for the same message objects on every candidate. For externalized tool results the latter reads the backing payload from disk, so the loop is quadratic in both calls and file I/O, and it runs inside the synchronous post-turn ingest hook, where a long stall can trip the gateway inactivity watchdog. Both results are now cached per message object (`id(message)`) for the duration of the pass. The message objects are live and unchanged during the pass, so comparisons are unchanged.
2. **Raise `_SESSION_END_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS` from 50 to 500** (`engine.py`), so session-end ingest waits out a writer that holds the lock for a few hundred milliseconds instead of dropping the final messages.

## Tests

- `tests/test_reconcile_identity_memoization.py`: identity resolutions per pass are at most one per message, and payload recovery calls stay bounded.
- `tests/test_vps_finalization_contract.py`: synthetic contention experiment (no real data) over timeouts 50 and 500 ms and lock holds of 0, 150, 350 ms and held-through-return. A final message is stored exactly when the hold is shorter than the timeout; the connections' own `busy_timeout` is restored afterwards; elapsed time stays bounded.
- `tests/test_lcm_engine.py`: the session-end elapsed-time bound is relaxed from 0.3 s to 0.75 s for the 500 ms wait.

`pytest tests/test_reconcile_identity_memoization.py tests/test_vps_finalization_contract.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py`: 784 passed.

The full suite has 2 failures in `tests/test_ingest_protection.py` (`test_import_lossless_claw_*`); they fail the same way on `main` at a13e709 without this change.

title: fix(sqlite): restrict artifact permissions without releasing live POSIX locks
body:
## Summary

Tightening permissions on the LCM SQLite artifacts (`lcm.db`, `-wal`, `-shm`) opened each existing file and called `fchmod`. In the process that owns the database, closing that extra descriptor releases the process's POSIX advisory locks on the file (POSIX drops all of a process's locks on a file when any of its descriptors for that file is closed), which can corrupt SQLite's locking while a session is live.

Three commits:

1. **Never open live SQLite artifacts to restrict permissions** (`sqlite_util.py`). An existing artifact is chmod'ed without opening it: by name relative to its directory with `follow_symlinks=False` where the platform supports that, or on Linux through an `O_PATH` descriptor (which holds no advisory locks). Opening the file is kept only as a last resort for platforms with neither (Windows).
2. **Isolate permission descriptors from live locks (macOS).** Darwin has no `O_PATH`, and a name-based chmod there can race a hardlink swap between check and chmod. The inode-pinned descriptor path therefore runs in a short-lived worker process that holds no SQLite locks, so closing its descriptor cannot affect the parent.
3. **Pin the artifact inode inside the worker; harden refusal parsing.** The worker re-checks the inode before acting, and the parent treats worker failures, malformed output and refusals as refusals (fail closed), never as success.

## Tests

- `tests/test_sqlite_lock_preservation.py`: a held write lock survives permission hardening; existing artifacts are never opened for I/O; symlinked and hardlinked sidecars are still refused.
- `tests/test_sqlite_process_locks.py`: live process locks preserved across journal modes; the parent never opens artifacts; worker failures and malformed refusals fail closed; the worker uses the inode-pinned path; a hardlinked sidecar is refused without touching its target.
- `tests/test_storage_permissions.py`: updated for the worker path.

`pytest tests/test_sqlite_lock_preservation.py tests/test_sqlite_process_locks.py tests/test_storage_permissions.py`: 33 passed, 3 skipped (platform-specific).

title: fix(engine): initialize a delegate child's own clone budget (subagents never compact)
body:
## Summary

Delegated subagents (`delegate_task` children) never compact under hermes-lcm. Their per-call context grows without bound: in production we saw children reach 470K–860K input tokens per call with zero compactions, against a configured threshold of ~220K on a 1M window. This was the largest single driver of token spend on our install.

## Root cause

The host builds each agent's context engine by calling `clone_for_agent()` on the registered prototype, then `update_model(...)` on that clone from inside the child agent's `__init__`.

`LCMEngine.update_model()` returns early whenever `_in_process_parent_session_id()` finds an auxiliary caller. That guard came in with #94 to stop a child from retargeting a **shared, already-bound** engine. But a child's own fresh clone is also called from an auxiliary frame, so the guard throws away the clone's only configuration call:

- `context_length` stays `0`, so `threshold_tokens` stays `0`
- `should_compress()` / `should_compress_preflight()` return `False` for a non-positive threshold
- the bypass path never reaches the host fallback compressor

The child still gets classified as auxiliary/stateless correctly. It just never gets a budget.

### Why it can look intermittent

If the plugin fails to load or clone for an agent (e.g. load timeout or a locked database), the host falls back to its built-in compressor, which compacts normally. While plugin loading was flaky, some children happened to compact. Once loading became reliable, every child hit this path.

## Fix

```diff
-        if parent_session_id:
+        if parent_session_id and self._session_id:
```

Only skip the update when the engine is already bound to a session. A fresh per-agent clone has no bound session, so it now receives its own window and threshold. A bound shared engine is still protected, and the child keeps its auxiliary/stateless classification: no child rows are written to the LCM store.

## Tests

`tests/test_child_compaction_budget.py` reproduces the host order without mocking auxiliary detection: unconfigured prototype → `clone_for_agent()` → `update_model()` from a subagent-shaped frame → `on_session_start()`.

- clone receives its own model, provider, window, and threshold; prototype unchanged (empty and parent-primed prototypes)
- compaction gates flip exactly at the threshold (219,999 → False, 220,000 → True, 468,000 → True), and preflight agrees
- a due child reaches the host fallback compressor with the child's 1M window
- a bound shared parent is still protected from a child's `update_model()`, and a later model switch on the child's own clone still works
- no child or parent rows written to the store

Against current `main` with the CI `ContextEngine` stub: **6 failed / 1 passed without the fix, 7 passed with it.**

## Live verification

Deployed on our install and exercised with a real Sonnet delegate pushed past threshold: context grew 34K → 211K across six calls, compaction fired at ~225K and committed down to ~39K, and the next call ran at 62K. Before the fix, no delegate on the same setup had compacted.

title: fix(reconcile): replay containment + head-overlap cursor for rebind r…
body:
fix(reconcile): replay containment + head-overlap cursor for rebind re-ingest

Mitigation for #599 / #631 (rebind replay re-appends the stored tail):

- Skip replay batches that are fully contained in the store (fail-closed).
- Advance the ingest cursor to the head-overlap position *before* the
  ambiguous-delta fallback, bounding duplicate re-ingestion on session
  resume / desktop reconnect.

## Positioning

**Partial mitigation.** The cursor only advances on an exact stored prefix;
a store-only line (orphan-recovery tool row, background-review row, earlier
missed replay) breaks the suffix-exact proof and the fresh tail is still
re-inserted per rebind — the residual described in #631. The storage-layer
guarantee for that residual is tracked by **PR #600** (unique identity index
on the same 5-tuple), which this PR deliberately does not duplicate.

This PR targets the engine-side coordination: it makes the *common* rebind
shape (clean stored prefix + fresh tail) idempotent without relying on the
storage constraint being merged.

## Production validation

Ran in a live hermes-lcm v1.0.0-rc.1 deployment (desktop + TUI gateway,
~35k stored messages):

- **Run 1** (2026-10-12 23:18 -> 2026-10-18 17:02, patch alone):
  10,274 ingested messages, 20 head-overlap advances, 0 skip-full,
  0 persist-ambiguous, 0 crashes, `PRAGMA integrity_check` clean.
- **Run 2** (2026-10-18 17:02 -> 2026-10-20, 48h, with a #600-style unique
  index in place): 367 ingested messages, **0 duplicate groups**,
  0 reconciliation anomalies, integrity clean, journal_mode=delete holding.

Pre-patch, the same deployment measured 388 duplicate identity groups
concentrated in ~5 high-reconnect sessions (worst: 270 extra rows, one
user message stored 19x; 84->143->202->261->320->379 rows across rebinds) —
the exact compounding shape of #631.

## Tests

No reconcile.py test regressions: existing ingest/replay/compaction suites
pass unmodified (`test_ingest_protection.py`, `test_auxiliary_first_ingest.py`,
`test_h3_composition_replay.py`, `test_h5_state_semantic_replay.py`:
158 passed). The guard is a no-op when there is no overlap (cursor stays
put), so all pre-existing reconcile behavior is preserved.

Complements #633 (which the maintainer noted requires reverting 6 tests):
this change is additive to `reconcile.py` only, touches no existing
function's contract, and needs no test reversals.

Refs #599, #631, #633

title: fix(lcm): harden lcm.db against file-level corruption (journal_mode=D…
body:
fix(lcm): harden lcm.db against file-level corruption (journal_mode=DELETE)

Corrects the diagnosis made in the 2026-10-12 patch (local commit `d3e085b`).
That commit blamed the recurring lcm.db corruption (2026-09-27, 10-03,
10-06, 10-12) on the SQLite WAL-reset bug in 3.45.1. Forensics show that is
wrong:

- The live dashboard process runs cpython-3.11.16 with a **static**
  SQLite 3.53.1 (no libsqlite3.so mapping). 3.53.1 is patched and OUT of
  the WAL-reset window (3.7.0-3.51.2), so that bug cannot fire in this
  process.
- All three corrupted artifacts (09-27, 10-06, 10-12) carry the 3.53.1
  build stamp in the file header (offset 96 = 3053001), i.e. a 3.53.1
  writer, not 3.45.1.

The signatures point elsewhere: the 10-06 file has ~86 KB of binary junk
prefixed before a valid SQLite header (whole DB shifted forward); 10-12
is a valid-header file truncated mid-page. That profile matches a **RAW
COPY of the live database** (cp / tar / a .backup taken while writers held
the file), not an in-process race. dmesg is clean (no disk I/O errors).

This is therefore a **HARDENING, not a root-cause fix**:

- `journal_mode=DELETE` removes the WAL file, its checkpoints and the
  stale-mmap surface — the least-attack-surface mode for a DB that must
  never be copied raw.
- `mmap_size=0` (pointless in DELETE mode, kept for symmetry).
- `synchronous=FULL` retained.

The operational rule lives in `skills/hermes-lcm/SKILL.md`: raw
cp/mv/tar of the live lcm.db is forbidden; use `sqlite3 .backup`,
`VACUUM INTO`, or `safe_lcm_ops.py`, and verify writer death before
restoring.

## Relation to #681 / #682

Our incident class is **complementary, not identical**, to #681:

- #681: multi-process writers racing SQLite's *per-connection page
  allocator* inside concurrent write transactions (in-DB corruption,
  freelist/b-tree inconsistency). #682's flock gate addresses it.
- Ours: a raw file-level copy of the live DB taken from outside the
  process (header shift / truncation artifacts). No transaction was in
  flight; the DB itself was intact at the moment of the copy.

Both hardenings are worth keeping: the flock gate fixes in-DB races,
DELETE mode removes the surface that makes a stray copy corruptible.
Happy to rebase this onto #682 if the maintainer prefers a single
"SQLite safety" PR.

## Validation

- `journal_mode=delete` holding in the live deployment for 8 days
  (2026-10-12 -> 2026-10-20), 10,641 ingested messages,
  `PRAGMA integrity_check` clean at every check.
- No test regressions: `test_db_bootstrap_fts.py`, `test_rollup_store.py`,
  `test_schema_stamp_remediation.py` (116 passed) + store/bootstrap subset
  of `test_lcm_core.py` (108 passed).

Refs #681, #682

title: clone_for_agent() silently corrupts lcm.db SQLite file under heavy concurrent load (recurring)
body:
## Summary
Under sustained heavy load (long session, many subagent/context clones in quick succession), `clone_for_agent()` on the LCM context engine produces SQLite btree corruption in `lcm.db`. This has now happened twice on the same install under similar conditions, hours/days apart, after a full restore in between.

## Symptom sequence
1. Repeated warning in `agent.log` during heavy load:
```
WARNING run_agent: Context engine 'lcm' could not be safely copied for this agent (disk I/O error) — falling back to built-in compressor. Plugin engines that hold uncopyable state (locks, DB connections) should override clone_for_agent() (or __deepcopy__) to copy only mutable budget state.
```
2. `PRAGMA integrity_check;` on `lcm.db` then shows real btree corruption, e.g.:
```
Tree 8 page 199284: btreeInitPage() returns error code 11
Tree 210656 page 210657: btreeInitPage() returns error code 11
Tree 210643 page 210655: btreeInitPage() returns error code 11
...
```
(Journal mode is WAL.)

## Root cause (hypothesis, from the first occurrence's RCA)
`clone_for_agent()` appears to copy the engine's live SQLite connection object itself (or something holding a reference to its locks/fds) rather than only the mutable budget state, as the warning text itself suggests. Under concurrent clone attempts from multiple subagents/contexts hitting the same backing DB file in a short window, this produces torn/overlapping writes to the SQLite file, visible as btree corruption on the next integrity check.

## Environment
- hermes-lcm v1.0.0-rc.1
- Hermes Agent core v0.22.2+1979
- lcm.db ~1GB+, WAL journal mode
- Linux (Debian-based LXC container), SQLite via stdlib `sqlite3` module

## Reproduction conditions
- Both occurrences happened during very long (8-10+ hour), continuous, heavy-load sessions: many sequential subagent dispatches, frequent context engine clones, high tool-call volume.
- No crash, no OOM, no host reboot either time — the corruption is silent until a `PRAGMA integrity_check` is run.

## Suggested fix
Per the warning's own guidance: `clone_for_agent()` (or `__deepcopy__`) on the LCM engine should be overridden to copy only the mutable budget/state fields, never the underlying DB connection, cursor, or any lock object. If a clone genuinely needs its own DB handle, it should open a fresh connection to the same file rather than duplicating the existing one.

## Workaround currently in use
Manual restore from the last clean backup/snapshot after each occurrence. This is not a fix — the underlying defect causes repeat corruption under the same load pattern. Filing this so there's an upstream fix instead of a recurring manual restore.

title: fix(engine): honor host threshold_tokens_cap in LCMEngine
fix(storage): pin the WAL generation with OFD locks so a stray close cannot unlink it
body:
## Summary

- Pins the live WAL generation with OFD locks so a stray `close()` in any process cannot unlink
  the WAL/SHM sidecars out from under processes still attached to them.
- Adds `wal_generation_guard.py` plus `arm`/`disarm` call sites, and a forensics playbook at
  `skills/hermes-lcm/references/wal-generation-corruption.md`.
- Carries the three commits from #682 (mmap_size pin, advisory flock write gate, diagnostics
  playbook) because the guard is **not** separable from them: cherry-picking the guard commit alone
  onto `main` conflicts in `lifecycle_state.py` and `skills/hermes-lcm/references/diagnostics.md`.
  **This PR supersedes #682.** Reviewing this one reviews all of it; #682 can be closed.

## Why

Recurring `database disk image is malformed` on `lcm.db`, several times per day on a host running
long-lived sessions with concurrent writers (agent, cron jobs, gateway).

Three independent defects compounded. Each is necessary but not sufficient on its own:

1. **`mmap_size` compaction race.** Memory-mapped I/O let a compacting writer and a concurrent
   reader disagree about page state. Pinned to `mmap_size=0`.
2. **Unserialized cross-process writes.** Multiple processes wrote with no barrier between them.
   Now fenced behind one advisory flock on a `<db>.lock` sidecar, held for the duration of each
   write transaction. In-process writers queue FIFO on a per-path mutex acquired *before* the flock
   and released *after*, so no thread ever waits on a mutex it already owns. Fails **open**: if
   flock is unavailable (some network filesystems), behavior degrades to current behavior rather
   than erroring.
3. **WAL generation unlinking.** The actual producer of the malformed-image symptom. A close path
   could unlink the live WAL while other processes still held it open; those processes then wrote
   through a stale generation. OFD locks now pin the generation so the sidecars survive a stray
   close.

Long-running sessions do not cause this, they widen the window: more concurrent writers, held open
longer, so all three races fire far more often.

### Relationship to other open PRs

- **#682** (mine): superseded by this PR, as described above.
- **#687** proposes `journal_mode=DELETE` for the same class of symptom, from a different
  diagnosis, and also edits `db_bootstrap.py`. These two approaches are mutually exclusive in
  spirit: #687 abandons WAL, this PR keeps WAL and makes the generation durable. Flagging rather
  than resolving, since picking between them is a maintainer call. If #687 lands first this needs
  rebasing and item 3 above may become moot.
- **#684 / #675 / #663** all concern permission helpers releasing live POSIX locks on SQLite
  artifacts. Same failure family (lock/sidecar lifetime), non-overlapping code paths. No conflict
  expected.

## Validation

Run with `PYTHON=/usr/bin/python3` (CPython 3.11, static SQLite 3.53.1) on Linux 7.2.11 /
ext4-backed `/mnt/fastdata`.

- [x] Focused validation: `pytest tests/test_cross_process_write_gate.py tests/test_wal_generation_guard.py tests/test_crash_safe_wal.py -q` -> **25 passed**
- [x] Default validation, via `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going` -> **13/13 gates pass, exit 0**:
  - [x] `pytest -q` (full) -> pass
  - [x] `bash -lc 'ulimit -n 1024 && pytest -q'` (low-fd) -> pass
  - [x] `python -m compileall -q .` -> pass
  - [x] `python -m py_compile scripts/import_lossless_claw.py` -> pass
  - [x] `bash -n scripts/install.sh scripts/update.sh` -> pass
  - [x] `git diff --check` (working tree, staged, and `origin/main...HEAD`) -> pass
  - [x] dependency contract -> valid, version 1.0.5, 10 external imports, 4 Python versions
  - [x] benchmark smoke, stress smoke, stress release -> pass
- [ ] Workflow validation: no workflow files changed, `actionlint` not applicable.

### Field evidence

The fix has carried a production workload for 61 hours on the reporting host. Counting the guard's
own forensics snapshot directories, one per detected corruption:

| Window | Corruption events |
|---|---|
| Oct 17 to Oct 18, pre-fix | 7 |
| Oct 19 20:00 onward, post-fix | 0 |

Post-deploy monitor log contains only `snapshot` and `heartbeat` records, 62 and 10 respectively,
through 2026-10-22T11:29. Zero `corruption_detected`, zero repair actions. `lcm_doctor` against the
live database reports `database_integrity` ok, `messages_fts_integrity` ok, `nodes_fts_integrity`
ok, `sqlite_storage` quick_check ok, FTS sync 853/853.

One honest caveat on that timeline: 79 `unavailable` records appear *after* the files were written
at 20:00, confined to 21:08-22:26 and ending in `recovered` at 22:27:55. Those are the tail of the
final pre-fix incident, not a regression. The files were on disk at 20:00 but the already-running
processes were still executing the previous code from memory. The fix prevents recurrence; it
cannot heal an already-poisoned open handle, which is why that window needed the processes to
reopen the file.

## Notes

- `wal_generation_guard.py` is self-contained and import-light. Reverting is mechanical: delete it
  and remove the `arm`/`disarm` call sites plus the imports.
- The `<db>.lock` sidecars are inert artifacts. Leaving them in place or deleting them is safe
  either way; they carry no state.
- An empty `/proc/locks` between writes is expected, not evidence the gate is inactive: the flock
  is held only for the duration of a write transaction.
- Tests cover the gate and guard directly, including cross-process acquisition ordering and the
  fail-open path, rather than asserting on timing.

Refs #682, #687

title: fix(engine): honor host threshold_tokens_cap in LCMEngine
body:
## Summary

The host's live compression sync (`tui_gateway/session_compression.py`)
calls `_coerce_threshold_tokens_cap` on the active context engine and
installs the result on `engine.threshold_tokens_cap` every turn. The
built-in `ContextCompressor` implements this contract; `LCMEngine` did not.

On every turn the sync raised `AttributeError`, the host caught it and
logged `Could not apply live compression config ...`, and — as a side
effect — the whole live compression apply aborted, so
`compression.threshold_tokens` from `config.yaml` never reached the engine.

## Changes (engine.py only, +40 lines)

- `_coerce_threshold_tokens_cap(value)`: `@staticmethod` mirroring
  `ContextCompressor._coerce_max_tokens` (positive int, or None = no cap).
- `threshold_tokens_cap`: property (getter + setter). The host installs
  the value each turn without re-deriving the trigger, so the setter
  re-applies the clamp immediately.
- `_effective_threshold_tokens(...)`: now clamps against the host cap after
  the LCM assembly-cap logic, matching `_apply_threshold_tokens_cap`
  semantics (the host cap is strictly tighter than both).

## Safety

Conservative: a None/invalid cap means "no cap" (unchanged behavior); a
numeric cap only ever lowers the trigger (earlier compaction), never
raises it. No new dependencies, no config required.

## Tests

`pytest tests/test_db_bootstrap_fts.py tests/test_import_lossless_claw.py tests/test_trajectory_store.py`
→ **203 passed, 1 pre-existing failure**
(`test_doctor_repair_apply_joins_background_scans_first` — `LCMEngine` import
error present on `origin/main`, unrelated to this change).

No new tests: this is a 40-line engine.py extension mirroring an existing
`ContextCompressor` contract; the host-side test suite covers it.

title: fix(lcm): collapse message re-ingestion with identity + tool_call_id unique indexes
body:
## Summary

Two re-ingestion shapes produced **duplicate rows** in `lcm.db`:

1. **Exact re-ingest** — the same message re-ingested with identical
   `session_id + role + observed_at + tool_call_id + content`. Upstream had no
   guard, so a replay wrote a second row.
2. **Tool-call re-ingest with a shifted clock** — the same `tool_call_id`
   re-ingested with a *different* `observed_at` (host replay / session re-bind).
   This slipped past any content-based dedup and duplicated the tool result.

Observed in production: 18 `tool_call_id`s each duplicated once (36 rows), all
in one session, with 0.5-15 min gaps between the two `observed_at` values.

### Why a content hash is the wrong key

A naive `hash(session_id + content)` dedup would **not** be safe: it would
collapse legitimate **parallel tool calls** that return identical content but
carry *distinct* `tool_call_id`s (292 such groups in the production DB).
`tool_call_id` is the stable event identifier, so it is the correct dedup key -
with `session_id` to scope it.

## Changes

### 1. v6 unique message-identity index (db_bootstrap.py)
Partial unique index on `(session_id, role, observed_at, tool_call_id, content)`
for non-empty tool rows. Rejects exact re-ingests at write time. Backfill
dedups any pre-existing exact duplicates (remaps summary-node `source_ids` and
lifecycle frontiers to the canonical `store_id` before deleting).

### 2. `tool_call_id` partial unique index (db_bootstrap.py)
Partial unique index on `(session_id, tool_call_id) WHERE tool_call_id IS NOT
NULL AND tool_call_id != ''` - guards the shifted-clock re-ingest shape
without touching the 292 parallel-content groups. Backfill collapses the 18
observed re-ingests.

### 3. Write-path fallback (store.py)
`_insert_message_conflict_safe` gains a `(session_id, tool_call_id)` fallback:
a re-ingested tool message resolves to the existing row instead of raising.

### 4. Tests (tests/test_message_identity_constraint.py, 14 cases)
Partial-index creation, re-ingest-with-different-`observed_at` dedup, parallel
same-content / distinct-`tool_call_id` preservation, distinct-content
preservation, and a legacy-DB migration backfill that remaps references.

## Tests

```
pytest tests/test_message_identity_constraint.py tests/test_rollup_store.py tests/test_import_lossless_claw.py tests/test_trajectory_store.py
-> 226 passed, 0 failed
```

Verified against the production DB (37,141 rows): migration collapses the 18
redundant re-ingests (37,141 -> 37,123), 0 `tool_call_id` violations, 0 dangling
summary `source_ids`, 0 dangling lifecycle frontiers, all parallel tool calls
preserved. `test_rollup_store.py` is updated because it hard-asserted
`SCHEMA_VERSION == 5`; with v6 now being the message-identity constraint it
expects the named `v6_message_identity_constraint` step to be present on a
fresh DB.

title: fix(sqlite_util): chmod existing SQLite artifacts via O_PATH so live POSIX locks survive
body:
## Problem

`sqlite_util._chmod_sqlite_artifact_at()` opens an **existing** `lcm.db` / `-wal` / `-shm` read-write, `fchmod`s it, and closes the fd. On POSIX, closing *any* descriptor to a file releases **every** fcntl lock the process holds on that file. The live `sqlite3` connection in the same process therefore silently loses its DB and WAL locks; when a sibling process (cron fire, CLI, dashboard) performs its last close, SQLite believes it is the last reader and unlinks the WAL under the still-open connection.

This is the mechanism behind #588 and #660 and matches the recurring `database disk image is malformed` / deleted-WAL reports. Reproduced on 2026-10-23 with a controlled two-process script (open connection, call the helper, observe `fcntl` locks gone via `/proc/locks`, then WAL unlink from the second process).

## Fix

For an existing file, pin the inode with `O_PATH` and chmod through `/proc/self/fd/<fd>`. Closing an `O_PATH` descriptor does not interact with advisory locks on Linux. Creation (`O_CREAT|O_EXCL`) keeps the original read-write path; platforms without `O_PATH` or `/proc` fall back to the previous behaviour, so nothing changes where the bug cannot occur.

## Testing

- Running as a local patch on `local/hermes-patches` since 2026-10-23 on a 1.1 GB `lcm.db` (592k messages) under gateway + cron + CLI concurrency; zero corruption since (previously ~weekly).
- `PRAGMA quick_check` ok; `fcntl` locks on the live connection persist across the helper (checked via `/proc/locks`).

Fixes #588, fixes #660.

title: fix(engine): add LCMEngine._coerce_threshold_tokens_cap for live compression config
body:
## Problem

hermes-agent's `tui_gateway/session_compression.py::_apply_live_compression_config()` duck-types the agent's compressor as `cc` and, when `compression.*` is edited live (Desktop/TUI config save), calls:

```python
cc.threshold_tokens_cap = cc._coerce_threshold_tokens_cap(compression.get("threshold_tokens", ...))
```

`agent.context_compressor.ContextCompressor` defines `_coerce_threshold_tokens_cap = _coerce_max_tokens`. When LCM is the context engine the compressor slot holds an `LCMEngine`, which did not, so every live config save logged

```
WARNING tui_gateway.server: Could not apply live compression config for <sid>: 'LCMEngine' object has no attribute '_coerce_threshold_tokens_cap'
```

and the new cap was never applied. Observed every 20-30 min across sessions on hermes-agent `v0.22.5+477` and `+800`.

## Fix

Add the method as a `staticmethod` mirroring upstream's normalization exactly (positive int, else `None`). LCM's own pacing (`context_threshold`, fresh tail) does not read `threshold_tokens_cap`, so this is a compatibility value only; no behaviour change for compaction.

## Testing

- Parity check of the shim against the real `ContextCompressor._coerce_max_tokens` over `None, 0, -5, 100, "200", "abc", 3.9, "0", "-1"`: identical.
- Running as a local patch since 2026-10-25; the warning stopped after gateway restart.

title: fix(reconcile): dedupe ambiguous rebind replays with a multiset delta
body:
## Summary
- Adds a multiset-difference fallback to ingest-cursor reconciliation, used before the "persisted ambiguous delta" path and after a scaffold-only prefix (compacted sessions). Only rows that are genuinely absent from the store get persisted.
- Rows that carry provider ids (`tool_call_id`, assistant `tool_calls` ids) are matched by id, because ids are unique within a session. Rows with no id are matched by count over a hashed `(role, stripped content, tool_calls identity)` key, so a user really sending "ok" twice still produces two rows.
- Fail-closed size gate: the fallback applies only to replay-sized batches. That means 8 or more effective messages, or 4 to 7 when no provider id repeats inside the batch. A short batch carrying a retry (an id reused with new content) keeps the legacy path, so it is still stored. Per-turn deltas that align on the existing paths never reach this code.
- `lcm_status` → `ingest_reconciliation` reports `persisted multiset delta` with `already_stored` and `persisted` counts, so operators can see it working.
- Adds a scrubbed synthetic fixture (`tests/fixtures/reingest_duplication.json`, no transcript text) and `tests/test_reingest_duplication.py` (9 tests). One expectation in `tests/test_lcm_engine.py` changes: the compacted-restart test no longer expects the durable fresh tail to be stored twice.

Refs #599, #631. Related open work: #550, #613, #686, #692 (see "Relation to other PRs" below).

## Why
On our gateway (Matrix and Discord with cron and subagents, about 2.5 months of history), `lcm.db` grew to 4.15 GB. 1,178,049 of its 1,431,266 message rows (82%) were exact same-session replays: 1,058,320 id-carrying rows and 119,729 plain-text rows inside replayed blocks, across 435 sessions.

Trigger: a fresh engine for an existing session gets the whole transcript on its first `ingest()`. That happens after a gateway restart, and also after idle agent eviction, which rebuilds the engine with no restart. `_reconcile_ingest_cursor_from_store` could not align the replay with the stored tail, so it fell back to cursor 0 and re-stored everything. Classifying the first divergences on real sessions gave four causes:
1. The host strips user/assistant text on reload (`hermes_state_messages._loaded_view_content` → `sanitize_context(content).strip()`), while LCM stored the live, unstripped string.
2. Earlier replays already sit in the store, so each failure makes the next alignment harder (they compound).
3. Parallel tool results come back in a different order.
4. Gateway notification turns land at different positions.

Exact-suffix alignment (#686) and contiguous-block alignment (#550) cover the clean shapes. Causes 2 to 4 break positional proofs. A multiset difference doesn't depend on position, and provider ids keep it safe.

## Relation to other PRs
- #692 / #600 (unique indexes): a storage-layer backstop. This PR complements it at the engine layer. With this change the replay is never offered to the store, which also covers assistant and text rows the tool-id index does not.
- #686 / #550: positional alignment. This fallback runs only when alignment has already failed, so it can sit beside either.
- #613: covers mutated stored tails (pruning, redaction). The approach is different; overlap is limited to the reconcile fallback point.

Happy to rebase onto whichever of these lands first.

## Validation
- [x] Reproduction on unpatched `main` (a13e709): `pytest tests/test_reingest_duplication.py` → 9 failed (for example, 41 stored rows vs 26 expected; reason `persisted ambiguous delta`)
- [x] Focused validation on this branch: `pytest tests/test_reingest_duplication.py -q` → 9 passed
- [x] Default validation:
  - [x] `pytest tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q` → 1110 passed
  - [x] `pytest -q` → 3038 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed (base `main`: 3029 passed, 1 skipped, 12 xfailed)
  - [ ] `scripts/validate_release.sh --full --keep-going ...` → not run locally; relying on CI
  - [x] `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` → clean
- [x] Production: before this branch, the gateway re-stored 2,796 duplicate rows in about 6 hours. It has been running the change on v0.21.0-rc1 since 2026-10-27, with 0 duplicate rows among the 59 id-carrying rows ingested since then. No restart or eviction has exercised the rebind path on the live system yet, so the regression tests are the evidence for that path for now.

title: fix(config): read compression.threshold + auxiliary timeout from the context-local hermes home
body:
### Summary

`_hermes_compression_threshold()` and `_hermes_auxiliary_compression_timeout_ms()` in `config.py` resolve the Hermes home with a raw environment read:

```python
home = Path(os.environ.get("HERMES_HOME") or Path.home() / ".hermes")
```

On a **multiplexed gateway** one process serves every profile, so `HERMES_HOME` is the ROOT home (`G:/Hermes`) for all of them. A profile's own `config.yaml` is therefore never consulted: `compression.threshold` and `auxiliary.compression.timeout` are always read from the ROOT config.

The plugin's own `__init__.py` already resolves the home correctly, via `hermes_cli.config.get_hermes_home()`, which honours the context-local home override. That is why the plugin stores data under the right profile (`LCM rebound storage for Hermes home G:\Hermes\profiles\pc_technician`) while its threshold comes from the wrong one. Two home resolutions, two different answers, in the same plugin.

`hermes_constants.get_hermes_home()` documents the intended precedence: **context-local override -> `HERMES_HOME` env var -> platform default**. `config.py` bypasses the first term.

### Impact

A profile's `compression.threshold` is silently ignored. On a live multiplexed gateway:

| profile | `compression.threshold` in its config.yaml | threshold the engine actually used |
|---|---|---|
| `pc_technician` | `0.9` | `0.5` (ROOT's value) |
| `assistant` | `0.85` | `0.5` (ROOT's value) |
| all others | `0.5` | `0.5` (correct by coincidence) |

The same defect applies to `auxiliary.compression.timeout`.

Consequence: an operator who raises a profile's threshold to delay compaction gets the ROOT's threshold instead. With ROOT at `0.5`, a profile configured at `0.9` compacts at 50% of its window instead of 90% - roughly 1.8x more compaction than intended.

### Reproduction

```python
import os, sys
from pathlib import Path
sys.path.insert(0, "<hermes-agent>")
from hermes_constants import set_hermes_home_override, reset_hermes_home_override
from hermes_lcm.config import _hermes_compression_threshold

os.environ["HERMES_HOME"] = "G:/Hermes"                 # ROOT, as the gateway has it
tok = set_hermes_home_override("G:/Hermes/profiles/pc_technician")
try:
    print(_hermes_compression_threshold(0.35))
finally:
    reset_hermes_home_override(tok)
```

Before this fix: `0.5` (ROOT's value).
After this fix: `0.9` (the profile's value).

### Proposed change

Replace both raw environment reads with `hermes_constants.get_hermes_home()`, matching what `__init__.py` in this same plugin already does, with a fallback that preserves current behaviour if the import is unavailable:

```python
try:
    from hermes_constants import get_hermes_home
except Exception:  # pragma: no cover
    def get_hermes_home():
        from pathlib import Path
        import os
        return Path(os.environ.get("HERMES_HOME") or Path.home() / ".hermes")
```

```python
home = get_hermes_home()
```

Two call sites: `config.py` line 76 (`_hermes_compression_threshold`) and line 146 (`_hermes_auxiliary_compression_timeout_ms`).

### Tests

`tests/test_lcm_scope_aware_threshold.py` covers both call sites:

- `test_override_reads_profile_not_env` - an override pointing at a profile with `threshold: 0.99` must return `0.99`.
- `test_clear_override_reads_env` - with the override cleared the env/default path still resolves.
- `test_aux_override_reads_profile` - an override pointing at a profile with `compression.timeout: 99` must return `99000` ms.

The threshold test fails against the current code and passes against the patched code (verified in both directions).

### Environment

Hermes Agent `v0.22.4`, Windows 10, Python 3.11. Multiplexed gateway serving 13 profiles from one process.

title: fix(storage): bound initialization contention and preserve transaction ownership
body:
## Problem

Healthy SQLite reopen can repeat schema/marker writes and automatic FTS maintenance. A concurrent writer can consume the host's plugin-load budget; failed initialization and owned-write paths also need reliable transaction and connection cleanup.

## Change

- Check healthy schema readiness without unnecessary writes, and share one cooperative initialization deadline across nested stores.
- Leave interrupted or contended automatic FTS maintenance pending. Defer automatic checks before entering caller-owned transactions, since SQLite VM interruption can roll back the entire transaction despite a savepoint.
- Release owned transactions/connections on failure; do not acknowledge raw ingestion as durable after merely releasing a caller-owned savepoint.
- Track and dispose returned registration handles if cancellation wins after registration completes.
- Preserve normal `sqlite3.executescript` semantics and use explicit statement execution where initialization must preserve transaction ownership.

This is a cumulative integration against current `main`, including the SQLite lock-preservation and bounded-wait behavior proposed in #675 and #607. It preserves the already-existing timestamp migration-marker contract discussed in #638; it does not add a second legacy timestamp backfill. #670 is a related closed proposal with a different deferred-binding approach. This change does not add lazy first-use storage binding or claim to resolve every contention cause.

The companion Hermes core change publishes the host's absolute monotonic load deadline before import/register work, including nested loads and timeout-disabled operation. The plugin also bounds initialization when the host does not publish that deadline.

## Verification and limits

The accepted source was applied to the exact upstream base and reversed to the exact base tree. Earlier focused candidate and upstream runs each passed 311 tests. Those are historical source acceptance results, not a fresh full-suite claim. A subsequent portability-only derivative replaces a machine-specific loader-test path with a repository-local baseline fixture; its two host-loader variants passed independent bounded verification. Other production bytes are unchanged by that derivative.

Cooperative deadlines cannot preempt arbitrary kernel/filesystem stalls. This does not establish historical message recovery, universal losslessness, production activation, or resolution of an unknown historical lock holder. No database repair or manual historical backfill is included.

title: fix(lifecycle): rebuild lcm_lifecycle_state when damage is confined to it
body:
Recurring reports (#643, #681) show page damage confined to `lcm_lifecycle_state` while `messages`, `summary_nodes` and both FTS indexes stay readable. In that state every lifecycle read/write keeps failing, the engine silently degrades to the built-in compressor, and the table stays rotten until an operator runs `PRAGMA integrity_check` by hand.

This adds a narrow, self-contained recovery path for exactly that signature.

## What it does

- `lifecycle_repair.table_check()` — table-scoped `PRAGMA quick_check('lcm_lifecycle_state')`, so the healthy path never scans the whole multi-hundred-MB file.
- `lifecycle_repair.classify()` — resolves bare `Tree N ... Rowid M out of order` errors to their owner through `sqlite_master.rootpage`, and refuses to repair if any error points at a content table.
- `lifecycle_repair.heal_if_corrupt()` — rebuilds the table with the same DDL `db_bootstrap` uses, then `VACUUM`: `DROP TABLE` leaves the old pages on the freelist, and a bare rebuild otherwise trips `Page N: never used`.
- `LifecycleStateStore._init_db()` checks once at startup.
- `_synchronized()` repairs and retries the operation once on a corruption error instead of poisoning the process for its whole lifetime.
- Physically unreadable pages cannot be dropped in-process; the helper returns `healed=False` with the reason rather than raising.

Only bookkeeping rows are ever lost: current binding, frontier markers and compaction debt — all recreated on the next bind. Content tables are never touched; if the full `integrity_check` blames anything outside the lifecycle table, the helper declines and the operator procedure stands.

## Evidence

Third episode on one deployment in three weeks (18.10, 02.11, 03.11.2026), each with the identical lifecycle-only signature, each repaired by exactly this rebuild (drop + recreate + `VACUUM`), with 100% of messages preserved.

```
Tree 17 page 17 cell 7: Rowid 295 out of order
wrong # of entries in index sqlite_autoindex_lcm_lifecycle_state_1
row N missing from index idx_lcm_lifecycle_current_session
```

## Tests

`tests/test_lifecycle_repair.py` — 11 tests: table-scoped detection, tree-root classification (lifecycle vs content), rebuild preserving `messages`, decline on physically damaged pages, corruption-error matching, and DDL drift against the bootstrap schema.

This is complementary to #690/#682 (root cause: cross-process WAL/allocator races). It does not try to prevent corruption; it makes a lifecycle-only corruption non-fatal instead of disabling LCM until someone notices.

title: fix: preserve context on summary publication contention
body:
## Summary

Gracefully abort or partially finalize LCM compaction when summary-node publication exhausts SQLite's existing busy timeout, instead of failing the user turn or discarding usable context.

The change also makes `SummaryDAG.add_node()` roll back failed writes before releasing its lock and assigns `node_id` only after commit. Rollback failures remain fatal because transaction state is then unknown.

This closes #431 and complements #429: that PR retries the narrower `SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT` case, while this change handles exhausted ordinary `SQLITE_BUSY`/`SQLITE_LOCKED` publication safely without adding another retry.

## Behavior

- First publication contention returns the original transcript unchanged and marks compression aborted.
- Later contention preserves already committed summaries and the remaining raw-message coverage.
- Condensation contention preserves committed leaf progress.
- Non-contention SQLite errors still propagate.
- Post-contention bookkeeping writes are skipped for that attempt.

## Validation

- `360 passed` across the publication-contention regressions, `test_lcm_core.py`, and compaction telemetry tests.
- Real two-connection SQLite contention, commit failure, rollback failure, first/later publication, condensation, and subsequent retry behavior are covered.
- Ruff and `git diff --check` pass.

Closes #431
Related: #421
Complements: #429

title: One emoji (or CJK fragment) in a query routes the whole query to the unbounded LIKE path; lcm_grep(mode="full_text") has no deadline
body:
## Summary

`search_query.requires_like_fallback()` returns `True` whenever the **raw** query contains any emoji or CJK text. That sends the **entire query** — including ordinary, perfectly indexable words — to `MessageStore._search_like()`. The LIKE path scores every matching row in SQL, so a mixed query like `🐧 report` costs orders of magnitude more than the emoji contributes.

Two user-visible outcomes:

- `lcm_recall`: the 8 s deadline interrupts the query → `total_results: 0`, `timeout: true` — a silent miss.
- `lcm_grep(mode="full_text")`: no deadline is installed on this path, so the call blocks for the full duration (183 s measured) instead of failing fast.

## Environment

- `hermes-lcm 1.0.0-rc.1` (`8d1b1e6`), Linux, Python 3.11, SQLite 3.53.1
- 159,276 messages / 354 summary nodes / 594 MB `lcm.db`
- embeddings disabled (`degraded_reason: semantic retrieval is disabled`)
- Reproduces on `0.20.0` as well; measurements below are from a copy of the production DB, not the live file.

## Reproduction

```text
lcm_grep(query="🐧",                        mode="full_text", session_scope="all")  -> ~5 s cold / 1.35 s warm, hits
lcm_grep(query="🐧 report",                 mode="full_text", session_scope="all")  -> >45 s (probe cap)
lcm_grep(query="📊 Telegram outage",        mode="full_text", session_scope="all")  -> >45 s (probe cap)
```

The full uncapped run of a mixed query (`🐧 emoji probe`, same DB) took **183.7 s**. A pure-emoji query is comparatively cheap because few rows contain the emoji; adding one ordinary word (e.g. `report`) pulls tens of thousands of rows into per-row scoring.

The same query shape through `lcm_recall` is cut off at the 8 s deadline and returns:

```json
{"total_results": 0, "timeout": true, "degraded": true,
 "provenance": {"arms_run": ["fts"], "coverage": {"fts": "none"}}}
```

## Mechanism

1. `requires_like_fallback()` — `if contains_cjk(raw) or contains_emoji(raw): return True`. The check intentionally uses the raw query because sanitization strips exactly those characters.
2. `store.search()` therefore calls `_search_like()` for the whole query. `_search_like` ORs `content LIKE '%term%'` over all terms and orders by per-term occurrence counts (`LENGTH(LOWER(content)) - LENGTH(REPLACE(...))`).
3. The `LIMIT ?` added in #54/#61 bounds rows **returned**, but the `ORDER BY` score/directness expressions are evaluated for every row in the LIKE match set before the limit applies. That is why the bound does not bound the work.
4. `lcm_grep(mode="full_text")` calls `_lcm_grep_full_text()` directly, without a deadline or `set_progress_handler`. Only `lcm_recall` and the semantic/hybrid grep arms build a deadline (`embedding_query_timeout_s` / `recall_query_timeout_s`).

## Expected behavior

- An emoji should narrow a result set, not choose the retrieval engine. If the query also contains indexable terms, those terms should run on FTS5; the emoji should act as an additional filter.
- No tool call should be able to block for minutes. `lcm_grep(full_text)` should have the same bounded deadline behavior as the recall arm.

## Suggested direction

1. **Split the query.** Run FTS on the sanitized textual terms; apply the emoji as an extra `content LIKE` condition over that candidate set (or post-filter in Python). Route the whole query to LIKE only when sanitization leaves no indexable terms at all.
2. **Bound the LIKE path before scoring**, not just on output: prefilter candidates with `store_id IN (SELECT rowid FROM messages_fts WHERE messages_fts MATCH <OR terms> ORDER BY rank LIMIT N)`. This also removes the residual cost that #54/#61 only partially addressed.
3. **Add a deadline to `lcm_grep(full_text)`** with a progress handler, matching recall, so a pathological query returns a bounded timeout error instead of blocking the turn.

## Related

- #460 — LIKE fallback exhausts the recall deadline (same cost class, different trigger)
- #54, #61 — bounded LIKE fetch; bounds rows returned, not rows scored
- #577 — FTS arm subdeadline
- #19 — introduced the CJK/emoji-aware fallback routing

title: fix: close shared sqlite connections under the store lock (use-after-close raises StoreClosed)
body:
## Summary
- Add `StoreClosed` (a `sqlite3.Error` subclass) and `GuardedConnection` / `GuardedCursor` to `sqlite_util.py`. A guarded connection runs every call, every cursor fetch and `close()` under one leaf `RLock`. `close()` is idempotent, and any use after close raises `StoreClosed` instead of reaching freed memory. That includes a handle or cursor taken before the close.
- Wrap every long-lived store connection with `guard_connection(...)`: `MessageStore`, `SummaryDAG`, `LifecycleStateStore`, `RollupStore`, `VectorStore`, `QueryViewStore`, `AssertionStore`, `TrajectoryStore`.
- `LifecycleStateStore`: the readers (`row_count`, `get_by_conversation`, `get_by_session`, `get_fragmentation_stats`, `clear_debt`, `delete_safe_rows_for_sessions`, `advance_frontier`) are now `@_synchronized`. The decorator raises `StoreClosed` on a closed store, and `close()` takes `self._lock`.
- `SummaryDAG` / `RollupStore` / `VectorStore` / `MessageStore`: `close()` now takes the lock the store's own execute paths already hold (`_db_lock` / `_write_lock`). `QueryViewStore`, `AssertionStore` and `TrajectoryStore` already did this, so they only get the wrapper.
- New `tests/test_store_close_race.py`.

## Why
- The store connections are opened `check_same_thread=False` and shared across threads. Several `close()` methods released the connection without holding the lock their queries take. Separately, the public `.connection` property hands the raw connection to diagnostics that take no lock at all. If `close()` runs while another thread is inside `execute`/`fetch` on the same connection, that is a use-after-free inside `_sqlite3`, and CPython segfaults. A wrong answer or an exception would at least be catchable; this kills the whole process.
- We hit this twice in a long-running host process: a store was shut down while a background hook was still running a lifecycle lookup on it.
- Use-after-close now raises `StoreClosed`. Because it subclasses `sqlite3.Error`, the existing fail-open `except sqlite3.Error` call sites keep working unchanged.

## Validation
- [x] Focused validation, red-first. The new test file on unmodified `main` (a13e709) with only the test added: `pytest tests/test_store_close_race.py -q` -> `11 failed, 1 passed`. Eight of the failures are a SIGSEGV in the racing subprocess (the lifecycle hammer, plus the raw-handle hammer for dag / rollup / vector / query_views / assertions / lifecycle / messages). The other three are the missing `StoreClosed` and the source contract. The one pass is the contract's own self-check, which is meant to pass on both trees.
- [x] Focused validation with the fix: `pytest tests/test_store_close_race.py -q` -> `12 passed in 8.12s`
- [ ] Default validation:
  - [x] `pytest tests/test_lcm_core.py tests/test_lcm_engine.py tests/test_packaging_install.py -q` -> `1109 passed, 1 skipped`
  - [x] `pytest -q` (run under `ulimit -n 1024`, see the next line)
  - [x] `bash -lc 'ulimit -n 1024 && pytest -q'` -> `3040 passed, 2 skipped, 12 xfailed in 370.47s`
  - [x] `python -m compileall -q .` -> clean
  - [x] `python -m py_compile scripts/import_lossless_claw.py` -> clean
  - [x] `bash -n scripts/install.sh scripts/update.sh` -> clean
  - [x] `git diff --check` -> clean
- [ ] Workflow validation, if workflows changed: `actionlint`. Not run: no workflow changed.
- [x] `ruff check .` (0.15.13) -> `All checks passed!`
- [x] `python scripts/validate_dependency_contract.py` -> `dependency contract valid`

## Notes
- Environment: macOS, Python 3.14.7, the CI `agent/` ContextEngine stub, `ulimit -n 1024`. The parent "Default validation" box is unchecked only because the template groups `actionlint` near it. Every listed sub-item was run and is checked.
- Environmental reds: none fired on this branch in this run. On our Macs, two known families sometimes go red on unmodified `main` as well: wall-clock deadline asserts in `test_embedding_provider.py` / `test_embedding_search_modes.py`, and the macOS `/var` -> `/private/var` symlink in `test_path_containment.py` / `test_path_security.py`. Which tests fail changes from run to run. I ran those four files on a clean `main` worktree in the same session and got `108 passed`. So there is nothing on this branch to explain, and no failure here is hidden behind that family.
- How the racing tests work: they run the race in a `python -X faulthandler` subprocess and assert on its exit status, so a segfault fails one test instead of killing the pytest run. Each hammer runs 8 or 6 threads against a fresh store per round, 40 / 15 rounds, which takes about 8 s total.
- `test_every_shared_lcm_connection_is_guarded` is a source contract (AST walk over the root modules). It fails on any new `sqlite3.connect(` unless the call is wrapped in `guard_connection`, or is listed in `_FUNCTION_LOCAL_CONNECTIONS`: handles opened and closed inside one function on one thread, such as in-memory scratch DBs, deadline-bounded readers and backup destinations. Each entry gives a reason. If you would rather not carry a source contract, it drops out cleanly.
- Cost: one uncontended `RLock` acquire per call on an already-serialized connection. Nothing acquires another lock while holding the guard lock.
- All values in the tests are synthetic (`s1`, `s{i}-{n}`, temp-dir databases). No transcripts, credentials or real `lcm.db` were used.

---
Head: `Kyzcreig/hermes-lcm@8ca2dffedc2e` · CI: https://github.com/Kyzcreig/hermes-lcm/commit/8ca2dffedc2e45d5f5e4f67d615e7ecdce25d044/checks

title: Startup FTS integrity-check is a write operation: concurrent plugin loads corrupt messages_fts ("database disk image is malformed"); failure-recorder upsert can latch a permanent plugin load failure
body:
### Expected behavior

lcm.db stays FTS5-integrity-check-clean across multi-process startup (gateway + UI windows loading the plugin at once). A transient FTS problem must never be able to block the plugin from loading permanently: the failure recorder must not itself be a failure mode.

### Actual behavior

At gateway startup the plugin's background FTS scan reports index corruption that did not exist 45 minutes earlier:

    2026-10-23 09:23:44,759 WARNING hermes_plugins.hermes_lcm: Background FTS integrity-check found corruption in 'messages_fts': database disk image is malformed. Run /lcm doctor repair apply to rebuild the index.

The context engine still registers (lcm active); only FTS-dependent search is degraded; no data loss (messages/messages_fts 3906/3906 before, 3956/3956 after rebuild; PRAGMA integrity_check ok).

Timeline (2026-10-23, MDT):
- 08:42-08:48: gateway restart window (install rollback); three consecutive hermes-lcm load failures, root error the metadata table's corrupt unique autoindex (see 'Earlier related incident' below).
- 08:5x: database repaired in place (metadata table rebuilt; backup lcm.db.bak-20261023). PRAGMA integrity_check: ok. FTS5 integrity-check command ok on messages_fts AND nodes_fts verified at 08:56 - the file was green.
- 09:23:09 plugin load #1 (UI process): engine registered, no warning.
- 09:23:17 plugin load #2 (second UI process, 8 s later).
- 09:23:44 plugin load #3 (gateway, pid 4173429): background scan finds messages_fts malformed; the recorder persists metadata key fts_integrity_failed:messages_fts at=1792769048.
- 09:2x: /lcm doctor repair apply rebuilds the index; lcm_doctor all-green after.

Relation to #681/#682: #681 documents the multi-process writer race on SQLite's per-connection page allocator, and #682's flock gate fences 'db_bootstrap's own stamp writers and the FTS integrity/repair paths' - so if #682 lands it should also serialize this scan race. This report adds two things that issue/PR does not cover: (1) the named write actor - FTS5's 'integrity-check' command is itself a write against the shadow tables, and the 09:23 race was three STARTUP SCANS, not user-data writers; (2) a second defect #682 does not address: the failure-recorder upsert running against the damaged database (below).

Analysis (inference, labeled):
1. FTS5's integrity-check performs writes against shadow tables while it runs - it is not a read-only probe.
2. A restart with UI windows open loads the plugin in near-simultaneous processes (here two UI loads 8 s apart, then the gateway); each starts the background scan; concurrent scans race on messages_fts shadow-table writes.
3. #570 serializes FTS bootstrap repair; the startup background integrity-check appears not covered by the same serialization - corruption reproduced on a build that includes #570.
4. Earlier related incident (same db, different table): 2026-10-18 the metadata table's unique autoindex lost its row for key fts_integrity_failed:messages_fts (PRAGMA integrity_check: 'row 189 missing from index sqlite_autoindex_metadata_1'; plugin's own recorded failure at=1792380152 ~2026-10-18 21:22 MDT). The failure recorder's upsert hit the damaged index and raised sqlite3.DatabaseError from db_bootstrap.py _run_background_integrity_scan -> _record_integrity_failed, so the plugin failed to load on EVERY gateway start - a persistent loop a restart cannot fix. The failure path is itself a failure mode.

(Analysis done by an agent assistant from this host's own logs; every quoted line is from the plugin's own log.)

### Minimal reproduction

context:
  engine: lcm
hermes-lcm in enabled plugins

### Version and branch

v1.0.0-rc.1 @ main a13e709c25476fa9dc145c61f33f1f4a0443a05 (2026-10-17), clean tree - includes #570, #623, #624. Upstream main unchanged as of filing (2026-11-12).

### Environment

Hermes Agent v0.22.2 (d923a5eb48), WSL2 / Ubuntu 24.04, Python 3.14.7; lcm.db journal_mode=wal

### Relevant config

```yaml

```

### Logs, traceback, or failing test

```text
- agent.log 09:23:44,759 WARNING 'Background FTS integrity-check found corruption in messages_fts: database disk image is malformed'
- Recorder persisted: metadata.fts_integrity_failed:messages_fts = {"at": 1792769048.8092887, "detail": "database disk image is malformed"}
- 2026-10-18 latched loop: sqlite3.DatabaseError: database disk image is malformed raised from db_bootstrap.py _run_background_integrity_scan -> _record_integrity_failed; plugin load failed on every gateway start until the metadata table was rebuilt
- agent.log 09:23:09 / 09:23:17: two plugin loads 8 s apart; warning on the third load at 09:23:44
- Happy to provide the full 09:23:09-09:23:45 window excerpts.
```

### Validation attempted

Local repairs, no data loss: metadata table rebuilt in place (206 rows preserved, backup lcm.db.bak-20261023); messages_fts rebuilt via /lcm doctor repair apply; lcm_doctor all-green afterwards (only the benign lifecycle_fragmentation inspect warning).

Suggested fixes:
1. Run the startup background integrity-check under the same serialization as #570's repair path (or #682's flock gate), or make the startup check read-only and leave all writes to /lcm doctor repair apply.
2. Isolate the failure recorder from the path it diagnoses: if the metadata upsert raises sqlite3.DatabaseError, log the detail and continue instead of failing plugin load. A recorder must never be able to latch a permanent load failure.
3. Consider a file-level advisory lock around ANY operation that writes FTS shadow tables, regardless of which process initiated it.

title: skill_view of the bundled hermes-lcm skill fails: register() passes the skill directory instead of the SKILL.md path (Errno 13 / IsADirectoryError)
body:
## Environment

- Hermes Agent plugin loader, Windows 11 (on POSIX this fails as `IsADirectoryError` instead)
- Plugin `hermes-lcm` v1.0.0-rc.1 (`8d1b1e6`) — still present at current `main` tip `a13e709`

## Symptom

The bundled skill appears in the skill catalog, but reading it fails:

```
[Errno 13] Permission denied: 'C:/Users/mgser/AppData/Local/hermes/plugins/lcm/skills/hermes-lcm'
```

The `SKILL.md` file itself is intact and readable when opened directly — the failure is only through the skill registry.

## Root cause

`plugin/__init__.py` registers the bundled skill with the **directory** as the path:

```python
skill_root = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'skills' / 'hermes-lcm'
register_skill = getattr(ctx, 'register_skill', None)
if callable(register_skill):
    register_skill(
        'hermes-lcm',
        skill_root,          # <-- directory, not SKILL.md
        ...,
    )
```

The host's `register_skill()` contract expects the **`SKILL.md` file path** (its docstring notes that plugin helpers pass the SKILL.md location); the reader then does `path.read_text()`. When a directory is registered, `skill_view` resolves to the directory and `read_text()` raises `Permission denied` on Windows (`Errno 13`) / `IsADirectoryError` on POSIX.

The plugin itself loads fine — only the qualified skill read (`skill_view('lcm:hermes-lcm')`) breaks.

## Suggested fix

Pass the file path instead of the directory:

```diff
    skill_root = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'skills' / 'hermes-lcm'
+    skill_md = skill_root / 'SKILL.md'
    register_skill = getattr(ctx, 'register_skill', None)
    if callable(register_skill):
        try:
            register_skill(
                'hermes-lcm',
-                skill_root,
+                skill_md,
                description=(
```

Verified locally (Windows 11, Hermes, 2026-11-13): with this one-line change the bundled skill loads through the normal `skill_view` path, and the plugin registration stays compatible with hosts that lack `register_skill` (the existing `try/except` guard already covers older hosts).

title: fix(tools): hide LCM tools whose backing feature is disabled
body:
## Summary

`lcm_retrieve` and `lcm_query_state` are advertised to the model on every turn even when their backing features are off, though their handlers can only return a disabled status in that state. This hides them from both exposure paths unless the feature is enabled:

- `lcm_retrieve` requires `adaptive_retrieval_enabled`
- `lcm_query_state` requires `assertions_enabled`

Both paths check one shared helper, `schemas.is_tool_enabled(name, config)`, against the resolved config: plugin-registry registration in `__init__.py` and `LCMEngine.get_tool_schemas()`. With a flag on, schemas and their order are unchanged.

## Why

Disabled tools can do no useful work, but their schemas cost context on every request: `lcm_retrieve` is 3,910 bytes and `lcm_query_state` is 1,620. With default config this drops 5,534 bytes (15 → 13 tools) from each request. The recall-policy guidance mentions neither tool, so it needs no change.

## Audit of the other tools

None of the other 13 tools can be fully disabled by a flag. `lcm_grep`/`lcm_recall` fall back to full-text search, `lcm_recent` falls back to leaf summaries, `lcm_compute` accepts raw spans without assertions, and `lcm_compile_evidence`/`lcm_evidence_pack` work on explicit invocation. Load-session, describe, expand, expand-query, status, inspect and doctor have no disabling flag.

## Tests

- New tests cover all four flag combinations for both paths, including byte equality when enabled. Existing contract expectations, docs and changelog are updated.
- Focused: `test_host_capability`, `test_tool_contracts`, `test_recall_guidance`, `test_adaptive_retrieval`, `test_assertion_lifecycle_tools` → 47 passed.
- `test_packaging_install` + the files above with the standalone host stub: 63 passed, 4 failed. The same 4 fail on unchanged `main` in the same environment, because the host package is absent.
- Full standalone suite: the remaining failures (lock-timing deadlines, legacy data-URI expansion, embedding-provider tests) reproduce on unchanged `main`.
